The distinction between the unexpected loss marginal contribution (a derivative) and the unexpected loss contribution (a derivative multiplied by the position's own UL).

Option (c) conflates two related but distinct quantities.

**Unexpected loss marginal contribution (ULMC)** is the derivative. It measures the sensitivity of portfolio unexpected loss to a marginal change in the position:

$$ULMC_{i} = \partial UL_{P} / \partial UL_{i}$$

**Unexpected loss contribution (ULC)** is that derivative scaled by the position's own unexpected loss:

$$ULC_{i} = ULMC_{i} \times UL_{i}$$

Two corruptions are present in option (c). It calls ULC a derivative when ULC is a derivative multiplied by $UL_{i}$, and it takes the derivative with respect to the position's weight rather than with respect to its unexpected loss.

**Why the distinction matters.** Only ULC has the additivity property that lets the ULCs sum to portfolio unexpected loss, which is what makes capital allocation exact. The marginal quantity ULMC does not sum to anything meaningful. In practice ULC is computed as:

$$ULC_{i} = UL_{i} \times \frac{\sum_{j} \rho_{ij} UL_{j}}{UL_{P}}$$

a.reason: Incorrect, the statement is accurate. The insurance pool analogy is Schroeck's own framing: expected loss is a predictable, premium-like cost recovered through the loan spread.

b.reason: Incorrect, the statement is accurate. This is the definition of unexpected loss in this chapter, one standard deviation of the credit loss distribution around its mean.

c.reason: Correct answer, because the statement is false. The derivative described is the marginal contribution (ULMC), taken with respect to $UL_{i}$, not with respect to the weight. ULC is ULMC multiplied by $UL_{i}$.

d.reason: Incorrect, the statement is accurate. Economic capital is exactly the distance from the expected outcome out to the adverse outcome at the chosen confidence level, which is why it is a multiple of UL rather than UL itself.

trap.explanation: This distractor is built from a true statement about a neighbouring quantity, with one word changed in the differentiation variable. It is difficult because the marginal-versus-total contribution distinction mirrors marginal VaR versus component VaR in market risk, where candidates often carry over the wrong mapping. The memory hook: ULC is the one that adds up.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the variance of default probability assuming a binomial distribution [stated Numerical]
questions.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
questions.question: Which distribution is most appropriate to generate the variance of the loss rate (LR)?

options.text: Binomial or Poisson
Uniform or exponential
Chi-squared or gamma
Normal or beta distribution

questions.solution:
Default is binary and therefore binomial; the loss rate is continuous on [0, 1] and requires a flexible continuous distribution.

The two inputs to unexpected loss are parameterised by different distributional assumptions, and the reason is structural.

| Input | Nature of the variable | Distribution used | Variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Probability of default | Binary: default or not | Binomial (Bernoulli) | $PD(1-PD)$, determined mechanically |
| Loss rate (LGD) | Continuous on [0, 1] | Normal or beta | Must be assumed or estimated from sparse data |

**Why the loss rate is the harder one.** Default is binary, so its variance follows mechanically from $p(1-p)$ with no distributional choice required. The loss rate is continuous, bounded between 0 and 1, and can take almost any shape depending on collateral, seniority and jurisdiction. Historical workout data is scarce, so practitioners must select a reasonable distribution rather than estimate one. The beta distribution is the popular choice because it is bounded on [0, 1] and extremely flexible in shape; the normal is also used as a simpler approximation despite being unbounded.

a.reason: The binomial is the distribution of the default event, not of the loss rate, and the Poisson models counts of rare events. This is the most tempting wrong answer precisely because the binomial genuinely does appear in this chapter, just applied to the other input.

b.reason: The uniform assigns equal probability across its range, which is unrealistic for recovery outcomes. The exponential is unbounded above and used for waiting times, not for a ratio confined to [0, 1].

c.reason: Chi-squared and gamma are both non-negative but unbounded above, so neither respects the natural ceiling of 100% loss. Neither is named in the reading.

d.reason: Normal or beta distribution. The beta is preferred for its bounded support and shape flexibility; the normal is a common simpler alternative.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the sibling swap that catches candidates who remember that a binomial assumption appears in this chapter but attach it to the wrong input. The learning objective wording, estimate the variance of default probability assuming a binomial distribution, reinforces the binomial in memory and makes the misattribution easy. Say it explicitly: binomial for PD, beta or normal for LR.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus an SPV, and distinguish between the three main SPV structures
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question: A structuring team at an originating bank is deciding whether to issue a securitisation through a trust or through a special purpose vehicle. Which of the following most accurately describes the difference in mechanics?

options.text: A trust holds legal title to the assets on behalf of noteholders as beneficiaries, whereas an SPV is a separate legal entity that purchases the assets outright and funds the purchase by issuing notes.
A trust is a separate legal entity that buys the assets and issues notes against them, whereas an SPV holds legal title purely as a custodian and issues no securities of its own.
Both structures leave legal ownership of the assets with the originator, so neither achieves a true sale and neither delivers bankruptcy remoteness.
A trust can only be used for revolving asset pools and an SPV only for amortising pools, so the choice is determined entirely by the collateral type.

questions.solution:
The legal mechanics that deliver bankruptcy remoteness: a trust holds title for beneficiaries; an SPV takes ownership through a true sale funded by note issuance.

Both routes exist to achieve the same commercial objective, which is to separate the assets from the originator's insolvency estate. They do it differently.

| Feature | Trust | Special purpose vehicle |
|---|---|---|
| Legal nature | A fiduciary relationship, not a company | A separate legal entity, typically a company |
| Who holds title | The trustee, on behalf of beneficiaries | The SPV itself, following a true sale |
| How investors hold | As beneficiaries with a beneficial interest in the trust assets | As creditors holding notes issued by the SPV |
| Balance sheet | None; assets are held on trust | The SPV records assets and issued liabilities |
| Typical use | Repeat issuance from one pool, for example a master trust | Single discrete transaction |

The common purpose: bankruptcy remoteness. In either structure the originator's creditors cannot reach the securitised pool if the originator fails, and the noteholders' recourse is to the pool rather than to the originator. That separation is the entire point, and it is what allows the notes to be rated above the originator's own rating.

The practical distinction. An SPV is a company, so it has a balance sheet: it records the purchased assets and the notes it has issued, and it requires a true sale of the receivables from the originator. A trust is not a company; it is a legal relationship in which a trustee holds title for beneficiaries. Trust structures are common where the same pool supports multiple issuances over time, which is why the master trust developed as a trust-based structure.

a.reason: A trust holds legal title for beneficiaries; an SPV purchases the assets outright and issues notes to fund the purchase.

b.reason: A straight role misassignment: the two descriptions have been swapped. It is the SPV that is a separate legal entity issuing notes, and the trust that holds title on behalf of others.

c.reason: Both structures are specifically designed to remove the assets from the originator's estate. If legal ownership stayed with the originator there would be no true sale, no bankruptcy remoteness, and no basis for rating the notes above the originator.

d.reason: A manufactured scope condition. Collateral type influences which of the three SPV structures is chosen, amortising, revolving or master trust, but it does not dictate the trust versus SPV question.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the role misassignment and the only serious distractor: both descriptions are individually accurate and only the labels are exchanged, so it survives any reader who recognises the vocabulary without holding the mapping. Option (c) is an absolute claim that denies the defining feature of the whole technique. Option (d) invents a constraint by importing the structure taxonomy into the wrong decision.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus an SPV, and distinguish between the three main SPV structures
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
A securitisation adviser is matching three prospective issuers to the appropriate SPV structure.

- Issuer 1: a one-off securitisation of a static pool of fully amortising auto loans, with principal repaid to noteholders as it is received
- Issuer 2: a securitisation of credit card receivables, where the short-dated collateral repays far faster than the notes and the pool must be replenished during an initial period
- Issuer 3: a frequent issuer that wishes to launch several series of notes at different times, all supported by a single large pool of receivables

Which sequence correctly matches each issuer to its structure?

options.text: 1 amortising, 2 revolving, 3 master trust
1 revolving, 2 amortising, 3 master trust
1 amortising, 2 master trust, 3 revolving
1 master trust, 2 revolving, 3 amortising

questions.solution:
Distinguishing the three SPV structures by how principal is treated and by whether the vehicle supports one issuance or many.

The three structures are separated by two questions: what happens to principal received during the deal's life, and whether the vehicle supports one issuance or several.

| Structure | Treatment of principal | Typical collateral | Number of issuances |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amortising | Passed through to noteholders as received | Auto loans, residential mortgages, other fully amortising assets | One |
| Revolving | Reinvested in new receivables during a revolving period, then amortised | Credit cards, trade receivables, other short-dated revolving assets | One |
| Master trust | Allocated across multiple series from a single pool | Credit cards and other large homogeneous pools | Many, issued over time |

Issuer 1. A static pool of fully amortising auto loans with principal passed straight through is the definition of an amortising structure. The note balance declines in step with the collateral.

Issuer 2. Credit card receivables have very short average lives, so passing principal straight through would repay the notes within months. A revolving structure solves this: during the revolving period, principal collections are reinvested in new receivables so the note balance stays constant, and amortisation begins only at the start of the controlled amortisation or accumulation period.

Issuer 3. A single large pool supporting multiple series issued at different times is a master trust. Each series takes a defined share of the pool's cash flows, which lets the issuer come to market repeatedly without assembling a new pool each time.

a.reason: Static amortising pool gives an amortising structure, replenished short-dated pool gives a revolving structure, and a single pool supporting multiple series gives a master trust.

b.reason: Reverses issuers 1 and 2. A static, fully amortising auto pool has nothing to revolve, and a credit card pool cannot be passed through without repaying the notes almost immediately.

c.reason: Confuses revolving with master trust. The distinguishing feature of a master trust is multiple series from one pool, not the reinvestment of principal. Credit card deals are frequently both revolving and issued from a master trust, which is the source of the confusion, but the two labels answer different questions.

d.reason: Misassigns all three. A one-off static pool is never a master trust, and a frequent multi-series issuer is not served by a simple amortising structure.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the trap that matters, and it is a sibling swap between revolving and master trust. Both are associated with credit cards in practice, so the two labels feel interchangeable. Hold the discriminator: revolving describes what happens to principal, master trust describes how many series the vehicle supports. A master trust can contain revolving collateral, and a revolving deal can be a standalone single issuance.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL)
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
Tahoma Bank issues credit cards to consumers. The aging analysis of its receivables is as follows.

| Aging bucket | Amount |
|---|---|
| 0 to 30 days | USD 600 million |
| 31 to 60 days | USD 250 million |
| 61 to 90 days | USD 170 million |
| 91 to 120 days | USD 130 million |
| 121 days and more | USD 60 million |
| Total | USD 1,210 million |

The amount written off during the period was USD 35 million. Based on this information, the delinquency ratio and the default ratio for Tahoma Bank are closest to:

options.text: Delinquency ratio 4.96%; default ratio 15.7%
Delinquency ratio 2.89%; default ratio 4.96%
Delinquency ratio 15.7%; default ratio 2.89%
Delinquency ratio 10.7%; default ratio 3.84%

questions.solution:
The delinquency ratio measures receivables more than 90 days past due as a share of the pool; the default ratio measures amounts actually written off as a share of the pool.

Delinquency ratio. Receivables more than 90 days overdue, divided by the total pool.

$$\text{Delinquency ratio} = \frac{91\text{ to }120\text{ days} + 121\text{ days and more}}{\text{Total receivables}} = \frac{130 + 60}{1{,}210} = \frac{190}{1{,}210} = 15.70\%$$

Default ratio. The amount actually written off, divided by the total pool.

$$\text{Default ratio} = \frac{\text{Amount written off}}{\text{Total receivables}} = \frac{35}{1{,}210} = 2.89\%$$

Why the cut-off is 90 days. Delinquency measures receivables that are late but not yet abandoned; the 90 day threshold is the industry convention for identifying seriously impaired balances. The default ratio is a step further down the same path: the servicer has given up on collection and charged the balance off. Delinquency is therefore a leading indicator of the default ratio, which is why both are reported for credit card collateral.

Direction check. The delinquency ratio should exceed the default ratio in a functioning pool, since not every seriously overdue balance is ultimately written off. Here 15.70% against 2.89% is consistent.

a.reason: The two figures are transposed and one is wrong. It reports 4.96% as delinquency, which is 60 / 1,210, that is, only the oldest bucket, and 15.7% as the default ratio.

b.reason: Reports the correct default ratio of 2.89% as the delinquency ratio, and 4.96% as the default ratio. A pure role misassignment between the two measures.

c.reason: Delinquency 15.70%, default 2.89%.

d.reason: 10.7% is 130 / 1,210, the 91 to 120 day bucket alone, which omits the 121+ day bucket. 3.84% does not follow from the stated write-off.

trap.explanation: Two traps. The first is the 90 day cut-off: including the 61 to 90 day bucket gives (170 + 130 + 60) / 1,210 = 29.75%, and taking only the 121 day bucket gives 4.96%, which appears in options (a) and (b). The second is role misassignment between the two ratios, which is what makes (b) dangerous, since both of its numbers are quantities that appear somewhere in the correct working. Fix the definitions: delinquency is more than 90 days overdue; default is written off.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL)
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
An analyst is monitoring a credit card master trust. In the most recent collection period the trust reported the following.

- Principal collections: USD 210 million
- Interest and fee collections: USD 90 million
- Total receivables outstanding at the start of the period: USD 1,500 million
- Amounts written off during the period: USD 12 million

Which of the following is nearest to the monthly payment rate, and what does a sustained decline in this measure indicate?

options.text: 20.0%, indicating that cardholders are repaying more slowly, which lengthens the life of the notes and raises the risk of early amortisation.
14.0%, indicating that cardholders are repaying more slowly, which lengthens the life of the notes and raises the risk of early amortisation.
20.0%, indicating that cardholders are repaying more quickly, which shortens the life of the notes and reduces credit risk.
6.0%, indicating that write-offs are consuming an increasing share of collections and that the excess spread is being eroded.

questions.solution:
The monthly payment rate measures total collections against outstanding receivables; a falling MPR signals slower repayment, extends note life, and is an early amortisation trigger in credit card structures.

The calculation. MPR takes total collections, both principal and finance charges, against the receivables balance.

$$\text{MPR} = \frac{\text{Principal collections} + \text{Interest and fee collections}}{\text{Total receivables outstanding}} = \frac{210 + 90}{1{,}500} = \frac{300}{1{,}500} = 20.0\%$$

Why MPR matters and only for revolving collateral. In an amortising deal the repayment schedule is contractual, so there is nothing to monitor. In a credit card structure the cardholder chooses how much to repay each month, so the speed at which the pool turns over is a behavioural variable, and it determines how quickly the notes can be repaid once amortisation begins.

What a falling MPR signals. Cardholders are paying down balances more slowly, typically because household finances are deteriorating. Three consequences follow: the expected life of the notes lengthens, the pool is exposed to credit deterioration for longer, and if MPR falls through the level specified in the documentation it triggers early amortisation, which forces principal to be repaid to investors immediately. MPR is therefore one of the standard early amortisation triggers alongside excess spread.

Do not deduct write-offs. The USD 12 million charged off is used in the default ratio, not in MPR. MPR measures cash collected, and written-off balances are by definition not collected.

a.reason: 300 / 1,500 = 20.0%, and a sustained decline signals slower repayment, longer note life and early amortisation risk.

b.reason: 14.0% is 210 / 1,500, that is, principal collections only. Omitting finance charge collections is the dropped term error; MPR is a total collections measure.

c.reason: The number is right but the interpretation is reversed. A declining MPR means slower repayment, not faster. This is a polarity flip on the direction of the signal.

d.reason: 6.0% is 90 / 1,500, the finance charge collections alone, and the interpretation describes the excess spread rather than MPR.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the trap for a candidate who computes correctly and then reverses the economic reading. State the direction explicitly: MPR down means repayment slower means note life longer means risk higher. Option (b) is the dropped term, taking principal only, and it is tempting because repayment intuitively means principal. Option (d) is a sibling swap with excess spread, the other principal early amortisation trigger.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL)
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
A manager of special purpose vehicles holding commercial mortgage-backed securities reports net operating income from the mortgaged properties of USD 68 million. Total debt payments on the notes issued against those mortgages are USD 54 million. The total value of assets in the mortgage pool is approximately USD 5 billion.

Given this information, the debt service coverage ratio is closest to:
questions.solution:
DSCR measures the cushion between the income a property generates and the debt service it must fund; it is a coverage multiple, not a balance sheet ratio.

$$\text{DSCR} = \frac{\text{Net operating income}}{\text{Debt service}} = \frac{68}{54} = 1.26$$

Interpretation. The properties generate 1.26 times the income needed to meet debt payments, a cushion of 26%. Income could fall by roughly 20% before coverage is lost.

$$\text{Breakeven decline} = 1 - \frac{1}{1.26} = 20.6\%$$

Why it is the key CMBS metric. Commercial mortgages are repaid from the cash flow the property generates rather than from a borrower's personal income, so the ratio of that cash flow to debt service is the direct measure of default risk. A DSCR below 1.00 means the property cannot service its debt from operations. Lenders typically require 1.20 or higher at origination, so 1.26 is adequate but not generous.

The pool value of USD 5 billion is a red herring. DSCR is a flow ratio comparing income to payments. Asset value belongs in the loan-to-value ratio, which is the complementary stock measure. The two are used together precisely because each misses what the other captures.

b.reason: 0.79 is 54 / 68, the ratio inverted. This is a debt service to income ratio, which is not a defined measure, and it also fails the sanity check that an adequately underwritten property should show coverage above 1.00.

c.reason: 0.0136 is 68 / 5,000, that is, net operating income divided by the pool value. This is a yield on assets, and it substitutes the red-herring stock figure for the debt service flow.

d.reason: 0.0108 is 54 / 5,000, debt service divided by pool value. The same wrong input twin as option (c), applied to the other flow.

trap.explanation: Options (c) and (d) exist to punish reflexive use of the supplied but irrelevant pool value; both are wrong input twin errors substituting a stock for a flow. Option (b) is the inversion, and the check that catches it is directional: a higher DSCR is safer, so income must sit in the numerator. Any DSCR below 1.00 describes a property that cannot pay its own debt, which is inconsistent with a performing pool.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL)
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
A mortgage pool manager reports that its mortgage-backed security is composed of four pools.

- USD 24 million of apartment mortgages yielding 8.4%
- USD 32 million of villa mortgages yielding 7.0%
- USD 16 million of penthouse mortgages yielding 6.8%
- USD 8 million of farmhouse mortgages yielding 5.6%

Using this information, the weighted average coupon is closest to:
questions.solution:
WAC weights each mortgage rate by its share of the outstanding principal balance, not by the number of loans.

$$\text{WAC} = \sum_i \left(\frac{\text{balance}_i}{\text{total balance}}\right) \times \text{coupon}_i$$

Step 1. Total balance.

$$24 + 32 + 16 + 8 = \text{USD } 80 \text{ million}$$

Step 2. Weight each coupon by its principal share.

| Pool | Balance | Weight | Coupon | Weighted contribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apartment | 24 | 30.0% | 8.4% | 201.6 |
| Villa | 32 | 40.0% | 7.0% | 224.0 |
| Penthouse | 16 | 20.0% | 6.8% | 108.8 |
| Farmhouse | 8 | 10.0% | 5.6% | 44.8 |
| Total | 80 | 100% | | 579.2 |

$$\text{WAC} = \frac{579.2}{80} = 7.24\%$$

Why weighting matters. The simple arithmetic average of the four rates is (8.4 + 7.0 + 6.8 + 5.6) / 4 = 6.95%, which is materially lower. The two largest pools, apartments at 8.4% and villas at 7.0%, carry 70% of the balance between them, so the weighted figure is pulled upward. Using an unweighted average would understate the pool's gross coupon and therefore the cash available to pay noteholders.

Where WAC is used. WAC less the pass-through rate paid to investors, less servicing, is the residual available to the issuer and to credit enhancement, that is, the excess spread.

a.reason: 6.95% is the simple arithmetic average of the four coupons, ignoring balances entirely. The single most common error on this calculation.

c.reason: 5.70% is close to the lowest coupon in the pool and below every weighted result. It cannot be a weighted average of values ranging from 5.6% to 8.4% unless the smallest pool dominated, which it does not.

d.reason: 7.60% would require the highest-yielding pool to carry a much larger share than its 30%. It overshoots the correct weighting.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the dropped term error, omitting the weights, and it is the answer a candidate produces in fifteen seconds by averaging four numbers. The structural check: a weighted average must lie between the minimum and maximum inputs, here 5.6% and 8.4%, which does not eliminate any option, so the weighting must actually be performed. Note that the correct answer sits above the simple average because the high-coupon pools are the large ones.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL)
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
A servicing agent reports that its commercial mortgage pool is composed of the following.

- USD 26 million of superstore mortgages with a maturity of 82 days
- USD 67 million of office space mortgages with a maturity of 169 days
- USD 22 million of cinema mortgages with a maturity of 253 days
- USD 17 million of restaurant mortgages with a maturity of 336 days

What is the weighted average maturity of these mortgage pools?

options.text: 145 days
210 days
187 days
273 days

questions.solution:
WAM weights the remaining term of each loan by its share of the outstanding principal balance.

$$\text{WAM} = \sum_i \left(\frac{\text{balance}_i}{\text{total balance}}\right) \times \text{maturity}_i$$

Step 1. Total balance.

$$26 + 67 + 22 + 17 = \text{USD } 132 \text{ million}$$

Step 2. Weight each maturity.

| Pool | Balance | Weight | Maturity (days) | Weighted contribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Superstore | 26 | 19.7% | 82 | 2,132 |
| Office | 67 | 50.8% | 169 | 11,323 |
| Cinema | 22 | 16.7% | 253 | 5,566 |
| Restaurant | 17 | 12.9% | 336 | 5,712 |
| Total | 132 | 100% | | 24,733 |

$$\text{WAM} = \frac{24{,}733}{132} = 187.4, \text{ that is, } 187 \text{ days}$$

The structural driver. The office pool at USD 67 million is more than half the total balance, so its 169 day maturity dominates and the result sits close to it. The two longest pools, cinema at 253 days and restaurant at 336 days, together carry only 29.5% of the balance and cannot pull the average far.

WAM against WAL. WAM uses the final maturity of each loan. Weighted average life uses the timing of principal repayments, so for any amortising pool WAL is shorter than WAM. The two coincide only for bullet loans that repay all principal at maturity.

a.reason: 145 days is well below the correct 187 days. The superstore pool (82 days) is the only shorter pool and carries under 20% of the balance, so it cannot pull the average below the 169-day office pool that makes up over half the balance.

b.reason: 210 days is the simple arithmetic average of the four maturities, (82 + 169 + 253 + 336) / 4 = 210. The dropped-weights error.

c.reason: 187 days.

d.reason: 273 days would require the two longest pools to dominate, whereas together they carry under 30% of the balance. It overweights the tail.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is again the dropped term error, and here it is more seductive than in the WAC question because 210 is a round, plausible-looking figure. The structural check that resolves it in seconds: the office pool is over half the balance at 169 days, so the answer must sit modestly above 169 and well below the midpoint of the range. That reasoning alone eliminates (a), (b) and (d).

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL)
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
Consider the amortisation schedule for a USD 1.0 million mortgage loan that fully amortises over ten years at a yield of 6.0%. The loan's scheduled cash flows are fixed. Summing the relevant weighted columns gives the following.

- Sum of $t \times$ principal repayment, divided by the original balance: 5.98
- Sum of $t \times$ discounted total cash flow, divided by the loan value: 5.02

Each of the following statements is true EXCEPT which one?

options.text: The Macaulay duration is 5.02 years.
If the yield increases to 7.0%, the Macaulay duration will decrease to 4.95 years.
The weighted average life is 5.98 years.
If the yield increases to 7.0%, the weighted average life will increase to 6.05 years.

questions.solution:
Weighted average life weights the timing of undiscounted principal repayments and is therefore independent of yield; Macaulay duration weights discounted total cash flows and does depend on yield.

The two measures look similar and differ on two dimensions that decide this question.

| | Weighted average life | Macaulay duration |
|---|---|---|
| Cash flows weighted | Principal repayments only | Total cash flow, principal and interest |
| Discounted | No | Yes |
| Sensitive to yield | No | Yes |
| Value here | 5.98 years | 5.02 years |

$$\text{WAL} = \frac{\sum t \times \text{principal repaid at } t}{\text{total principal}}$$

$$\text{Macaulay duration} = \frac{\sum t \times PV(\text{total cash flow at } t)}{\text{price}}$$

Why WAL cannot change with yield. The numerator contains the scheduled principal repayments and the denominator the original balance. Neither is discounted, so no interest rate enters the calculation anywhere. Changing the yield from 6.0% to 7.0% leaves WAL at 5.98 years. Statement (d) is therefore false.

Why Macaulay duration does change with yield. Every cash flow is discounted at the yield. Raising the yield reduces the present value of distant cash flows by proportionally more than near ones, which shifts weight toward the front of the schedule.

The direction in statement (b). The scheduled cash flows are fixed, so only the discount rate changes. A higher yield discounts distant cash flows more heavily, so Macaulay duration shortens, from 5.02 to 4.95 years, exactly as for a bullet bond. Statement (b) is true. (Even if the level payment were repriced at 7.0%, duration would still be 4.95: for a level-payment annuity the payment size cancels out of the duration ratio, so duration depends only on the discount rate.)

The ordering check. WAL of 5.98 exceeds Macaulay duration of 5.02, which is always the case for an amortising loan, because WAL ignores the interest cash flows that arrive early and pull duration forward.

a.reason: The statement is true. The discounted weighted sum gives a Macaulay duration of 5.02 years.

b.reason: The statement is true. Higher yield discounts distant cash flows more heavily, shifting weight toward the front of the schedule, so Macaulay duration shortens from 5.02 to 4.95 years.

c.reason: The statement is true. The undiscounted principal-weighted sum gives a WAL of 5.98 years.

d.reason: This is the credited answer because the statement is false. WAL contains no discounting, so it is invariant to the yield. It remains 5.98 years.

trap.explanation: The item works by placing a true yield-sensitivity statement (b) next to a false one (d), so a candidate who believes both measures behave alike will find one of them arbitrary. The discriminator is a single structural fact: WAL is undiscounted, so no yield can touch it. Statement (b) checks direction: higher yield shortens Macaulay duration for an amortising loan just as for a bullet bond, because distant cash flows are discounted more heavily.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how the default probabilities and default correlations affect the credit risk in a securitization
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
A structurer is explaining to an investment committee how a rise in the default correlation of the collateral pool affects a securitisation, holding each individual asset's default probability constant.

Which of the following is correct?

options.text: The senior tranche becomes riskier and the equity tranche becomes safer, because higher correlation raises the probability of the extreme joint-default outcomes that reach the senior tranche while raising the probability that no assets default at all.
Both the senior and the equity tranche become riskier, because higher correlation increases the expected number of defaults in the pool.
The senior tranche becomes safer and the equity tranche becomes riskier, because higher correlation concentrates losses in the first-loss position.
Neither tranche is affected, because the expected loss of the pool depends only on the individual default probabilities, which are unchanged.

questions.solution:
Correlation redistributes risk across the capital structure without changing pool expected loss: it fattens both tails, hurting the senior tranche and helping the equity tranche.

The invariant. Expected loss on the pool is the sum of individual expected losses and is unaffected by correlation, because expectation is linear:

$$E[\text{pool loss}] = \sum_i PD_i \times EAD_i \times LGD_i, \text{ independent of } \rho$$

What correlation changes is the shape of the loss distribution around that unchanged mean.

What higher correlation does. It fattens both tails simultaneously. Assets increasingly default together or survive together, so the probability of very many defaults rises and the probability of very few or none also rises. Intermediate outcomes become less likely.

| Outcome | Effect of higher correlation | Tranche affected |
|---|---|---|
| Very few or no defaults | More likely | Equity tranche benefits |
| An intermediate number of defaults | Less likely | Mezzanine, ambiguous |
| Very many defaults | More likely | Senior tranche is harmed |

The senior tranche. It suffers only in the extreme scenario where losses breach all the subordination beneath it. That scenario requires many simultaneous defaults, and higher correlation makes it more likely. The senior tranche is therefore long correlation risk, or equivalently short correlation.

The equity tranche. It absorbs the first losses and is wiped out by even a modest number of defaults. Its only good outcome is that almost nothing defaults, and higher correlation makes that clustering-at-zero outcome more likely. The equity tranche therefore benefits from higher correlation.

The practical statement. At a correlation of zero, diversification makes the senior tranche close to riskless and the equity tranche near certain to be impaired. At a correlation of one, the pool behaves as a single credit, so every tranche defaults together or none does, and the tranching provides no protection at all. This is why correlation is the single most important assumption in rating a structured product.

a.reason: Higher correlation fattens both tails, harming the senior tranche and benefiting the equity tranche.

b.reason: The expected number of defaults is $n\pi$ and does not change with correlation; only the dispersion around it changes. The option also claims both tranches move the same way, whereas correlation redistributes risk between them.

c.reason: A clean polarity flip: the directions are exactly reversed. It is intuitively attractive because concentrating losses in the first-loss position sounds like what correlation should do, but higher correlation makes the no-loss outcome more likely, which is what the equity tranche needs.

d.reason: The premise is right and the conclusion wrong. Pool expected loss is indeed unchanged, but tranche risk depends on the distribution, not the mean. Tranching exists precisely to slice that distribution, so any change to its shape changes the risk of every tranche.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the dominant trap and a textbook polarity flip, because the correct answer is counterintuitive: raising a risk parameter makes the riskiest tranche safer. Option (d) is the scope error, correctly identifying that pool expected loss is invariant and then wrongly concluding that nothing else can change. Say it once and hold it: correlation does not change the mean, it fattens both tails; equity is long correlation, senior is short correlation.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how the default probabilities and default correlations affect the credit risk in a securitization
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question:
Two collateral pools support otherwise identical securitisations with the same tranche attachment points. Pool 1 contains assets with a 2% individual default probability and a pairwise default correlation of 0.05. Pool 2 contains assets with the same 2% individual default probability and a pairwise default correlation of 0.40.

Which statement most accurately describes the difference between the two structures?

options.text: The two pools have the same expected loss, but Pool 2's senior tranche requires more subordination to achieve the same rating.
Pool 2 has a higher expected loss and therefore requires more subordination throughout the capital structure.
The two pools have the same expected loss and the same tranche risk, since attachment points are identical.
Pool 1 requires more subordination for its senior tranche, because lower correlation means defaults are less predictable.

questions.solution:
Raising the individual default probability shifts the whole loss distribution; raising correlation changes only its shape, and it is the shape that determines how much subordination a senior tranche needs.

Separate the two levers. They act on different features of the loss distribution.

| Lever | Effect on pool expected loss | Effect on the tail | Effect on senior tranche |
|---|---|---|---|
| Higher individual PD | Increases | Shifts the whole distribution right | More subordination needed |
| Higher default correlation | Unchanged | Fattens both tails | More subordination needed |

Expected loss is identical. Both pools have individual PD of 2%, so:

$$E[\text{pool loss}] = n \times 0.02 \times LGD, \text{ identical across the two pools}$$

Tail risk is not. The senior tranche is impaired only when cumulative losses exceed the subordination beneath it, which is a tail event. Pool 2's higher correlation makes clustered defaults more likely, so the probability of breaching any given attachment point is higher. To restore the same expected loss on the senior tranche, and therefore the same rating, the attachment point must be raised, which means more subordination.

Why this is the central lesson of structured credit. Two pools can look identical on every asset-level metric that a rating on the underlying collateral would capture, and still support very different amounts of senior debt. The difference lives entirely in an unobservable correlation assumption, which is why senior tranche ratings are far more sensitive to model assumptions than corporate bond ratings of the same nominal grade.

a.reason: Expected loss is identical; Pool 2's fatter tail means the senior tranche needs more subordination for the same rating.

b.reason: Expected loss depends on individual default probabilities, which are identical at 2%. Correlation does not change the mean. This is the standard confusion of correlation with the level of default risk.

c.reason: The first clause is right and the second wrong. Identical attachment points with different loss distributions produce different tranche risk; that is the whole reason correlation is modelled.

d.reason: A polarity flip. Lower correlation means more diversification and a thinner tail, so Pool 1's senior tranche needs less subordination, not more. The justification offered, that lower correlation makes defaults less predictable, also inverts the relationship.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the most common error and a scope error conflating two independent parameters: it treats correlation as though it were a level of risk rather than a dependence structure. The discipline is to ask which moment of the loss distribution a parameter touches. PD moves the mean; correlation moves the tails. Option (c) is the trap for a candidate who correctly identifies the invariant expected loss and then stops one step short of asking what tranching actually prices.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe common types of structured products
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question: Which of the following gives a notable difference between commercial mortgage-backed securities and residential mortgage-backed securities?

options.text: CMBS are always issued through a master trust, whereas RMBS use amortising structures.
RMBS are exposed to commercial property values, whereas CMBS are exposed to household incomes.
CMBS pools contain a very large number of small homogeneous loans, whereas RMBS pools are concentrated in a small number of large loans.
CMBS loans typically carry prepayment protection such as lockouts and yield maintenance, whereas RMBS borrowers can generally prepay freely, so prepayment risk is a far greater concern in RMBS.

questions.solution:
The defining economic difference between the two mortgage-backed classes is the treatment of prepayment, which follows from the difference between commercial loan documentation and residential borrower rights.

Both are mortgage-backed, and the temptation is to distinguish them by property type alone. The examinable difference is what the borrower is permitted to do.

| Feature | RMBS | CMBS |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying | Residential mortgages, repaid from household income | Commercial property loans, repaid from property cash flow |
| Pool composition | Thousands of small homogeneous loans | Tens of large heterogeneous loans |
| Prepayment | Largely unrestricted, so prepayment risk is central | Restricted by lockouts, penalties and yield maintenance |
| Key credit metric | Loan to value, borrower credit score | DSCR and loan to value at property level |
| Analytical approach | Statistical, pool level | Loan by loan |

Prepayment. Residential borrowers in most markets may repay early with little or no penalty, so when rates fall they refinance and the pool prepays. That gives RMBS negative convexity: the security shortens exactly when the investor would prefer it to lengthen. Commercial mortgage documentation typically prevents this through lockout periods, defeasance, prepayment penalties or yield maintenance provisions, so CMBS cash flows are far more predictable.

The corollary. Because prepayment is contained, CMBS analysis concentrates on credit, principally DSCR and loan-to-value at the individual property level. RMBS analysis must model prepayment behaviour as well as credit, which is why PSA, CPR and SMM conventions exist for residential pools.

Granularity. RMBS pools contain thousands of small loans and are analysed statistically. CMBS pools contain tens of large loans and are analysed loan by loan, which makes single-asset concentration a genuine risk in CMBS and a negligible one in RMBS.

a.reason: Master trusts are associated with revolving short-dated collateral such as credit cards, not with commercial mortgages. Both CMBS and RMBS typically use amortising structures. A sibling swap importing the wrong SPV structure.

b.reason: The exposures are transposed. RMBS depend on household incomes and residential property values; CMBS depend on commercial property cash flows. A straightforward role misassignment.

c.reason: Also transposed. RMBS pools are the granular ones containing many small loans; CMBS pools are concentrated in a small number of large loans. This reversal matters because it determines whether the pool can be analysed statistically.

d.reason: Prepayment protection in commercial loan documentation, against largely free prepayment for residential borrowers, is the defining difference.

trap.explanation: Options (b) and (c) are both role misassignments created by transposing the two asset classes, and each is individually plausible to a reader who has the concepts but not the mapping. Option (a) imports the master trust from the credit card world. The one-line discriminator worth holding: residential borrowers can prepay, commercial borrowers usually cannot, and everything else follows from that.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe common types of structured products
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question: A risk analyst is preparing a briefing note on the principal categories of structured credit product. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A collateralised loan obligation is backed by a pool of corporate loans, a collateralised bond obligation by a pool of bonds, and a synthetic CDO obtains its credit exposure through credit default swaps rather than by purchasing the assets.
A synthetic CDO is backed by a pool of physical assets purchased by the SPV, whereas a cash CDO obtains its exposure through credit default swaps.
In a collateralised debt obligation, credit tranching and time tranching are the same mechanism, since both allocate losses in order of seniority.
A collateralised loan obligation differs from a collateralised bond obligation only in that the CLO issues a single tranche while the CBO issues multiple tranches.

questions.solution:
The taxonomy of structured credit products by collateral type and by whether exposure is obtained physically or synthetically.

Two independent classification axes are in play, and confusing them generates most of the errors here.

Axis 1: what the collateral is.

| Product | Collateral |
|---|---|
| Collateralised loan obligation (CLO) | A pool of corporate loans, typically leveraged loans |
| Collateralised bond obligation (CBO) | A pool of bonds |
| Collateralised mortgage obligation (CMO) | Mortgage pass-through securities, time tranched |
| Collateralised debt obligation (CDO) | The general category, covering loans, bonds or other debt |

Axis 2: how the exposure is obtained. A cash CDO buys the assets, funding the purchase by issuing notes. A synthetic CDO does not buy anything: the SPV sells protection through credit default swaps on a reference portfolio and invests the note proceeds in safe collateral. Credit risk is transferred without the assets moving, which is faster, cheaper and avoids the need for a true sale.

The two tranching mechanisms, which option (c) conflates. Credit tranching allocates losses in order of seniority, so the equity tranche absorbs the first losses. Time tranching allocates principal repayments in sequence, so one class is repaid before another begins. They are independent: a deal can have both, and time tranching redistributes prepayment risk rather than credit risk.

a.reason: CLO on loans, CBO on bonds, and synthetic CDOs obtain exposure through credit default swaps rather than purchase.

b.reason: The definitions of cash and synthetic are exactly reversed. A cash CDO buys the assets; a synthetic CDO takes exposure through derivatives.

c.reason: Credit tranching allocates losses by seniority; time tranching allocates principal repayments in sequence and addresses prepayment risk, not credit risk. Treating them as one mechanism is a sibling swap.

d.reason: Both CLOs and CBOs are multi-tranche structures. The difference between them is the collateral, loans versus bonds, not the number of tranches.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is a clean polarity flip on the cash versus synthetic definition, and it is the single most examined distinction in this area. Option (c) is the credit versus time tranching sibling swap, which is worth holding precisely because both are described as sequential and both appear in the same documents: credit tranching orders losses, time tranching orders principal.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: A risk manager is outlining the tools appropriate for measuring different types of VaR. Given the characteristics of market price fluctuations versus credit events, what approach should be specified for the measurement of credit VaR?

options.text: Historical simulation models, because they account for the high-frequency nature of credit events.
Sophisticated models that encompass credit correlations and rating transitions, reflecting the infrequency and interconnectedness of credit events.
Continual mark-to-market valuation methods, to capture the volatile and high-impact nature of credit defaults and downgrades.
Volatility-based models similar to those used for market risk VaR, to capture the variability of credit spreads.

questions.solution:
Credit events are rare, discrete and correlated, so credit VaR requires correlation and transition modelling rather than the high-frequency price-history methods used for market VaR.

The two measures share a definition but almost nothing else.

| Dimension | Market VaR | Credit VaR |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Maximum loss from market price moves at a confidence level over a horizon | Maximum credit loss at a confidence level over a horizon |
| Typical horizon | One day to ten days | One year |
| Confidence level | 95% or 99% | 99.9% or higher, aligned to a target rating |
| Event frequency | Continuous price movement | Rare, discrete events |
| Loss distribution | Approximately symmetric | Highly skewed with a long right tail |
| Principal tool | Historical simulation, variance-covariance, Monte Carlo on price history | Credit correlation and rating transition models |

Why historical simulation fails for credit. Market VaR can be estimated from a year of daily returns because prices move every day, giving hundreds of observations. Defaults are rare: an investment-grade issuer may default once in decades, so a comparable history simply does not exist. Estimating a 99.9% quantile from a sample containing almost no defaults is not possible.

Why correlation modelling is unavoidable. Credit losses are driven by joint default, and the tail of the loss distribution is entirely determined by how often obligors fail together. Since joint defaults are rarer still than single defaults, the dependence structure must be modelled, typically through a Gaussian copula or a single systematic factor, rather than observed.

Why rating transitions enter. Credit loss is not only default. A downgrade widens the required spread and reduces the value of a held position without any default occurring. Mark-to-market credit VaR frameworks such as CreditMetrics therefore work from a full transition matrix, not a single default probability.

a.reason: Credit events are infrequent, not high frequency. The justification inverts the very characteristic that makes historical simulation unusable here.

b.reason: Credit correlation and rating transition models, reflecting the rarity and interconnectedness of credit events.

c.reason: Continual mark to market is the market risk approach and is only partially available for credit, since most loans and many bonds are illiquid and have no observable continuous price. This option also mislabels credit defaults as volatile in the continuous sense.

d.reason: Applying market risk volatility methods to credit is precisely the error the reading warns against. Credit loss distributions are highly skewed and driven by rare joint events, so a volatility-based symmetric model understates the tail.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is a polarity flip hidden in the justification: the technique named is a real one, and the reason given, high frequency, is the exact opposite of the truth. Option (d) is the sibling swap that imports the market risk toolkit wholesale. Both are caught by the same question: how many observations of the event do we actually have? For market moves, thousands. For defaults, almost none.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: A newly appointed risk committee member asks why the bank's market risk VaR is reported at a one-day 99% level while its credit VaR is reported at a one-year 99.9% level. Which of the following best explains the difference in convention?

options.text: The horizons differ because market positions can be liquidated or hedged within days, whereas credit exposures are illiquid and must be held through the year; the confidence levels differ because credit capital is calibrated to a target solvency standard rather than to a trading limit.

The horizons differ because credit losses accumulate more slowly than market losses, and the confidence levels differ because credit loss distributions are approximately normal and therefore require a more extreme quantile.
The conventions are arbitrary regulatory choices with no economic basis, and either measure could be reported on either horizon without changing its interpretation.
The horizons differ because market risk is measured under the risk-neutral measure and credit risk under the real-world measure, and the confidence levels follow from that difference in measure.

questions.solution:
The horizon reflects how quickly a position can be exited; the confidence level reflects what the number is used for, a trading limit versus a solvency standard.

Two separate design choices, each with its own justification.

The horizon reflects liquidity and management action. A trading book position can be sold or hedged within a day or two, so the relevant question is how much can be lost before the desk can act. Loans and unhedged counterparty exposures cannot be exited quickly, and the annual balance sheet and capital planning cycle imposes a natural one-year frame. Credit risk models therefore use a one-year horizon almost universally.

The confidence level reflects the purpose.

| | Market VaR | Credit VaR |
|---|---|---|
| Horizon driver | Time to liquidate or hedge, one to ten days | Illiquidity and the annual review cycle, one year |
| Confidence driver | Trading limit and backtestability, 95% to 99% | Target solvency standard and credit rating, 99.9% and above |
| Distribution shape | Approximately symmetric | Highly skewed with a long right tail |
| Can the model be backtested | Yes, exceptions occur often enough | Barely, the events are too rare |

Market VaR at 99% supports limit setting and backtesting: a 1% exception rate produces roughly two or three exceptions per year, which is enough to test the model. Credit VaR at 99.9% or above supports a solvency standard: the confidence level is chosen to match the default probability implied by the bank's target senior debt rating, so it must be far more extreme.

Note the tension in (b). Credit loss distributions are not approximately normal. They are bounded below at zero, highly skewed, and fat tailed, which is why a normal approximation understates capital and why the beta distribution and Monte Carlo simulation are used instead.

a.reason: Horizon follows liquidity and management action; confidence level follows the intended use, a solvency standard rather than a trading limit.

b.reason: The first clause is loosely defensible, but the second is factually wrong: credit loss distributions are strongly non-normal, and it is that skewness rather than any normality that drives the extreme quantile.

c.reason: An absolute claim denying any economic content. Both conventions follow directly from the liquidity of the exposures and the purpose of the number, and changing the horizon would materially change what the measure means.

d.reason: The measure distinction is imported from derivative valuation and does not determine VaR conventions. Both market and credit VaR are computed under the real-world measure, because both are forecasting actual losses rather than pricing an instrument.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the sharpest, because it pairs a plausible first clause with a factual reversal in the second, and a candidate who validates only the opening will accept it. Option (d) is a scope error importing the real-world versus risk-neutral distinction, which governs valuation rather than risk measurement. Both VaR measures forecast real losses and therefore use real-world probabilities.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question: A USD 1 million portfolio of credits is divided into 100 equally weighted credits, each with default probability $p$. The default correlation is zero and the recovery rate is zero. If $p = 0.03$ and the 95th percentile of the number of defaults is assumed to be 4, calculate the credit VaR.

options.text: USD 0.01 million
USD 0.004 million
USD 0.09 million
USD 0.001 million

questions.solution:
Credit VaR is the loss at the confidence level less the expected loss, computed from a default count distribution.

Step 1. Value of each credit.

$$\text{Each position} = \frac{\text{USD } 1{,}000{,}000}{100} = \text{USD } 10{,}000$$

Step 2. Loss at the 95th percentile. With zero recovery, each default costs the full position value.

$$\text{Loss}_{95\%} = 4 \text{ defaults} \times \text{USD } 10{,}000 = \text{USD } 40{,}000$$

Step 3. Expected loss.

$$EL = n \times p \times \text{position value} = 100 \times 0.03 \times 10{,}000 = \text{USD } 30{,}000$$

Equivalently, the expected number of defaults is $np = 3$, costing USD 30,000.

Step 4. Credit VaR.

$$\text{Credit VaR} = \text{Loss}_{95\%} - EL = 40{,}000 - 30{,}000 = \text{USD } 10{,}000 = \text{USD } 0.01 \text{ million}$$

Interpretation. Three defaults are expected and are paid for through the spread. The fourth default, costing USD 10,000, is the unexpected loss that capital must absorb at a 95% standard.

Note on the given percentile. The question fixes the 95th percentile at 4 defaults by assumption. Under an exact binomial with $n = 100$ and $p = 3\%$ it would be 6 defaults ($P(\le 5) = 91.9\%$, $P(\le 6) = 96.9\%$), giving a credit VaR of $6 \times 10{,}000 - 30{,}000 = \text{USD } 30{,}000$. Either way, with 100 independent credits the quantile sits only a few defaults above the mean of 3, which is why credit VaR is small relative to the notional.

a.reason: USD 40,000 less USD 30,000 equals USD 10,000, or USD 0.01 million.

b.reason: USD 0.004 million is USD 4,000, which corresponds to 4 defaults valued at USD 1,000 each, that is, a unit error in the position size.

c.reason: USD 0.09 million is USD 90,000. It does not follow from a defined step; it appears to combine the 3% default probability with the portfolio value in a mis-scaled way.

d.reason: USD 0.001 million is USD 1,000, one tenth of the correct answer, a decimal slip on the position size.

trap.explanation: The dominant error is not offered but must be guarded against: reporting the quantile loss of USD 40,000 without subtracting expected loss. That is the intermediate-result trap and it is the single most common credit VaR mistake. The distractors here are unit and decimal errors on the position size, which is easy to misstate because the portfolio total and the position count differ by two orders of magnitude. Write the position value down explicitly before computing anything.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question:
Portfolio Y has a notional value of USD 1,000,000 spread across 30 credit positions. Each credit has a default probability of 3% and a zero recovery rate. All credit positions in the portfolio are exposures to the same obligor, so the portfolio has a default correlation equal to 1.

Determine the credit VaR at the 99% confidence level.
questions.solution:
At a default correlation of one, a portfolio behaves as a single credit, so diversification disappears and credit VaR approaches the full notional less expected loss.

The key structural insight. With $\rho = 1$ every position defaults together or none does. The 30 positions collapse into a single Bernoulli outcome, and the number of positions becomes irrelevant.

$$\text{Loss} = \text{USD } 1{,}000{,}000 \text{ with probability } 3\%, \text{ and USD } 0 \text{ with probability } 97\%$$

Step 1. Loss at the 99th percentile. The probability of zero loss is 97%, which is less than 99%. The 99th percentile therefore falls in the default state.

$$\text{Loss}_{99\%} = \text{USD } 1{,}000{,}000$$

Step 2. Expected loss.

$$EL = 0.03 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = \text{USD } 30{,}000$$

Step 3. Credit VaR.

$$\text{Credit VaR} = 1{,}000{,}000 - 30{,}000 = \text{USD } 970{,}000$$

Contrast with the same 30 positions if they were independent: the 99th percentile of a binomial with $n = 30$ and $p = 3\%$ is 4 defaults, so credit VaR would be only about USD 103,000 ($4 \times 33{,}333 - 30{,}000$). The expected loss is identical in both cases; only the shape of the distribution has changed. This is the clearest available demonstration that correlation drives the tail and leaves the mean untouched.

The threshold check. Had the confidence level been 95% rather than 99%, the 95th percentile would fall in the no default state, since $P(\text{no default}) = 97\%$ exceeds 95%. Credit VaR would then be floored at zero. Confidence level and default probability must be compared before computing anything.

a.reason: USD 1,000,000 less USD 30,000 equals USD 970,000.

b.reason: USD 980,000 corresponds to subtracting a 2% expected loss rather than 3%, or to using 29 of the 30 positions. A wrong input twin on the default probability.

c.reason: USD 30,000 is the expected loss itself, reported as the answer. The intermediate-result trap, and the most likely miss under time pressure.

d.reason: USD 200,000 does not follow from any defined step. It resembles a partial-diversification result, which is precisely what a correlation of one rules out.

trap.explanation: The structural trap is treating the portfolio as diversified. A candidate who reaches for a binomial distribution with n = 30 and p = 3% will find a 99th percentile of 4 defaults and compute a credit VaR near USD 103,000 ($4 \times 33{,}333 - 30{,}000$), which is not offered and should prompt a rethink. The phrase all positions feature the same obligor is the instruction to collapse the portfolio to one credit. Option (c) is the intermediate-result trap of stopping at expected loss.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: A bank uses a simplified ratings transition matrix for its corporate bond portfolio to calculate credit VaR. What do the transition probabilities in such a matrix represent?

options.text: The likelihood that credit ratings will deteriorate or improve within a certain timeframe, impacting the valuation of bonds.
The estimated probability that a bond will experience a rating upgrade or downgrade within the next fiscal year based on economic forecasts.
The likelihood that a company's credit rating will migrate from one specific category to another over a specified time frame, such as one year.
The frequency of credit rating changes within the portfolio over the past year, used as a predictor for future transitions.

questions.solution:
Each cell of a transition matrix is a conditional probability of moving from one specific rating to another specific rating over a stated horizon.

A transition matrix is a grid of conditional probabilities. Each row is a starting rating, each column an ending rating, and each cell answers a specific question: given that the issuer is rated X today, what is the probability it is rated Y in one year?

| From \\ To | A | B | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0.90 | 0.09 | 0.01 |
| B | 0.05 | 0.85 | 0.10 |
| Default | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.00 |

Three properties follow and each is examinable.

Rows sum to one. Every issuer must end somewhere, including in the same rating or in default.

Default is absorbing. The default row is all zeros except a one in the default column; an issuer cannot recover out of default within the matrix.

The diagonal dominates. Ratings are deliberately stable, because agencies rate through the cycle and avoid reversals, so the largest entry in each row is the probability of staying put.

How it produces credit VaR. Each end-state rating implies a revaluation of the bond at that rating's credit spread. Combining the probability of each migration with the value in that state builds a full distribution of end-of-horizon portfolio values, and credit VaR is read off its tail. This is the CreditMetrics mark-to-market approach, and it captures loss from downgrade as well as from default.

Multi-period extension. Under the Markov assumption, the $n$-year matrix is the one-year matrix raised to the power $n$. Squaring the one-year matrix gives the two-year matrix.

a.reason: Directionally true but imprecise. It describes deterioration or improvement in general, whereas a transition probability is cell specific: from one named rating to another named rating. The distinction matters because it is the cell-level granularity that allows each end state to be revalued.

b.reason: Two defects. It restricts the matrix to upgrades and downgrades, omitting the largest entry in every row, which is the probability of remaining in the same rating, and it omits default. It also attributes the estimates to economic forecasts rather than to historical migration experience.

c.reason: The probability of migrating from one specific rating category to another over a specified horizon.

d.reason: Describes the historical sample from which the matrix is estimated rather than the matrix itself. A realised frequency over the past year is an input to estimation; a transition probability is a forward-looking conditional probability. It also restricts the matrix to the bank's own portfolio, whereas transition matrices are estimated from broad agency data.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the trap, and it is a scope error rather than a factual mistake: everything it says is true, but it describes the matrix at the wrong level of resolution. A candidate scanning for a true statement will accept it. The discriminator is the phrase from one category to another, which is what makes the matrix usable for revaluation. Option (d) is the estimate versus estimator confusion, describing the data rather than the parameter.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: An instructor is discussing how to extend a one-year credit rating transition matrix to estimate risk over different timeframes. Which method appropriately projects the transition probabilities for a two-year period?

options.text: Computing the geometric mean of the one-year transition probabilities.
Applying exponential smoothing to one-year transition data together with historical two-year transition trends.
Squaring the one-year transition matrix to estimate the two-year transition matrix.
Updating the one-year transition matrix with recent default and recovery rates before applying it to the second year.

questions.solution:
Under the Markov assumption, multi-period transition probabilities are obtained by matrix multiplication, so the $n$-period matrix is the one-period matrix raised to the power $n$.

The Markov property. The standard assumption is that the probability of migrating over the next year depends only on the current rating, not on the path that led there. Under that assumption transitions compose by matrix multiplication:

$$T(2\text{ years}) = T(1\text{ year}) \times T(1\text{ year}) = T^2, \quad T(n\text{ years}) = T^n$$

Why matrix multiplication and not scalar arithmetic. Reaching rating C in two years from rating A requires summing over every possible intermediate state:

$$P(A \rightarrow C \text{ over } 2 \text{ years}) = \sum_B P(A \rightarrow B) \times P(B \rightarrow C)$$

That summation over intermediate paths is exactly what the row-by-column product of matrix multiplication performs. Averaging individual cell probabilities discards the paths entirely.

The cumulative default probability. The two-year cumulative default probability for an A-rated issuer is the A-to-default entry of $T$ squared, which correctly counts the path A stays A then defaults, plus the path A migrates to B then defaults, and so on. It is not twice the one-year figure, and it is not $1 - (1-PD)^2$, because those shortcuts ignore migration.

The caveat worth knowing. The Markov assumption is an approximation. Empirically ratings display momentum: an issuer recently downgraded is more likely to be downgraded again than a stable issuer of the same rating. Matrix powers therefore understate multi-year migration risk somewhat.

a.reason: A geometric mean averages values along a single dimension and produces a number, not a matrix. It cannot capture migration through intermediate ratings, which is the entire content of a multi-period transition.

b.reason: Exponential smoothing is a time series estimation technique used to weight recent observations more heavily when estimating the one-year matrix in the first place. It is not a method for projecting one horizon onto another. A sibling swap between estimation and extrapolation.

c.reason: Squaring the one-year matrix gives the two-year matrix under the Markov assumption.

d.reason: Updating the matrix with recent data improves the inputs but does nothing to extend the horizon. Applying an updated one-year matrix to the second year still requires the multiplication step that this option omits.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (d) both fail on the same point: they operate on the matrix's contents without performing the composition that moves from one horizon to two. The mechanical check is to ask what object the method produces; a two-year transition matrix must itself be a matrix of the same dimensions, which immediately rules out an averaging operation. Option (b) is a genuine technique misapplied, which is the hardest kind of distractor to reject without knowing what each technique is for.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: A credit risk officer is explaining the challenges of adjusting VaR for credit spread risk. What significant risk should the officer highlight when discussing the limitations of using historical simulation for credit VaR calculations?

options.text: The risk of overestimating credit spread changes, due to the assumption of continuously increasing spreads over time.
The challenge of capturing jump-to-default risk, which arises from the possibility that a company could default abruptly without prior indication.
The issue of underestimating market liquidity risk, due to a narrow focus on credit spreads instead of the broader market impacts on portfolio value.
The limitations in assessing interest rate risk, since historical simulation for credit VaR is strictly confined to credit spread changes.

questions.solution:
Credit spread risk is the risk of loss from spread widening without default; historical simulation of spread moves cannot capture the discontinuous jump to default.

Credit spread risk defined. The risk that the credit spread on a position widens, reducing its value, without any default occurring. It is a mark-to-market risk driven by changing market perception of credit quality, and it affects any position valued off a credit curve.

Why historical simulation is attractive here. Spreads are observable and move continuously, so a history of daily spread changes can be applied to the current portfolio in exactly the way market risk VaR is computed. That works well for the continuous part of credit risk.

Where it breaks: jump to default. Default is a discontinuous event. A bond trading at 98 does not decline smoothly to its recovery value of 40; it gaps there on the announcement. A historical sample of spread changes contains almost no such jumps, because defaults are rare and the surviving names that populate the sample by construction did not default.

| Component of credit risk | Nature | Captured by historical simulation of spreads |
|---|---|---|
| Spread widening without default | Continuous, observable daily | Yes |
| Rating migration | Discrete but gradual | Partially, through the spread change it causes |
| Jump to default | Discontinuous and rare | No |

The consequence. Historical simulation of spread changes captures the body of the credit loss distribution and systematically misses the tail, which is precisely where credit VaR is read. This is why credit VaR frameworks add a default or transition component rather than relying on spread histories alone.

a.reason: Historical simulation makes no assumption that spreads increase continuously; it resamples observed historical changes in both directions. The stated assumption is invented, and the direction of the resulting error, overestimation, is the reverse of the true problem, which is understatement of tail risk.

b.reason: Jump-to-default risk, the abrupt discontinuous loss that a spread history cannot contain.

c.reason: Liquidity risk is a genuine limitation of VaR generally, but it is not the specific defect that credit spread simulation introduces, and the option describes a breadth problem rather than the discontinuity problem.

d.reason: Interest rate risk is separable from credit spread risk and is handled in the market risk framework. The claim that credit VaR by historical simulation is strictly confined to spread changes is also an absolute claim that does not hold, since transition-based approaches exist.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is a polarity flip on the direction of the error: the true failure of spread-based historical simulation is understating tail risk, not overestimating spread changes. Option (c) names a real limitation of VaR but attaches it to the wrong mechanism, a scope error. The discriminating idea is continuity: historical simulation resamples what has been observed, and a default has not been observed in the history of a surviving issuer.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR; assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question: A risk manager is evaluating the impact of default correlation on a credit portfolio's risk. Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between default correlation and credit portfolio risk?

options.text: Higher default correlation reduces credit portfolio risk, because it indicates a greater likelihood of joint defaults.
Higher default correlation increases credit portfolio risk, because it indicates a greater likelihood of joint defaults.
Default correlation has no impact on credit portfolio risk, as it only measures the co-movement of credit events.
It is impossible to determine the relationship between default correlation and credit portfolio risk without further information.

questions.solution:
Higher default correlation increases the dispersion of portfolio losses and therefore credit VaR, while leaving expected loss unchanged.

The mechanism. Default correlation measures the tendency of obligors to fail together. Raising it makes clustered outcomes more likely, which fattens the right tail of the loss distribution.

$$UL_P = \sqrt{\sum_i \sum_j \rho_{ij} UL_i UL_j}, \text{ increasing in every } \rho_{ij}$$

Because credit VaR is a tail quantile net of the mean, it increases with correlation.

The invariant that makes option (a) tempting and wrong. Expected loss is unchanged:

$$E[\text{loss}] = \sum_i PD_i \times EAD_i \times LGD_i, \text{ independent of correlation}$$

So correlation raises risk without raising expected loss, which is exactly why it consumes capital rather than spread.

The two boundary cases.

| Correlation | Portfolio behaviour | Credit VaR |
|---|---|---|
| $\rho = 0$ | Fully diversified; defaults arrive independently | Smallest, and it shrinks further as $n$ grows |
| $0 < \rho < 1$ | Partial diversification | Intermediate |
| $\rho = 1$ | Behaves as a single credit; no diversification at all | Largest, approaching the full notional less expected loss |

The same USD 1 million notional at a 3% default probability produced a credit VaR of USD 10,000 with independent credits and USD 970,000 at a correlation of one.

a.reason: A polarity flip. The justification given, a greater likelihood of joint defaults, is correct and is precisely the reason risk increases. The option pairs the right mechanism with the wrong conclusion.
