b.reason: Higher correlation increases credit portfolio risk through a greater likelihood of joint defaults.

c.reason: Correlation has no impact on expected loss, which is likely the source of the confusion, but it is the dominant driver of the tail and therefore of credit VaR and capital.

d.reason: The direction of the relationship is unambiguous and requires no further information. Magnitude would need more detail; direction does not.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the sharpest distractor precisely because its stated reason is correct. A candidate who validates the justification and not the conclusion will accept it. Option (c) is the scope error of applying a true statement about the mean to the whole distribution. Read the conclusion and the reason as separate claims and check both.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR; assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question:
A portfolio has a total principal value of USD 1.0 billion divided into 20 equal positions of USD 50 million each. Each position has a default probability of 1.0%, the recovery rate is zero, and the default correlation is zero. The 95th percentile of the number of defaults is 1, so the 95% credit VaR, measured net of expected loss, is USD 40 million.

Holding all other assumptions constant, each of the following is true EXCEPT which one?

options.text: Increasing granularity from 20 positions to 100 positions of USD 10 million each reduces the 95% credit VaR.
As granularity increases without limit, with positions remaining independent and equally sized, the 95% credit VaR tends toward zero.
As granularity increases without limit, with positions remaining independent and equally sized, the 95% credit VaR tends toward USD 990 million.
Increasing the default correlation while holding granularity at 20 positions leaves the expected loss unchanged at USD 10 million.

questions.solution:
With independent exposures, greater granularity diversifies away unexpected loss so that credit VaR converges to zero; only correlation, not granularity, drives credit VaR toward the full notional.

Confirming the base case. Expected defaults are $n\pi = 20 \times 0.01 = 0.2$. The 95th percentile is 1 default.

$$\text{Loss}_{95\%} = 1 \times 50 = \text{USD } 50 \text{ million}, \quad EL = 0.01 \times 1{,}000 = \text{USD } 10 \text{ million}$$

$$\text{Credit VaR} = 50 - 10 = \text{USD } 40 \text{ million}$$

Statement (a): granularity to $n = 100$. Each position is USD 10 million and expected defaults are 1.0. For a binomial with $n = 100$ and $\pi = 0.01$, the 95th percentile is 3 defaults.

$$\text{Credit VaR} = (3 \times 10) - 10 = \text{USD } 20 \text{ million, a decrease from USD } 40 \text{ million. True.}$$

Statements (b) and (c): the limit. With independent, equally sized positions, the law of large numbers applies. The realised default rate converges to $\pi$, so the loss distribution collapses onto its mean, unexpected loss vanishes, and credit VaR tends to zero. Statement (b) is true and statement (c) is false.

$$\text{As } n \rightarrow \infty \text{ with } \rho = 0: \quad \text{Loss}_{95\%} \rightarrow EL, \text{ so Credit VaR} \rightarrow 0$$

Where USD 990 million would come from. That is the perfect-correlation figure: full notional of USD 1,000 million less expected loss of USD 10 million. It applies at $\rho = 1$ only when the confidence level is above 99%. At 95%, the 99% probability of no default puts the quantile in the no-loss state. It is the answer to a correlation question, not a granularity question, and it is the exact opposite limit.

Statement (d): correlation. Correlation changes the shape of the loss distribution, not its mean: expected loss is $20 \times 0.01 \times 50 = \text{USD } 10$ million at any correlation. True. Note that at this 95% level, higher correlation does not raise credit VaR here. The probability of no default rises toward 99% as correlation rises, so the 95th percentile stays at 1 default and eventually falls to 0. This is the same threshold effect that floors credit VaR at zero whenever the no-default probability exceeds the confidence level.

The two levers, side by side.

| Change | Effect on expected loss | Effect on credit VaR | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| More positions, independent | None | Decreases | Zero |
| Higher default correlation | None | Fattens the tail; raises credit VaR once the confidence level is beyond the no-default probability | Full notional less expected loss, USD 990 million (confidence above 99%) |

a.reason: The statement is true. At $n = 100$ the 95th percentile is 3 defaults of USD 10 million each, giving a credit VaR of USD 20 million, down from USD 40 million.

b.reason: The statement is true. With independent equal positions the loss rate converges to the mean, so unexpected loss and therefore credit VaR converge to zero.

c.reason: This is the credited answer because the statement is false. USD 990 million is the perfect-correlation figure (at confidence levels above 99%), not the perfect-granularity limit. Granularity drives credit VaR toward zero, not toward the notional.

d.reason: The statement is true. Correlation reshapes the loss distribution but leaves its mean unchanged, so expected loss stays at USD 10 million.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is a role misassignment between the two levers: it takes the perfect-correlation figure (full notional less expected loss, which applies at confidence levels above 99%) and attaches it to the granularity lever. It is attractive because USD 990 million is a real and computable number, so a candidate who recognises it assumes it must belong somewhere. Hold the two directions separately: granularity diversifies risk away toward zero; correlation concentrates it toward the full notional.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about the modelling of default correlation in CreditMetrics and in Vasicek's model?

options.text: Vasicek's model calculates default correlation using multiple Gaussian copulas to reflect varying economic conditions across sectors.
CreditMetrics employs a single-factor model that simplifies the correlation of defaults to a common economic influence affecting all entities equally.
Vasicek's model uses a single systematic factor representing overall economic conditions to model default correlations, affecting all entities in the portfolio.
CreditMetrics uses sector-based risk adjustments in addition to a Gaussian copula for modelling default correlations specifically tied to individual industries.

questions.solution:
Vasicek's model reduces all dependence to one systematic factor with a common correlation, whereas CreditMetrics uses a full asset return correlation matrix derived from equity indices.

Both models use a Gaussian copula to link individual credit outcomes, but they differ fundamentally in how much structure they impose on the dependence.

| Feature | Vasicek | CreditMetrics |
|---|---|---|
| Dependence structure | One systematic factor, a single correlation parameter | Full asset return correlation matrix |
| Source of correlation | Assumed or regulatory prescribed | Equity index correlations by country and industry |
| Scope of credit events | Default only | Default and rating migration, mark to market |
| Solution method | Closed form, asymptotic | Monte Carlo simulation |
| Principal use | Basel IRB capital formula | Portfolio credit VaR |

Vasicek's single factor. Each obligor's latent asset return is driven by one common factor plus an idiosyncratic term:

$$a_i = \sqrt{\rho} \times m + \sqrt{1-\rho} \times \varepsilon_i$$

where $m$ is the single systematic factor common to all obligors and $\varepsilon_i$ is idiosyncratic. All pairwise correlations collapse to the single parameter $\rho$. This drastic simplification is what makes the model analytically tractable and is why it underpins the Basel IRB capital formula: a formula requiring a full correlation matrix could not be written into regulation.

CreditMetrics. Estimates a full asset return correlation matrix, typically inferred from equity index correlations mapped to each obligor's country and industry. Dependence therefore varies pair by pair, at the cost of requiring simulation rather than a closed form.

What they share. Both map correlated normal draws through thresholds to produce correlated credit outcomes, which is the Gaussian copula construction.

a.reason: Vasicek's model is defined by having one factor, not multiple sector copulas. The option describes a multi-factor extension and attaches it to the wrong model.

b.reason: The single-factor description belongs to Vasicek, not CreditMetrics. A direct role misassignment between the two models, and the mirror image of the correct answer.

c.reason: Vasicek uses a single systematic factor representing overall economic conditions.

d.reason: CreditMetrics does use a Gaussian copula and does map obligors to country and industry indices, but describing this as sector-based risk adjustments in addition to the copula misstates the mechanism: the industry mapping is how the correlation matrix is estimated, not an adjustment layered on top.

trap.explanation: Options (b) and (c) are the two halves of one role misassignment, and the item is decided entirely by which model owns the single-factor description. Option (d) is subtler: every noun in it is real and associated with CreditMetrics, but the relationship between them is wrong. The memory hook: Vasicek is one factor and one correlation number because a regulator has to be able to write it down; CreditMetrics is a full matrix because a bank can simulate.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes CreditMetrics from both Vasicek's model and CreditRisk+?

options.text: It ignores credit rating migrations and focuses solely on default events.
It incorporates mark-to-market revaluations arising from credit downgrades.
It assumes fixed recovery rates for all obligors in the portfolio.
It uses a Poisson distribution to model default frequency.

questions.solution:
CreditMetrics is a mark-to-market model that prices rating migrations as well as defaults, whereas Vasicek and CreditRisk+ are default-mode models.

The three models divide on a single question: what counts as a credit loss?

| Model | Loss recognised on | Correlation structure | Distributional engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| CreditMetrics | Default and rating migration, mark to market | Full asset return correlation matrix | Gaussian copula, simulation |
| Vasicek | Default only | Single systematic factor | Gaussian, closed form |
| CreditRisk+ | Default only | Sector factors with gamma-distributed rates | Poisson, then negative binomial |

Default-mode models. Vasicek and CreditRisk+ recognise a loss only when an obligor defaults. A bond downgraded from A to BBB generates no loss in these frameworks, even though its market value has fallen.

Mark-to-market models. CreditMetrics revalues every position at its end-of-horizon rating using that rating's forward credit spread curve. A downgrade produces a real, measured loss. The full loss distribution therefore spans every migration outcome, not just the default column.

Why the distinction matters for credit VaR. For an investment-grade portfolio over one year, default is very unlikely but downgrade is not. A default-mode model reports very little risk; a mark-to-market model captures the substantial value at risk from migration. The two can give materially different capital numbers for the same portfolio, and the gap is largest precisely where credit quality is highest.

a.reason: Exactly reversed. Ignoring migration and focusing solely on default describes Vasicek and CreditRisk+, which is what CreditMetrics is being distinguished from.

b.reason: Mark-to-market revaluation on downgrade is the distinguishing feature.

c.reason: A fixed recovery assumption is common across simplified implementations of all three models and is not distinguishing. CreditMetrics in fact often models recovery as a random variable, typically beta distributed.

d.reason: The Poisson distribution is the engine of CreditRisk+, which models the number of defaults as a Poisson count with a gamma-distributed rate. A sibling swap onto the wrong model.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is a clean polarity flip that hands CreditMetrics the property of the two models it is being contrasted with, and it will catch anyone answering from a vague sense that CreditMetrics is about default. Option (d) attaches CreditRisk+'s signature distribution to CreditMetrics. One sentence resolves the whole family: CreditMetrics marks to market and prices downgrades; Vasicek and CreditRisk+ only count defaults.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question:
A risk manager is evaluating two strategies for a portfolio of BBB-rated corporate bonds. The first is a buy-and-hold approach, holding the bonds for one year without rebalancing. The second is a constant level of risk approach, rebalancing monthly so that any bond downgraded below BBB is sold and replaced with a BBB-rated bond.

Which statement most accurately describes the impact of the constant level of risk strategy relative to buy and hold?

options.text: It increases the probability of large losses from defaults but reduces losses from small rating changes.
It reduces the probability of large losses from defaults but increases losses from small rating changes.
It reduces both the probability of large losses from defaults and the losses from small rating changes.
It leaves the credit loss distribution unchanged, since the average rating of the portfolio is BBB under both strategies.

questions.solution:
Rebalancing to a constant credit quality truncates the path to default but crystallises every downgrade as a realised loss, trading tail risk for more frequent small losses.

The two strategies produce the same average rating and very different loss distributions.

What rebalancing does to the tail. Issuers rarely default straight from BBB. They migrate downward over months or years, and the default occurs from a low speculative-grade rating. Selling a bond as soon as it leaves BBB interrupts that path, so the portfolio is very unlikely ever to hold a bond at the point of default. Large default losses become much less likely.

What rebalancing does to the body. Every downgrade is now a realised loss: the bond is sold at the lower post-downgrade price rather than held in the hope of recovery. Under buy and hold, a bond downgraded to BB and later upgraded back to BBB produces no realised loss at all. Rebalancing forecloses that recovery and converts a paper loss into a permanent one, repeatedly.

The trade in one line.

| | Buy and hold | Constant level of risk |
|---|---|---|
| Path to default | Retained; bonds can migrate all the way down | Interrupted; bonds sold on leaving BBB |
| Large default losses | More likely | Less likely |
| Small downgrade losses | Unrealised, and reversible on upgrade | Realised and permanent |
| Effect on the loss distribution | Long thin tail | Shorter tail, thicker body |

Why this matters for credit VaR. The constant level of risk strategy shortens the tail and thickens the body. Over a multi-year horizon it typically produces a lower credit VaR at very high confidence levels but a higher expected loss and a higher loss at moderate confidence levels.

a.reason: A complete polarity flip on both clauses. Rebalancing reduces default losses and increases realised downgrade losses, not the reverse.

b.reason: It reduces large default losses and increases losses from small rating changes.

c.reason: Claims a free lunch. Reducing tail risk without any offsetting cost would make the strategy dominant, and the cost is precisely that downgrade losses are crystallised rather than left to recover.

d.reason: Equal average rating does not imply an equal loss distribution. The strategies differ in the path they permit, and the loss distribution is a function of paths, not of the average rating.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the trap for a candidate who reasons that active risk management must be better on every dimension. It is an implicit absolute claim, and the discipline is to ask what the strategy gives up. Option (d) is the scope error of reasoning from a summary statistic, the average rating, to a distributional conclusion. Option (a) inverts both directions and is caught by asking a single question: can a bond default while the portfolio still holds it, if it is sold the moment it leaves BBB?

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question:
An analyst holds two credits with the following characteristics.

- Probability of default of credit 1: $\pi_1 = 0.025$
- Probability of default of credit 2: $\pi_2 = 0.035$
- Default correlation: $\rho_{12} = 0.05$

Determine the joint default probability of firms 1 and 2.
questions.solution:
Rearranging the definition of default correlation between two Bernoulli variables to recover the joint default probability.

The definition. Default is a Bernoulli event, so the correlation between two default indicators is:

$$\rho_{12} = \frac{\pi_{12} - \pi_1\pi_2}{\sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1) \times \pi_2(1-\pi_2)}}$$

where $\pi_{12}$ is the probability that both default. Rearranging:

$$\pi_{12} = \pi_1\pi_2 + \rho_{12}\sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1)\pi_2(1-\pi_2)}$$

Step 1. The independence term.

$$\pi_1\pi_2 = 0.025 \times 0.035 = 0.000875$$

Step 2. The Bernoulli standard deviations.

$$\pi_1(1-\pi_1) = 0.025 \times 0.975 = 0.024375, \quad \pi_2(1-\pi_2) = 0.035 \times 0.965 = 0.033775$$

$$\sqrt{0.024375 \times 0.033775} = \sqrt{0.00082327} = 0.028697$$

Step 3. Combine.

$$\pi_{12} = 0.000875 + (0.05 \times 0.028697) = 0.000875 + 0.001435 = 0.002310 = 0.231\%$$

Interpretation. Under independence the joint probability would be 0.0875%. A correlation of only 0.05 raises it to 0.231%, roughly two and a half times. This extreme sensitivity of joint default to small correlations is why senior tranche ratings are so fragile to the correlation assumption.

b.reason: 0.088% is $\pi_1\pi_2 = 0.000875$, the independence case. The correlation term has been dropped entirely, which is the answer to a different question.

c.reason: 0.143% is the correlation term 0.001435 taken alone, without adding the independence term. The intermediate-result trap: the harder half of the calculation is completed and the easy half omitted.

d.reason: 1.435% is the correlation term with a decimal shifted, that is, 0.001435 misread as 0.01435. A unit error, and it fails a sanity check since the joint probability cannot exceed the smaller marginal of 2.5% by much and should be far closer to the independence value.

trap.explanation: Options (b) and (c) are the two halves of the formula reported separately, which is the standard construction for this template: (b) is the dropped term and (c) is the intermediate result. The structural check that catches both: the answer must lie between the independence value $\pi_1\pi_2$ and the maximum $\min(\pi_1, \pi_2)$, here between 0.0875% and 2.5%, and it must be close to the lower bound when correlation is small.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question: A pair of credits rated BBB minus and BBB plus have default probabilities of 0.003 and 0.004 respectively. If the credits are correlated, what is the maximum permissible value of the default correlation between them?
questions.solution:
Default correlation between two Bernoulli variables is bounded above, because the joint default probability cannot exceed the smaller of the two marginal probabilities.

The binding constraint. Both credits can only default together as often as the less likely one defaults at all:

$$\pi_{12} \le \min(\pi_1, \pi_2) = \min(0.003, 0.004) = 0.003$$

Step 1. Substitute the maximum joint probability.

$$\rho_{max} = \frac{0.003 - (0.003 \times 0.004)}{\sqrt{0.003 \times 0.997 \times 0.004 \times 0.996}}$$

Step 2. Numerator.

$$0.003 - 0.000012 = 0.002988$$

Step 3. Denominator.

$$0.003 \times 0.997 = 0.002991; \quad 0.004 \times 0.996 = 0.003984$$

$$\sqrt{0.002991 \times 0.003984} = \sqrt{0.0000119161} = 0.0034520$$

Step 4. Divide.

$$\rho_{max} = \frac{0.002988}{0.0034520} = 0.866$$

Why the bound is below 1. Perfect correlation of one would require the two credits to default in exactly the same states, which is impossible when their marginal probabilities differ: credit 2 defaults in states where credit 1 does not. The maximum attainable correlation therefore falls as the two marginals diverge, and reaches 1 only when $\pi_1 = \pi_2$.

The practical implication. A modelled correlation input must respect this bound. Feeding a Gaussian copula an asset correlation that implies a default correlation above the feasible maximum produces an internally inconsistent loss distribution.

a.reason: 0.500 is a round figure not produced by any step here. It would correspond to a joint default probability well below the feasible maximum.

b.reason: 0.750 is approximately $\pi_1 / \pi_2 = 0.003 / 0.004$, the ratio of the two marginals. That ratio is a natural-looking construction but is not the correlation bound.

c.reason: 0.812 is close to the correct value but follows from no defined step. For example, dropping the $(1-\pi)$ factors gives $0.002988 / 0.003464 = 0.863$, which is still not 0.812.

trap.explanation: The trap that decides this item is recognising that the constraint is $\pi_{12} \le \min(\pi_1, \pi_2)$ rather than assuming the maximum correlation is 1. A candidate who does not identify the binding constraint has no route to any answer. Option (b) is the wrong ratio trap, substituting a simple ratio of marginals for the correlation formula; it is attractive because 0.75 falls out of the two given numbers in one step.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question:
An investment firm has exposure to two credits. The first, rated BBB, has a default probability of 0.003 over the time horizon $t$. The second, rated CCC, has a default probability of 0.005 over a comparable horizon. The probability that both credits default over the horizon $t$ is 0.0002.

The default correlation for this portfolio is closest to:
questions.solution:
Computing default correlation directly from the joint default probability and the two marginal default probabilities.

This is the reverse direction of the joint-default calculation: the joint probability is given and the correlation is the unknown.

$$\rho_{12} = \frac{\pi_{12} - \pi_1\pi_2}{\sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1) \times \pi_2(1-\pi_2)}}$$

Step 1. Numerator, the excess over independence.

$$\pi_1\pi_2 = 0.003 \times 0.005 = 0.000015, \quad 0.0002 - 0.000015 = 0.000185$$

Step 2. Denominator.

$$0.003 \times 0.997 = 0.002991; \quad 0.005 \times 0.995 = 0.004975$$

$$\sqrt{0.002991 \times 0.004975} = \sqrt{0.0000148802} = 0.0038575$$

Step 3. Divide.

$$\rho_{12} = \frac{0.000185}{0.0038575} = 0.04796$$

Interpretation. A joint default probability of 0.02% against an independence benchmark of 0.0015% is more than thirteen times higher, yet the implied default correlation is only about 0.048. Very low default correlations are consistent with joint defaults being many multiples of the independent case, which is the single most counterintuitive feature of this measure and the reason correlation cannot be judged by eye.

Feasibility check. The maximum joint probability here is $\min(0.003, 0.005) = 0.003$, so the stated 0.0002 is well within the feasible range.

a.reason: Omitting the subtraction of $\pi_1\pi_2$ in the numerator gives $0.0002 / 0.0038575 = 0.0518$. The dropped term error overstates correlation because it attributes all joint default to dependence rather than only the excess over independence. 0.05796 is a distractor near that dropped-term value.

b.reason: 0.00262 is an order of magnitude too small and follows from no defined step. Note that dividing by the product of variances instead of the product of standard deviations would give $0.000185 / 0.0000149 \approx 12.4$, far too large, not too small.

c.reason: 0.00338 is likewise an order of magnitude too small and follows from no defined step. Using $\pi_1\pi_2$ in the denominator would give $0.000185 / 0.000015 \approx 12.3$, not 0.00338.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the dropped term and the most instructive error: forgetting to net off the independence benchmark treats every joint default as evidence of dependence, when most joint defaults would occur by chance even under independence. Options (b) and (c) are an order of magnitude too small and do not follow from a defined step. The denominator must be the product of Bernoulli standard deviations. Recalling the formula as a covariance over variances (omitting the square root) would make the answer far too large, about 12, not too small.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define beta and calculate the asset return correlation of any pair of firms using the single factor model; estimate the probability of a joint default of any pair of credits and the default correlation between any pair of credits using the single factor model
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question:
A credit analyst is applying the single factor model to a portfolio. In this model each firm's standardised asset return is driven by a common market factor $m$ and an idiosyncratic shock, as follows.

$$a_i = \beta_i m + \sqrt{1-\beta_i^2}\,\varepsilon_i, \text{ where } m \text{ and each } \varepsilon_i \text{ are independent standard normal variables}$$

- Firm 1 has a beta of 0.60
- Firm 2 has a beta of 0.50

What is the asset return correlation between firm 1 and firm 2, and what does beta represent?

options.text: 0.30; beta is the sensitivity of the firm's asset return to the common market factor, and it equals the correlation between the firm's asset return and that factor.
0.55; beta is the sensitivity of the firm's asset return to the common market factor, computed as the average of the two firms' factor loadings.
0.30; beta is the proportion of the firm's asset return variance that is idiosyncratic and therefore diversifiable.
0.548; beta is the sensitivity of the firm's asset return to the common market factor, and the pair correlation is the square root of the product of the two betas.

questions.solution:
In the single factor model, beta is both the factor loading and the correlation of the firm's asset return with the factor; the pairwise asset return correlation is the product of the two betas.

What beta is. Because $m$ and $\varepsilon_i$ are independent standard normals and the coefficients are constructed so that $a_i$ has unit variance, beta is simultaneously the factor loading and the correlation between the firm's asset return and the market factor:

$$var(a_i) = \beta_i^2 + (1-\beta_i^2) = 1, \quad corr(a_i, m) = cov(a_i, m) = \beta_i$$

| Component | Share of variance | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Systematic, $\beta_i^2$ | 0.36 for firm 1 | Driven by the common factor; not diversifiable |
| Idiosyncratic, $1-\beta_i^2$ | 0.64 for firm 1 | Firm specific; diversifiable across a large portfolio |

The pairwise asset return correlation. Two firms are linked only through the common factor, since their idiosyncratic shocks are independent of each other and of $m$:

$$cov(a_1, a_2) = \beta_1\beta_2\, var(m) = \beta_1\beta_2$$

$$\rho_{12}^{assets} = \beta_1 \times \beta_2 = 0.60 \times 0.50 = 0.30$$

Why this matters for the portfolio. All pairwise correlations in the portfolio are determined by $n$ betas rather than by $n(n-1)/2$ separate parameters. That reduction is the entire practical appeal of the single factor model, and it is why the Basel IRB formula can be written in closed form.

Note the ordering. Asset return correlation of 0.30 is much larger than the default correlation it implies, which for typical default probabilities is a fraction of a per cent. The two are routinely confused; asset correlation is the model input, default correlation is the output.

a.reason: $0.60 \times 0.50 = 0.30$, and beta is both the factor loading and the correlation with the market factor.

b.reason: 0.55 is the arithmetic average of the two betas. Correlations transmitted through a common factor multiply, they do not average; averaging would imply a pair correlation higher than either firm's correlation with the factor itself, which is impossible.

c.reason: The correlation is right but the definition of beta is inverted. Beta squared is the systematic share of variance; the idiosyncratic and diversifiable share is 1 minus beta squared.

d.reason: 0.548 is $\sqrt{0.60 \times 0.50} = \sqrt{0.30}$. Taking the square root of the product is a correlation misuse: the square root appears in the homogeneous portfolio simplification $UL_C = UL \times \sqrt{\rho}$, and has been imported into the wrong formula.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the trap that separates recall from understanding: the arithmetic is correct and only the definition of beta is flipped, so a candidate who computes first and reads second will accept it. Option (d) is a correlation misuse importing a square root from a different result in the same syllabus. The structural check on option (b): a pair correlation transmitted through a common factor must be no larger than either firm's own correlation with that factor, so 0.55 is impossible when one beta is 0.50.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define beta and calculate the asset return correlation of any pair of firms using the single factor model; estimate the probability of a joint default of any pair of credits and the default correlation between any pair of credits using the single factor model
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question:
Two firms are modelled with the single factor structure $a_i = \beta_i m + \sqrt{1-\beta_i^2}\,\varepsilon_i$. Both have an unconditional default probability of 2.0% and a beta of 0.40 with respect to the common factor. A firm defaults when its asset return falls below its threshold $k_i$.

Which of the following correctly describes the steps required to estimate the joint default probability of the pair?

options.text: Set $k = N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054$ for both firms, then evaluate the bivariate standard normal cumulative distribution at $(k, k)$ with correlation equal to $\beta_1\beta_2 = 0.16$.
Set $k = N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054$ for both firms, then evaluate the bivariate standard normal cumulative distribution at $(k, k)$ with correlation equal to $\beta_1 + \beta_2 = 0.80$.
Multiply the two unconditional default probabilities to obtain 0.04%, since the single factor model assumes conditional independence between firms.
Set $k = N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054$, then evaluate the univariate standard normal at $k$ divided by $\sqrt{1-0.16}$, since the idiosyncratic component determines joint default.

questions.solution:
Joint default under the single factor model is a bivariate normal probability evaluated at the two default thresholds, with the asset return correlation equal to the product of the betas.

Step 1. Recover the default threshold from the unconditional default probability. Asset returns are standard normal, so the threshold is the inverse normal at the default probability:

$$\pi_i = P(a_i < k_i) = N(k_i) \rightarrow k_i = N^{-1}(\pi_i), \quad k = N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054 \text{ for both firms}$$

Step 2. Establish the asset return correlation. The pair correlation is the product of the betas:

$$\rho^{assets} = \beta_1\beta_2 = 0.40 \times 0.40 = 0.16$$

Step 3. Joint default is a bivariate normal probability. Both firms default when both asset returns fall below their thresholds:

$$\pi_{12} = P(a_1 < k, a_2 < k) = \Phi_2(k, k; \rho^{assets}) = \Phi_2(-2.054, -2.054; 0.16)$$

This evaluates to approximately 0.092%, against an independence benchmark of $2\% \times 2\% = 0.04\%$. An asset correlation of 0.16 therefore raises joint default by a factor of roughly 2.3.

Why conditional independence does not mean unconditional independence. Option (c) exploits a real property of the model. Firms are independent conditional on a given realisation of $m$, because their $\varepsilon$ terms are independent. But $m$ itself is random, and integrating over its distribution reintroduces dependence. Conditional independence is the computational device that makes the model tractable; it is not a claim that firms default independently.

The resulting default correlation.

$$\rho^{default} = \frac{0.00092 - 0.0004}{\sqrt{0.02 \times 0.98 \times 0.02 \times 0.98}} \approx 0.026$$

Note the ordering: asset correlation 0.16, default correlation about 0.026. Default correlation is always much smaller, because default requires crossing a far tail threshold.

a.reason: Thresholds from the inverse normal, correlation as the product of betas, and a bivariate normal evaluation at the two thresholds.

b.reason: Adding the betas instead of multiplying them. A correlation of 0.80 would exceed either firm's own correlation with the factor, which is impossible for dependence transmitted through that factor. A correlation misuse.

c.reason: Applies conditional independence unconditionally. Firms are independent only for a fixed realisation of the market factor; averaging across realisations of $m$ produces positive dependence. This option would set the joint probability to the independence benchmark and eliminate the entire point of the model.

d.reason: Uses a univariate rather than a bivariate distribution, so it cannot describe a joint event at all, and it attributes joint default to the idiosyncratic component. Idiosyncratic shocks are independent across firms and can never generate joint default; the systematic component is the sole source of dependence.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the most instructive distractor because its stated reason is a genuine and important property of the model. The scope error lies in applying conditional independence where unconditional dependence is required. Option (d) is a role misassignment between the systematic and idiosyncratic components: it names the term that cannot possibly cause co-movement. Option (b) is caught by the same structural check as elsewhere: a factor-transmitted pair correlation cannot exceed either individual loading.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model
questions.reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
questions.question:
In the single factor Gaussian copula model, the cumulative default probability conditional on the market factor $m$ is given by the expression below. A single firm has a beta of 0.60 and a default threshold $k$ of $-1.645$, so that its unconditional default probability is 5.0%.

If the economy enters a downturn such that the market factor $m$ takes the value $-1.41$, what is the conditional default probability?

$$p(m) = N\left[\frac{k - \beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$$
questions.solution:
Conditioning a firm's default probability on an adverse realisation of the systematic factor, which is the core computation of the one-factor Gaussian copula.

The structure. The firm defaults when $a = \beta m + \sqrt{1-\beta^2}\,\varepsilon$ falls below $k$. Conditional on a known $m$, only $\varepsilon$ remains random, so:

$$p(m) = P\left(\varepsilon < \frac{k-\beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right) = N\left[\frac{k-\beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$$

Step 1. Confirm the threshold. The unconditional default probability is 5.0%, so $k = N^{-1}(0.05) = -1.645$. This is consistent with the stem.

Step 2. Numerator.

$$k - \beta m = -1.645 - (0.60 \times -1.41) = -1.645 + 0.846 = -0.799$$

Step 3. Denominator.

$$\sqrt{1-0.60^2} = \sqrt{1-0.36} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.80$$

Step 4. Evaluate.

$$p(m) = N\left(\frac{-0.799}{0.80}\right) = N(-0.999) = 15.90\%$$

Interpretation. A one-and-a-half standard deviation downturn in the systematic factor triples the firm's default probability, from 5.0% unconditional to 15.9% conditional. That amplification is the entire content of the model: it is how a single common factor generates default clustering without any direct linkage between firms.

The direction to fix. The market factor enters with a negative sign in the numerator, so a fall in $m$ raises the conditional default probability. Set $m = 0$ and the expression returns $N(k) = 5.0\%$, the unconditional value, which is the check to run whenever the sign is in doubt.

Where this leads. Setting $m$ to an extreme quantile such as $N^{-1}(0.001)$ gives the worst case default rate that underpins the Basel IRB capital formula.

a.reason: 7.83% is approximately $N(-1.415)$, which is what results from using $\beta^2 = 0.36$ in place of $\beta$ in the numerator: $(-1.645 + 0.36 \times 1.41)/0.80 = -1.42$. This understates the downturn effect.

b.reason: 10.67% is close to $N(-1.245)$, consistent with dividing the numerator by 0.64 rather than by 0.80, that is, using the variance where the standard deviation is required.

d.reason: 22.75% is approximately $N(-0.75)$. It overstates the downturn effect and follows from no correct step. Omitting the denominator entirely gives $N(-0.799) = 21.2\%$, and a wrong sign on the market factor term gives $N(-3.11) \approx 0.09\%$.

trap.explanation: Two mechanical traps dominate. The first is variance versus standard deviation in the denominator, which produces option (b): the scaling is $\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 0.80$, not $1-\beta^2 = 0.64$. The second is the sign of the market factor: $m$ enters negatively, so an adverse (negative) $m$ increases default probability. The $m = 0$ check recovers the unconditional 5.0% and settles both questions in seconds.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question:
A risk manager is assessing the impact of default correlation on two credit portfolios. Portfolio A consists of uncorrelated bonds and Portfolio B consists of highly correlated bonds. Both have the same number of positions, the same individual default probabilities and the same total notional.

Which portfolio has the higher level of risk?

options.text: Portfolio A, because uncorrelated bonds carry less diversification benefit than highly correlated bonds.
Portfolio B, because highly correlated bonds produce a wider loss distribution than uncorrelated bonds.
Both portfolios have the same level of risk, because default correlation does not affect portfolio expected loss.
It is impossible to determine without knowing the recovery rates and the confidence level.

questions.solution:
Correlation is the primary determinant of the dispersion of portfolio credit losses, so the correlated portfolio carries greater unexpected loss and credit VaR for identical expected loss.

Both portfolios have identical expected loss, since expectation is linear and unaffected by dependence. They differ entirely in the dispersion around that mean.

$$E[\text{loss}_A] = E[\text{loss}_B] = n \times \pi \times EAD \times LGD$$

$$\sigma^2[\text{loss}] \text{ increases with every pairwise } \rho_{ij}$$

Portfolio A, uncorrelated. Defaults arrive independently, so the realised default rate clusters tightly around $\pi$. The law of large numbers applies and unexpected loss shrinks as the number of positions grows.

Portfolio B, highly correlated. Positions fail together or survive together. Most years produce few losses and occasional years produce catastrophic ones. The distribution is far more dispersed, so credit VaR and required economic capital are much larger.

Why this makes correlation estimation the central problem. Two portfolios that look identical on every observable asset-level metric can require dramatically different capital. Yet default correlation is the hardest parameter to estimate: joint defaults are rarer than single defaults, so the data is sparse, and credits are illiquid, so correlation cannot be read from market prices. The parameter that matters most is the one estimated least reliably.

a.reason: Reverses the logic entirely. Uncorrelated bonds carry more diversification benefit, not less, which is precisely why Portfolio A is the safer of the two.

b.reason: Portfolio B, because high correlation widens the loss distribution.

c.reason: The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. Correlation leaves expected loss unchanged but is the dominant driver of the tail, which is what determines credit VaR and capital.

d.reason: Recovery rates and confidence level affect the magnitude of the difference but not its direction. The ranking is unambiguous for any recovery assumption and any confidence level above the point at which either portfolio shows a loss.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the sharpest, because its stated reason is correct: correlation genuinely does not affect expected loss. The scope error is treating expected loss as though it were the whole of risk. Option (a) is a polarity flip on the meaning of diversification. Option (d) is the false-humility trap, declining to answer a question whose direction is fully determined.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models
questions.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
questions.question: A quantitative analyst is documenting the two families of model used to generate default correlation for a credit portfolio. Which of the following correctly distinguishes them?

options.text: Structural models derive correlated defaults from correlated firm asset values crossing default thresholds, whereas reduced form models treat default as an unpredictable event whose intensity is correlated across firms through common risk factors.
Structural models treat default as an unpredictable jump governed by a hazard rate, whereas reduced form models derive default from the firm's balance sheet by comparing asset value with liabilities.
Structural models are calibrated exclusively to CDS spreads, whereas reduced form models are calibrated exclusively to accounting statements.
Structural models cannot generate default correlation at all, since each firm's asset value is modelled independently; only reduced form models can produce correlated defaults.

questions.solution:
Structural models explain default through the capital structure and generate correlation through correlated asset values; reduced form models treat default as an exogenous intensity and generate correlation through common factors driving that intensity.

The two families answer different questions about why a firm defaults, and each generates correlation by a different route.

| Feature | Structural | Reduced form |
|---|---|---|
| Cause of default | Endogenous: asset value falls below the liability threshold | Exogenous: an unpredictable jump with intensity $\lambda$ |
| Source of correlation | Correlated asset values, typically through common factors | Correlated default intensities, through common risk factors |
| Typical calibration | Equity price and equity volatility | CDS and bond credit spreads |
| Examples | Merton, Moody's KMV, the single factor model | Jarrow-Turnbull, Duffie-Singleton, hazard rate models |
| Short horizon default probability | Implausibly low, since assets move continuously | Realistic, since default can arrive at any instant |

Structural models. Default is endogenous and predictable in principle: it occurs when asset value falls below the value of liabilities. Merton and Moody's KMV are the canonical examples. Correlation arises naturally, because asset values are correlated through common economic factors. The single factor model is a structural construction: correlated asset returns crossing thresholds.

Reduced form models. Default is exogenous and unpredictable: it arrives as the first jump of a point process with intensity $\lambda$, and the model does not ask why. Correlation is introduced by making the intensities depend on common observable factors, or by correlating the jump processes directly. Jarrow and Turnbull and Duffie and Singleton are the standard references.

The practical trade. Structural models offer economic interpretation and can be applied to any firm with observable equity, but they are hard to calibrate to market spreads and predict implausibly low short-horizon default probabilities, since asset value cannot jump. Reduced form models calibrate cleanly to CDS and bond spreads and handle short horizons well, but they offer no explanation of default and their correlation structure is imposed rather than derived.

a.reason: Structural models use correlated asset values crossing thresholds; reduced form models use correlated intensities driven by common factors.

b.reason: The two descriptions are exactly transposed. The hazard rate jump description belongs to reduced form models and the balance sheet description to structural models.

c.reason: An absolute claim on both sides. Structural models are typically calibrated to equity prices rather than CDS spreads, and reduced form models to credit spreads rather than accounting statements. Neither calibration is exclusive.

d.reason: Structural models generate correlation precisely by correlating asset values. The single factor model in this set is a structural model whose entire purpose is to produce correlated defaults.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the role misassignment and the only serious distractor: both descriptions are individually accurate and only the labels are exchanged, which is the standard construction whenever two model families sit side by side. The mnemonic worth carrying: structural models look at the balance sheet and ask why; reduced form models look at the spread and do not ask. Option (c) signals itself through the word exclusively.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe Altman's Z-score methodology and apply it to predict a firm's default and to classify a sample of firms by credit quality
questions.reading: Altman's Z-Score Model for Corporate Default Prediction
questions.question: An analyst is applying Altman's original Z-score model to a publicly traded manufacturing firm. Which of the following correctly states the model's construction and interpretation?

options.text: $Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 1.0X_5$, where $X_4$ is the market value of equity divided by the book value of total liabilities, and a score above 2.99 places the firm in the safe zone.
$Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 1.0X_5$, where $X_4$ is the book value of equity divided by the market value of total liabilities, and a score below 2.99 places the firm in the safe zone.
$Z$ is a logistic function of five accounting ratios returning a value between 0 and 1, interpreted directly as the firm's probability of default.
$Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 1.0X_5$, where the largest coefficient attaches to sales divided by total assets, reflecting the dominance of asset turnover in predicting default.

questions.solution:
The five ratios of the Altman Z-score, their coefficients, the market-over-book construction of $X_4$, and the direction of the zone cut-offs.

The original model for public manufacturers is a linear discriminant function of five ratios.

$$Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 1.0X_5$$

| Ratio | Definition | Coefficient |
|---|---|---|
| $X_1$ | Working capital / total assets | 1.2 |
| $X_2$ | Retained earnings / total assets | 1.4 |
| $X_3$ | EBIT / total assets | 3.3, the largest |
| $X_4$ | Market value of equity / book value of total liabilities | 0.6 |
| $X_5$ | Sales / total assets | 1.0 |

Zone cut-offs.

$$Z > 2.99 \rightarrow \text{safe zone} \quad | \quad 1.81 \le Z \le 2.99 \rightarrow \text{grey zone} \quad | \quad Z < 1.81 \rightarrow \text{distress zone}$$

Two facts that generate the distractors. First, $X_4$ uses the market value of equity over the book value of liabilities, and it is the only ratio in the model containing a market input. Second, the largest coefficient is 3.3 on $X_3$, earnings before interest and taxes over total assets, so operating profitability is the strongest single discriminator, not turnover.

Why the output is not a probability. The Z-score is a discriminant score on an unbounded scale, unitless, and it cannot be mapped to a default probability or a credit rating without a separate calibration. That is the structural difference from logistic regression, whose link function constrains the output to $[0,1]$ and delivers a probability directly.

This is a closed-book recall item: the five ratios and both cut-offs belong on the formula sheet.

a.reason: The coefficients, the market-over-book construction of $X_4$, and the 2.99 safe-zone threshold are all as stated.

b.reason: Two polarity flips. $X_4$ is inverted, and the zone direction is reversed: a higher Z means safer, so above 2.99 is safe. The threshold reversal is the more damaging of the two, since it inverts every conclusion drawn from the model.

c.reason: Describes logistic regression, not linear discriminant analysis. The Z-score is an unbounded linear score, not a probability, and requires a cut-off to classify.

d.reason: The formula is reproduced correctly and only the interpretation is corrupted: the largest coefficient is 3.3 on $X_3$, not 1.0 on $X_5$.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the sharpest because it reproduces the equation faithfully and corrupts only the reading of it, so a candidate checking the coefficients will pass over the error. Option (b) is a double polarity flip; the direction of the cut-off is the half that matters, because reversing it converts every safe firm into a distressed one. Option (c) is the LDA versus logistic confusion, which recurs across the credit scoring material.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe Altman's Z-score methodology and apply it to predict a firm's default and to classify a sample of firms by credit quality
questions.reading: Altman's Z-Score Model for Corporate Default Prediction
questions.question:
Everina Grande Corp has been reviewed using both Altman's Z-score and an internal rating system developed by its primary bank. The financial ratios from recent statements are as follows.

- Working capital / total assets ($X_1$): 0.254
- Retained earnings / total assets ($X_2$): 0.448
- EBIT / total assets ($X_3$): 0.0896
- Market value of equity / total liabilities ($X_4$): 1.583
- Sales / total assets ($X_5$): 3.284
- The bank's internal system, which emphasises cash flow analysis and current market conditions, classified the company just above the threshold for being at risk of financial distress.

How does Altman's Z-score differ from the bank's internal rating system in assessing this company's credit quality?

options.text: Altman's Z-score suggests a low risk of default, while the bank's internal system indicates potential risk, highlighting the weight the internal system places on current cash flow and market conditions.
Both the Z-score and the internal system suggest a high risk of default, reflecting a consistent evaluation across different methods.
Altman's Z-score identifies the company as high risk, whereas the bank's internal system gives it a stable outlook.
Both methods indicate the company is unlikely to default soon, showing a consistent outcome despite different analytical focuses.

questions.solution:
Applying the Z-score to classify a firm, then reconciling a backward-looking accounting score with a forward-looking internal assessment.

Step 1. Compute the Z-score.

| Term | Calculation | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| $1.2 \times X_1$ | $1.2 \times 0.254$ | 0.3048 |
| $1.4 \times X_2$ | $1.4 \times 0.448$ | 0.6272 |
| $3.3 \times X_3$ | $3.3 \times 0.0896$ | 0.2957 |
| $0.6 \times X_4$ | $0.6 \times 1.583$ | 0.9498 |
| $1.0 \times X_5$ | $1.0 \times 3.284$ | 3.2840 |
| Z-score | | 5.46 |

$$Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 1.0X_5 = 0.3048 + 0.6272 + 0.2957 + 0.9498 + 3.2840 = 5.46$$

Step 2. Classify. $Z = 5.46$ sits well above the 2.99 safe-zone threshold, so the model classifies the firm as low default risk. Note that $X_5$ alone contributes 3.28 of the total, so the score is dominated by asset turnover.

Step 3. Reconcile. The bank places the firm just above the at-risk threshold, which is a marginal pass rather than a clean bill of health. The two assessments diverge.

Why they diverge, which is the examinable point. The Z-score is a static function of historical accounting ratios. The bank's system weights current cash flow and market conditions, which are forward looking and can deteriorate well before accounting ratios reflect it. A firm with strong historical turnover and accumulated retained earnings can still face near-term liquidity strain. This is the backward-looking limitation of empirical models appearing in a concrete case.

a.reason: $Z = 5.46$ signals low risk; the internal system flags potential risk; the divergence reflects the internal system's use of current cash flow and market conditions.

b.reason: A Z-score of 5.46 is far above the distress threshold of 1.81 and well above the safe threshold of 2.99. It does not indicate high default risk.

c.reason: Reverses both assessments. The Z-score says safe and the internal system flags concern, not the other way round.

d.reason: Only the Z-score indicates low risk. Just above the at-risk threshold is a caution, not an all-clear.

trap.explanation: Two routes to a wrong answer. A candidate who does not compute the score guesses on the qualitative framing and finds (d) plausible, since just above the threshold can be misread as comfortable. A candidate who computes but reverses the cut-off direction picks (c). The phrase just above the threshold for at risk is deliberately soft language for a firm that has barely cleared a warning line.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR [stated Numerical]
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: A workshop participant asks for a definition of credit VaR. How should the instructor define it?

options.text: The minimum potential profit due to credit enhancements that could be gained over a specified time period at a certain confidence level.
The expected average credit loss that a portfolio is anticipated to incur over an extended time frame, without reference to a confidence level.
The maximum potential credit loss that could be experienced over a specified time period at a certain confidence level, in excess of the expected loss.
The guaranteed credit loss that will occur, taking into account the entire term structure of credit ratings, without the need for a confidence interval.

questions.solution:
Credit VaR is a quantile of the credit loss distribution measured net of expected loss, so that it captures unexpected loss only. The learning objective carries two verbs, define and calculate, and is stated as Numerical; this question exercises only the definitional verb and requires no arithmetic, so its demand does not match the stated type. It is retained because the definition it tests, specifically that credit VaR is measured net of expected loss, is the foundation of every credit VaR calculation in this tier.

$$\text{Credit VaR} = \text{Credit loss at the chosen confidence level} - \text{Expected credit loss}$$

Three elements must be present and only option (c) has all three: it is a maximum rather than an average, it requires a confidence level and horizon, and it is measured net of expected loss.

The third element is the one most often omitted and the reason it matters: expected loss is a predictable cost covered by the loan spread and by provisions, so capital must absorb only the unexpected portion.

| Quantity | What it is | How it is funded |
|---|---|---|
| Expected credit loss | The mean of the credit loss distribution | Loan pricing and provisions |
| Credit VaR | Quantile of loss minus the mean | Economic capital |
| Quantile loss itself | Total loss at the confidence level | Provisions and capital together |

a.reason: Inverts the sign of the quantity, describing a minimum profit rather than a maximum loss, and imports credit enhancements, which belong to securitisation structures rather than to a general definition.

b.reason: Defines expected credit loss and explicitly disclaims the confidence level, which is the defining parameter of any VaR measure. A sibling swap between the mean and a quantile.

c.reason: Maximum potential credit loss at a confidence level over a horizon, in excess of expected loss.

d.reason: An absolute-claim trap. Nothing about a loss distribution is guaranteed, and removing the confidence interval removes the parameter that makes the measure meaningful.

trap.explanation: Option (b) swaps the mean for the quantile, the same confusion that separates expected from unexpected loss throughout the credit syllabus. Option (d) signals itself through the word guaranteed; absolute claims in this material are almost always the corruption.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus an SPV, and distinguish between the three main SPV structures [stated Qualitative]
questions.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
questions.question: Besides being used to securitise a firm's assets, a special purpose vehicle can also be used to:

options.text: Transform illiquid assets into liquid ones.
Issue credit-linked notes.
Convert the currency of the underlying assets into another currency more acceptable to investors.
All of the above.

questions.solution:
The range of functions an SPV performs beyond balance sheet removal: liquidity transformation, synthetic issuance, and currency transformation. The objective's action verbs are analyze differences and distinguish between three named structures; this question asks what other functions an SPV can perform, which is adjacent background rather than a comparison of trust against SPV or of the three structures against one another. It is retained because the synthetic issuance function it names is examinable elsewhere.

An SPV is a general-purpose isolation and repackaging vehicle, and all three functions are standard.

Liquidity transformation. Individual loans are illiquid. Pooled inside an SPV and refinanced with rated notes, they become tradable securities.

Credit-linked note issuance. The SPV issues notes whose redemption is linked to a reference entity's credit performance, investing the proceeds in collateral and entering a credit default swap with the arranger. This is the synthetic structure, in which credit risk moves and the assets do not.

Currency transformation. An SPV holding assets in one currency can issue notes in another, hedging the mismatch internally with a currency swap and widening the investor base.

a.reason: Incorrect as a complete answer. True, but only one of three correct functions.

b.reason: True, and the basis of synthetic securitisation, but incomplete as a complete answer.

c.reason: True, and standard in cross-border deals, but incomplete as a complete answer.

d.reason: All three are recognised uses of a special purpose vehicle.

trap.explanation: An all-of-the-above item whose failure mode is stopping at the first individually correct option. Option (a) is the most familiar function and the most likely stopping point. Option (b) is the one most often missed, because a candidate who conceives of securitisation as moving assets off a balance sheet does not immediately recognise the synthetic case, in which no assets move at all.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define the hazard rate and use it to define probability functions for default time as well as to calculate conditional and unconditional default probabilities
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question:
Suppose the hazard rate, also called the default intensity and denoted $\lambda$, is constant and equal to 0.090.

In this case, each of the following is true EXCEPT which one is false?

options.text: The unconditional one-year default probability is approximately 8.6%.
The two-year cumulative default probability is approximately 16.5%.
The probability of the joint event of survival through the first year and default in the second year is approximately 7.9%.
The conditional one-year default probability, given survival through the first year, is approximately 17.3%.

questions.solution:
The memoryless property of a constant hazard rate: the conditional default probability over the next year is the same regardless of how long the obligor has already survived.

**Solution**

With a constant hazard rate, the survival and cumulative default functions are exponential.

Survival to time $t$: $S(t) = e^{-\lambda t}$

Cumulative default by time $t$: $F(t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$

**Check (a).** $F(1) = 1 - e^{-0.09} = 1 - 0.91393 = 8.607\%$ — true

**Check (b).** $F(2) = 1 - e^{-0.18} = 1 - 0.83527 = 16.473\%$ — true

**Check (c).** Survive year 1 and default in year 2: $S(1) - S(2) = 0.91393 - 0.83527 = 7.866\%$ — true

**Check (d).** Condition on survival through year 1 by dividing by $S(1)$: $[S(1) - S(2)] \div S(1) = 0.07866 \div 0.91393 = 8.607\%$, not 17.3% — false

The result worth internalising: the conditional one-year default probability equals the unconditional first-year default probability, both 8.607%. This is the memoryless property of the exponential distribution: with a constant hazard rate, surviving a year tells you nothing about the year ahead. Algebraically:

$$[e^{-\lambda t} - e^{-\lambda (t+1)}] \div e^{-\lambda t} = 1 - e^{-\lambda}, \text{ independent of } t$$

a.reason: Incorrect, the statement is true. $1 - e^{-0.09} = 8.607\%$.

b.reason: Incorrect, the statement is true. $1 - e^{-0.18} = 16.473\%$. Note it is less than twice the one-year figure, because cumulative default probabilities compound rather than add.

c.reason: Incorrect, the statement is true. $S(1) - S(2) = 7.866\%$, the marginal default probability for year 2 viewed from today.

d.reason: Correct answer, because the statement is false. The conditional one-year default probability given survival is 8.607%, equal to the unconditional first-year probability. The stated 17.3% is roughly double the correct value.

trap.explanation: 17.3% is close to 2 x 8.607% = 17.2%, so the distractor is built from doubling, the instinctive move for a candidate who thinks conditioning on survival should raise the figure materially. It also sits close to the two-year cumulative of 16.5%, so it can be reached by confusing conditional with cumulative default probability, two sibling concepts that are easy to swap. Both routes fail on the same principle: with a constant hazard rate the conditional probability is flat over time.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define the hazard rate and use it to define probability functions for default time as well as to calculate conditional and unconditional default probabilities
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question: A municipal bond analyst observes that in recent years there have been about 6.0 US municipal defaults per year. Making the simplifying assumption that 6.0 defaults per year is the average of a Poisson process, what is the probability that the next municipal default occurs within one month?
questions.solution:
The link between a Poisson arrival process and the exponential distribution of waiting time to the next event.

**Solution**

If events arrive as a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$, the waiting time to the next event is exponentially distributed with the same parameter. The cumulative distribution function of that waiting time is the familiar cumulative default probability:

$$P(T \le t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$$

**Step 1.** Set the parameters consistently. $\lambda = 6.0$ per year and $t =$ one month $= 1/12$ year. Either scale $\lambda$ to a monthly rate or express $t$ in years; do not do both.

$$\lambda t = 6.0 \times (1/12) = 0.50$$

**Step 2.** Apply the CDF.

$$P(T \le 1/12) = 1 - e^{-0.50} = 1 - 0.60653 = 39.35\%$$

**Sanity check.** With six defaults expected per year, half a default is expected in an average month, so a probability near 40% that at least one arrives is the right order of magnitude. A figure below 10% would be inconsistent with the stated frequency.

a.reason: 8.42% equals $1 - e^{-0.088}$, a mis-scaled exponent that corresponds to no consistent time conversion. For reference, converting to a monthly basis twice gives $\lambda t = 6/144 = 0.042$ and $1 - e^{-0.042} = 4.08\%$. The exponent must be exactly $6.0 \times 1/12 = 0.50$.

b.reason: 17.00% is approximately $1 - e^{-0.186}$, again a mis-scaled exponent rather than a coherent alternative horizon (a two-month horizon would give $1 - e^{-1.0} = 63.2\%$). Only $\lambda t = 0.50$ is consistent with six defaults per year over one month.

c.reason: Correct. 39.35%.

d.reason: 60.65% is $e^{-0.50}$ itself, that is, the survival probability, the probability that no default occurs within the month. Reporting the complement is the single most common error on exponential default questions.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the complement trap, and it is dangerous because 60.65% is a fully correct quantity answering the opposite question: it is a polarity flip between the probability of default and the probability of survival. Read whether the stem asks for default or survival. Options (a) and (b) come from mis-scaled exponents, the other recurring failure mode: the exponent must be lambda multiplied by time in consistent units, and applying a monthly conversion twice shrinks the exponent by a factor of twelve.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a rating migration matrix and calculate the probability of default, cumulative probability of default, and marginal probability of default
questions.reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
questions.question:
You are a risk analyst at Smith Incorporated, which holds a bond rated Caa by Moody's. Using the average cumulative default rate table below, calculate the probability that the bond will default during the fourth year, conditional on no earlier default.

| Rating | 1 yr | 2 yr | 3 yr | 4 yr | 5 yr | 7 yr | 10 yr |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aaa | 0.000 | 0.013 | 0.013 | 0.037 | 0.106 | 0.247 | 0.503 |
| Aa | 0.022 | 0.069 | 0.139 | 0.256 | 0.383 | 0.621 | 0.922 |
| A | 0.063 | 0.203 | 0.414 | 0.625 | 0.870 | 1.441 | 2.480 |
| Baa | 0.177 | 0.495 | 0.894 | 1.369 | 1.877 | 2.927 | 4.740 |
| Ba | 1.112 | 3.083 | 5.424 | 7.934 | 10.189 | 14.117 | 19.708 |
| B | 4.051 | 9.608 | 15.216 | 20.134 | 24.613 | 32.747 | 41.947 |
| Caa-C | 16.448 | 27.867 | 36.908 | 44.128 | 50.366 | 58.302 | 69.483 |

*Average cumulative default rates in per cent, 1970 to 2012, from Moody's.* Your calculation is closest to:
questions.solution:
Converting cumulative default rates into a marginal default probability, then into a conditional default probability by dividing by the survival probability.

**Solution**

Three quantities must be kept distinct. Read the Caa-C row.

**Step 1. Marginal (unconditional) default probability in year 4.** This is the increment in the cumulative rate, measured from the start:

$$\text{Marginal } PD_4 = \text{Cumulative}_4 - \text{Cumulative}_3 = 44.128\% - 36.908\% = 7.220\%$$

This is the probability, viewed today, that the bond survives three years and then defaults in the fourth.

**Step 2. Survival probability to the end of year 3.**

$$S_3 = 1 - \text{Cumulative}_3 = 1 - 0.36908 = 0.63092$$

**Step 3. Conditional default probability in year 4.** Condition on having survived, by dividing the marginal probability by the survival probability:

$$\text{Conditional } PD_4 = \text{Marginal } PD_4 \div S_3 = 7.220\% \div 0.63092 = 11.44\%$$

The three quantities side by side:

| Quantity | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Cumulative PD to year 4 | Default at any time in the first four years | 44.128% |
| Marginal PD in year 4 | Survive three years, then default in year four, viewed from today | 7.220% |
| Conditional PD in year 4 | Default in year four given survival to end of year three | 11.44% |

The conditional figure is always the largest, because the denominator is less than one. The intuition: among the 63% of Caa bonds still alive after three years, about one in nine defaults during year four.

a.reason: 69.94% is the ratio $44.128 / 63.092$, that is, the year-4 cumulative rate divided by the survival probability. It conditions the wrong numerator, using cumulative rather than marginal default.

b.reason: 19.51% is approximately $44.128 - 27.867 = 16.26$ divided by the wrong survival figure, or a similar two-year offset error. It arises from reading the cumulative table one column out of position.

c.reason: 63.092% is the survival probability to the end of year three, that is, the denominator of the calculation reported as the answer. A pure intermediate-result trap.

d.reason: Correct. 11.44%.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the intermediate result and the most common miss under time pressure, because 1 minus 36.908 is an easy first move and the number looks substantial enough to be an answer. Option (a) is the subtler error: it applies the correct conditioning step to the wrong numerator (cumulative instead of marginal), producing a figure that is internally coherent but answers a different question. Note also the distinction between marginal (7.220%, unconditional, viewed from today) and conditional (11.44%, given survival); this pair is tested constantly and the wording carrying the discrimination is 'conditional on no earlier default'.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a rating migration matrix and calculate the probability of default, cumulative probability of default, and marginal probability of default
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question:
A credit analyst is working from the following one-year rating migration matrix for a simplified three-state system. Migrations are independent from year to year, so the matrix satisfies the Markov property. Default is an absorbing state.

| From \\ To | A | B | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0.90 | 0.09 | 0.01 |
| B | 0.05 | 0.85 | 0.10 |
| Default | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.00 |

For a credit currently rated A, which of the following correctly gives the two-year cumulative default probability and the marginal default probability in year two?

options.text: Cumulative 2.80%; marginal 1.80%
Cumulative 2.00%; marginal 1.00%
Cumulative 1.80%; marginal 2.80%
Cumulative 2.80%; marginal 2.80%

questions.solution:
Building multi-period default probabilities from a migration matrix by enumerating paths, and separating the cumulative measure from the marginal increment.

**Solution**

**Step 1.** Enumerate the paths to default within two years, starting from A. Default is absorbing, so each path terminates at the first default.

| Path | Calculation | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| A $\to$ D in year 1 | 0.01 | 1.00% |
| A $\to$ A $\to$ D | $0.90 \times 0.01$ | 0.90% |
| A $\to$ B $\to$ D | $0.09 \times 0.10$ | 0.90% |

$$\text{Cumulative PD(2 years)} = 1.00\% + 0.90\% + 0.90\% = 2.80\%$$

Equivalently, square the matrix and read the A-to-default entry:

$$P(A \to D \text{ over 2 years}) = P(A\to A)P(A\to D) + P(A\to B)P(B\to D) + P(A\to D)\times 1$$
$$= (0.90 \times 0.01) + (0.09 \times 0.10) + (0.01 \times 1.00) = 0.0090 + 0.0090 + 0.0100 = 0.0280$$

**Step 2.** Marginal default probability in year two. This is the increment in the cumulative measure, that is, the probability of surviving year one and then defaulting in year two, viewed from today:

$$\text{Marginal PD(year 2)} = \text{Cumulative PD(2)} - \text{Cumulative PD(1)} = 2.80\% - 1.00\% = 1.80\%$$

**Why cumulative is not simply twice the one-year figure.** The naive answer of 2.00% ignores migration: a credit that survives year one may have been downgraded to B, from which the default probability is ten times higher. That migration channel contributes $0.09 \times 0.10 = 0.90\%$, which is as large as the stay-in-A channel. Migration risk is therefore not a second-order effect.

a.reason: Correct. Cumulative 2.80% and marginal 1.80%. The three default paths contribute 1.00% + 0.90% + 0.90% = 2.80%, and the year-two increment is 2.80% - 1.00%.

b.reason: 2.00% is $2 \times 1.00\%$, the naive doubling of the one-year default probability. It ignores the migration path through B entirely (worth 0.90%) and also overstates the stay-in-A path (0.90%, not 1.00%), so it falls 0.80% short of the correct 2.80%. The marginal figure of 1.00% follows from the same error.

c.reason: The two figures are transposed. 1.80% is the marginal and 2.80% the cumulative, not the reverse. A role misassignment between the two measures.

d.reason: Reports the cumulative figure twice. The marginal probability must be smaller than the cumulative, since the cumulative includes year one as well as year two.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the dropped path error: doubling the one-year default probability treats the credit as though it could not migrate, which discards the channel that contributes about a third of the two-year risk (0.90% of 2.80%). Option (c) is a straight role misassignment between cumulative and marginal. The structural check that catches both: cumulative must exceed marginal, and cumulative must exceed twice the one-year figure whenever downgrade is possible, because downgraded credits default more often.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a rating migration matrix and calculate the probability of default, cumulative probability of default, and marginal probability of default
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question: An instructor is discussing how to extend a one-year credit rating transition matrix to estimate risk over different timeframes. Which method appropriately projects the transition probabilities for a two-year period?

options.text: Computing the geometric mean of the one-year transition probabilities.
Applying exponential smoothing to one-year transition data together with historical two-year transition trends.
Squaring the one-year transition matrix to estimate the two-year transition matrix.
Updating the one-year transition matrix with recent default and recovery rates before applying it to the second year.

questions.solution:
Under the Markov assumption, multi-period transition probabilities are obtained by matrix multiplication, so the n-period matrix is the one-period matrix raised to the power n.

**Solution**

**The Markov property.** The standard assumption is that the probability of migrating over the next year depends only on the current rating, not on the path that led there. Under that assumption transitions compose by matrix multiplication:

$$T(2\text{ years}) = T(1\text{ year}) \times T(1\text{ year}) = T^2$$
$$T(n\text{ years}) = T^n$$

**Why matrix multiplication and not scalar arithmetic.** Reaching rating C in two years from rating A requires summing over every possible intermediate state:

$$P(A \to C \text{ over 2 years}) = \sum_B P(A \to B) \times P(B \to C)$$

That summation over intermediate paths is exactly what the row-by-column product of matrix multiplication performs. Averaging individual cell probabilities discards the paths entirely.

**The cumulative default probability.** The two-year cumulative default probability for an A-rated issuer is the A-to-default entry of $T$ squared, which correctly counts the path A stays A then defaults, plus the path A migrates to B then defaults, and so on. It is not twice the one-year figure, and it is not $1$ minus $(1$ minus $PD)$ squared, because those shortcuts ignore migration.

**The caveat worth knowing.** The Markov assumption is an approximation. Empirically ratings display momentum: an issuer recently downgraded is more likely to be downgraded again than a stable issuer of the same rating. Matrix powers therefore understate multi-year migration risk somewhat.

a.reason: A geometric mean averages values along a single dimension and produces a number, not a matrix. It cannot capture migration through intermediate ratings, which is the entire content of a multi-period transition.

b.reason: Exponential smoothing is a time series estimation technique used to weight recent observations more heavily when estimating the one-year matrix in the first place. It is not a method for projecting one horizon onto another. A sibling swap between estimation and extrapolation.

c.reason: Correct. Squaring the one-year matrix gives the two-year matrix under the Markov assumption.

d.reason: Updating the matrix with recent data improves the inputs but does nothing to extend the horizon. Applying an updated one-year matrix to the second year still requires the multiplication step that this option omits.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (d) both fail on the same point: they operate on the matrix's contents without performing the composition that moves from one horizon to two. The mechanical check is to ask what object the method produces; a two-year transition matrix must itself be a matrix of the same dimensions, which immediately rules out an averaging operation. Option (b) is a genuine technique (exponential smoothing) misapplied to a different job (horizon extrapolation), a sibling swap between two related but distinct statistical techniques, which is the hardest kind of distractor to reject without knowing what each technique is for.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe CDS spreads and explain how CDS spreads can be used to estimate hazard rates
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question:
Analysts at GlobalTech Corp are evaluating the firm's credit risk using market spreads. The following data is available.
