questions.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled
questions.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
questions.question: When modelling extreme credit losses using the beta distribution, which technique is typically employed to complement it, so as to obtain a more accurate representation of the tail of the credit loss distribution?

options.text: Logistic regression, to better estimate the correlation between defaults and recoveries.
Extreme value theory, to focus specifically on the tail behaviour of credit loss distributions.
Monte Carlo simulation, to account for a wider range of potential outcomes.
The Poisson distribution, given its suitability for modelling rare events.

questions.solution:
The analytical beta solution is combined with a numerical procedure, specifically Monte Carlo simulation, to fit the tail.

The chapter states the pairing explicitly: the tail fitting exercise is best accomplished by combining the analytical solution (the beta distribution) with a numerical procedure, namely Monte Carlo simulation.

**Why the combination is needed.** The beta is fitted from two moments, $EL_P$ and $UL_P$, which calibrates the body of the distribution. Economic capital is read from the 99.9% region and beyond, where a two moment analytic fit has no mechanism to reproduce extreme joint default behaviour. Monte Carlo populates that region empirically by generating many thousands of correlated default scenarios, capturing co-movement that the closed form smooths over.

$$\text{Beta distribution (analytical backbone, fitted from } EL_P \text{ and } UL_P\text{)} + \text{Monte Carlo simulation (numerical tail)} \rightarrow \text{economic capital}$$

**An important caution about option (b).** Extreme value theory is a legitimate and widely used tail modelling technique in practice, and Schroeck's own footnote acknowledges that EVT related distributions such as Cauchy, Gumbel and Pareto are among the alternatives for finding an analytic solution. But the technique named as the complement to the beta distribution for tail fitting is Monte Carlo simulation. Where general practice and the assigned reading diverge, answer the reading.

a.reason: Logistic regression is a classification technique used to estimate the probability of a binary event, which is how credit scoring models predict default. It is an input to PD estimation, not a method for shaping a loss distribution's tail. The option gains plausibility by referencing the genuine default-recovery correlation phenomenon.

b.reason: Extreme value theory is the general practice answer for tail modelling and is therefore the distractor that punishes knowledge rather than ignorance. In this reading the named complement to the beta distribution is Monte Carlo simulation.

c.reason: Monte Carlo simulation, the numerical procedure that complements the analytical beta solution.

d.reason: The Poisson distribution models the number of rare events and is the backbone of the CreditRisk+ framework. It addresses default counts, not the severity distribution's tail, and it would replace the beta rather than complement it.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the defining trap of this item. A weak candidate selects (c) by recognition; a strong candidate may select (b) because EVT is what tails genuinely call for in general practice. The rule to internalise: when a distractor is true in general practice but a different technique is named in the source reading, the reading wins.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk
questions.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
questions.question: Schroeck illustrates the bottom up approach to quantifying economic capital for credit risk, but cautions that despite its elegance and simplicity a number of caveats need to be addressed. According to Schroeck, each of the following is a problem with the quantification of credit risk EXCEPT which one?

options.text: The approach assumes that credits are illiquid assets.
The approach provides no way to aggregate economic capital across the major risk types of credit, market and operational risk.
In practice, to avoid undue complexity, internal credit risk models tend to use only a one year estimation horizon rather than a multi period horizon.

While the approach considers default correlation within the same risk type, it assumes that market and operational risk components are separated and are measured and managed in different departments within the bank.

questions.solution:
The three stated caveats of the bottom up approach, and the fact that aggregation across risk types is a strength of economic capital rather than a limitation.

The reading lists exactly three caveats, and options (a), (c) and (d) reproduce them.

| Stated caveat | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Credits are assumed to be illiquid | Measures only internal risk contributions, not correlation with risk factors as priced in liquid markets; a value based approach would be more suitable as loans become tradable |
| A one year estimation horizon is used | The multi period nature of credit and the correlated migration of credit quality are ignored, because precise numerical multi period solutions become very complex |
| Only within-risk-type correlation is considered | Market and operational risk are assumed separated and managed in different departments during measurement |

**Why option (b) is not a stated problem.** Economic capital is in fact well suited to aggregation across credit, market and operational risk. Expressing every risk type in a common currency amount at a common confidence level is one of the principal advantages of the economic capital framework over the regulatory approach, and Schroeck develops the aggregation method later in the same work.

**The fine distinction between (b) and (d).** These two options are deliberately close. Option (d) is a caveat about measurement practice: the bottom up credit calculation treats other risk types as separately measured and managed, so it does not itself perform the aggregation. Option (b) makes the much stronger claim that economic capital offers no way to aggregate at all, which is false. The corruption is an absolute claim built on top of a true observation about scope.

a.reason: Incorrect, this is a stated caveat. The illiquidity assumption means the model captures only internal betas to the existing credit portfolio, not market priced correlations.

b.reason: Correct answer, because this is NOT a stated problem. Economic capital is well suited to aggregation across risk types; this is presented as an advantage of the framework, not a caveat.

c.reason: Incorrect, this is a stated caveat. Almost all internal credit risk models use a one year horizon, which omits multi period credit quality migration.

d.reason: Incorrect, this is a stated caveat. The approach considers correlations only within the credit risk type and assumes other risk types are handled elsewhere.

trap.explanation: The discrimination is entirely between (b) and (d), and it rests on the difference between an absolute claim (no way to aggregate) and a scope statement (aggregation is not performed within this calculation). Absolute claims are disproportionately the wrong answer. A candidate who correctly recognises (d) as a genuine caveat may then reject (b) as a duplicate rather than identifying it as the false statement, which is precisely the reaction the item is engineered to produce.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the CAMEL system used for evaluating the financial condition of a bank
questions.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
questions.question:
Maple Consultants made the following observations on Marble Bank using the CAMEL system:

- Marble Bank maintains a capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio of 15%, well above the regulatory minimum of 10%.
- A significant portion of the loan portfolio is in long-term fixed-rate mortgages, which have started to show an increase in delinquencies over the past year.
- The management team has recently been restructured with several new appointments from within the banking sector, though their effectiveness in implementing strategy remains to be seen.
- Despite a challenging economic environment, the bank has reported a consistent increase in net income over the past three years.
- The bank's liquidity coverage ratio is below the required 100%.

Each option below combines two elements of the CAMEL evaluation. All of the following accurately reflect the bank's financial condition EXCEPT which one?

options.text: Capital adequacy is strong; management changes are recent but promising.
Asset quality is becoming a concern due to rising mortgage delinquencies; earnings have been consistently strong.
Liquidity is below regulatory requirements and asset quality shows signs of deterioration.
Management has been effective in strategy implementation; liquidity coverage ratios meet the required standards.

questions.solution:
Reading a bank's condition across all five CAMEL components and separating what the evidence supports from what it does not.

CAMEL assesses five dimensions. Map each observation to its component before evaluating any option.

| Component | Observation | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Capital adequacy | CRAR 15% versus 10% minimum | Strong |
| Asset quality | Rising delinquencies in long-term fixed-rate mortgages | Deteriorating |
| Management | Recently restructured; effectiveness not yet demonstrated | Uncertain, not yet proven |
| Earnings | Consistent net income growth over three years | Strong |
| Liquidity | LCR below the required 100% | Below requirement |

Option (d) fails twice. On M, the stem says effectiveness remains to be seen; the option asserts that management has already been effective. On L, the stem says LCR is below 100%; the option asserts the standard is met. The second clause is a direct contradiction of stated fact, which is what makes this the answer rather than merely the weakest option.

The examinable habit: in a five-bullet CAMEL vignette, tag each bullet with its letter and a plus or minus sign before reading the options. Marble Bank is C+, A-, M neutral, E+, L-.

a.reason: Incorrect, the statement is accurate. CRAR of 15% against a 10% minimum is strong, and describing recent management changes as promising but unproven matches the stem.

b.reason: Incorrect, the statement is accurate. Rising mortgage delinquencies are an asset quality concern and three years of rising net income is strong earnings.

c.reason: Incorrect, the statement is accurate. Both clauses restate the stem directly.

d.reason: Correct answer, because the statement is inaccurate. It converts management's unproven effectiveness into demonstrated effectiveness, and it reverses the liquidity finding.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the near miss: a candidate who reads promising as an overstatement may pick it. The discrimination is that promising is consistent with unproven, whereas has been effective is not. Option (d) also demonstrates the standard corruption pattern of pairing one soft overstatement with one hard factual reversal, so that a reader who checks only the first clause may pass over it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk: PD, LGD, EAD, expected loss, time horizon
questions.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
questions.question:
A junior credit risk analyst includes the following five statements in a credit risk assessment report. The credit risk manager reviews them.

1. The probability of default for a loan is identical to its hazard rate, directly indicating the instantaneous rate at which borrowers default per year, regardless of the loan's term or the time already elapsed without default.
2. LGD measures the total amount of credit extended to a borrower that is likely to be recovered immediately after a default event, indicating a direct recovery rate without considering the collateral's value or sale costs.
3. EAD is the minimum amount a lender is guaranteed to recover when a borrower defaults, fixed at the initiation of the loan and unaffected by changes in credit line usage or market conditions.
4. Expected loss is calculated solely on the historical default rate of similar loans and is a static measure that remains unchanged throughout the life of a loan.
5. The time horizon for assessing credit risk is set to a standard one-year period for all types of loans and facilities, regardless of loan term or borrower risk profile.

Which of the statements are incorrect?

options.text: 1 and 2 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 4 and 5 only
All of them

questions.solution:
Precise definitions of the five quantitative credit risk inputs, and the specific way each is commonly misstated.

Every one of the five statements contains at least one definitional error.

| Statement | The specific error | Correct position |
|---|---|---|
| 1. PD equals the hazard rate | Conflates a probability with an intensity, and denies conditioning | The hazard rate is an instantaneous conditional intensity; PD over horizon $T$ is $1 - e^{-\lambda T}$. PD depends on term and on survival so far |
| 2. LGD is what is recovered | Reverses the quantity and ignores costs | LGD is the fraction not recovered, that is, $1 - \text{recovery}$, and is measured net of collateral value and realisation costs |
| 3. EAD is a guaranteed minimum recovery | Confuses exposure with recovery, and freezes it at origination | EAD is the expected exposure at the moment of default, and it varies with drawdown on committed lines and with market conditions |
| 4. EL is static and historical only | Denies forward-looking recalibration | EL is recomputed as PD, EAD and LGD are updated; it is not a fixed historical average |
| 5. One year applies to everything | States a convention as a rule | One year is the common convention, following the annual review cycle, but the horizon should reflect the facility and the risk profile |

The unifying error across all five is the imposition of rigidity where the framework is conditional: PD depends on horizon and elapsed time, LGD depends on collateral and workout costs, EAD depends on facility usage, EL is recalculated as inputs move, and the horizon is a convention that can be varied.

$$EL = PD \times EAD \times LGD, \text{ with every input a function of horizon and current conditions}$$

a.reason: Statements 1 and 2 are indeed wrong, but so are 3, 4 and 5.

b.reason: Omits statements 2 and 5, both of which are wrong.

c.reason: Omits statements 1 and 3, both of which are wrong.

d.reason: Correct. All five statements are incorrect.

trap.explanation: All-of-the-above is psychologically hard to select, because a candidate who confidently identifies three errors tends to assume the remaining two must be the true ones by construction. Statement 5 is the most seductive, because the one-year horizon genuinely is standard practice; the error is the word regardless, which converts a convention into a universal rule. Statement 1 is the second trap: PD and the hazard rate are closely related but are a probability and an intensity respectively, and treating them as the same quantity is the classic twin-input confusion.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the judgmental approaches, empirical models, and financial models to predict default
questions.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
questions.question:
After an audit raised concerns about credit risk assessment at Mancus Lending Group, a UK real estate lender serving borrowers from individual homeowners to major developers, a board meeting was called to select a new credit risk model. Three board members proposed different alternatives.

- Moe: We cannot overlook the human element. Our judgment is nuanced and capable of catching what models might miss, especially in the real estate sector.
- Larry: Historical data is key. With CreditMetrics we have a systematic way to estimate defaults, applying a robust value-at-risk framework that is proven effective.
- Curly: But consider the Merton model's precision. It uses market data to assess the risk, bringing a level of financial insight that traditional methods cannot.

Which statement or statements accurately represent the approaches being discussed?

options.text: Moe's judgmental approach only
Larry's CreditMetrics approach only
Curly's Merton model approach only
All of them

questions.solution:
The three families of default prediction and what each legitimately claims: judgmental, empirical, and financial (market-based) models.

Each speaker describes his approach accurately. The three map onto the chapter's taxonomy.

| Family | Basis | Example | Principal strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| Judgmental | Expert analyst assessment | Internal credit committee review | Captures qualitative factors and unusual situations |
| Empirical / statistical | Historical data and statistical estimation | Altman Z-score, logistic regression, CreditMetrics | Systematic, replicable, testable |
| Financial / market-based | Option pricing theory applied to the capital structure | Merton, Moody's KMV | Uses forward-looking market information |

Moe is right that judgmental assessment captures qualitative and situational factors that no dataset encodes, which matters in a heterogeneous real estate book.

Larry is right that CreditMetrics is data-driven, works through rating transitions, and produces a portfolio loss distribution within a value-at-risk framework.

Curly is right that the Merton model draws on market data, specifically equity price and equity volatility, rather than on accounting history, and so reflects information as it arrives.

The item tests whether the candidate can recognise correct descriptions rather than rank the approaches. None of the three claims is overstated: note that no speaker claims his method is best or free of limitations.

a.reason: Moe's characterisation is accurate, but so are the other two. Selecting this alone is a scope error.

b.reason: Larry's characterisation of CreditMetrics as historical-data-driven within a VaR framework is accurate, but incomplete as the full answer.

c.reason: Curly's characterisation of Merton as market-data-based is accurate, but incomplete as the full answer.

d.reason: Correct. All three descriptions are accurate representations of their respective approaches.

trap.explanation: The item exploits the instinct to rank rather than to verify. A candidate who believes market-based models are superior selects (c); one who distrusts models selects (a). The stem asks only which descriptions are accurate. Read the verb: represent, not recommend. A useful secondary check is that none of the three statements contains an absolute claim, which is unusual and signals that all may stand.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the judgmental approaches, empirical models, and financial models to predict default
questions.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
questions.question: Which of the following statements is most likely true about linear discriminant analysis?

options.text: The analysis produces a non-linear scoring function.
Variables are selected from a large set of accounting ratios, qualitative features and judgments, with little regard to their statistical significance.
The score produced by the function must lie between 0 and 1.

When a good discriminant function has been estimated using historical data on performing and defaulted borrowers, any new borrower can be assigned to a predefined group based on the score the function produces.

questions.solution:
What linear discriminant analysis does: estimate a linear combination of variables that separates known groups, then classify new observations by score.

LDA fits a linear function of explanatory variables that maximises separation between two known groups, typically performing and defaulted borrowers:

$$Z = w_1 X_1 + w_2 X_2 + \ldots + w_n X_n$$

Once the weights are estimated on a historical sample containing both groups, the function is applied to a new borrower and the resulting score is compared with a cut-off to assign membership. That classification step is exactly what option (d) describes, and it is the purpose of the technique.

The canonical application is Altman's Z-score, which is an LDA function of five accounting ratios.

**Two properties worth fixing, because they generate the distractors.** The output is a score on an unbounded real line, not a probability, so it does not lie in $[0, 1]$ and cannot be read directly as a default probability. And variables are chosen precisely for their statistical discriminating power, not without regard to it.

a.reason: The clue is in the name. LDA produces a linear scoring function. Non-linear alternatives exist, such as logistic regression and quadratic discriminant analysis, but they are different techniques.

b.reason: Variable selection in LDA is driven by statistical discriminating power. The phrase with little regard to statistical significance describes a purely judgmental approach.

c.reason: The Z-score is unbounded and unitless; it is not a probability. This is the sharpest distractor because it confuses LDA with logistic regression, whose output is constrained to $[0, 1]$ by the logit link.

d.reason: A well-estimated discriminant function classifies new borrowers into predefined groups by their score.

trap.explanation: Option (c) catches candidates who blur the two workhorse classification techniques. Say the contrast out loud: LDA gives an unbounded score requiring a cut-off; logistic regression gives a probability in $[0, 1]$ directly. This matters beyond definitions, because it is why an Altman Z-score cannot be mapped to a default probability without a separate calibration step.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare agencies' ratings to internal credit rating systems
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question: Considering the internal ratings-based approach used by banks to assess the creditworthiness of companies, especially those without external agency ratings, which of the following best describes an advantage of internal rating systems over agency ratings?

options.text: Internal ratings can provide a more detailed evaluation of a company's ability to service its debt through specific financial metrics and cash flow analysis.
Agency ratings offer more consistent results because they are applied uniformly across industries and geographic regions.
Internal ratings are generally more accessible to the public and provide a broader understanding of a company's financial health.
Agency ratings are quicker to update and reflect recent market changes more efficiently than internal systems.

questions.solution:
What internal rating systems add over agency ratings: coverage of unrated obligors and borrower-specific depth, at the cost of comparability and transparency.

The two systems differ on four dimensions, and only one of them favours internal ratings unambiguously.

| Dimension | Agency ratings | Internal ratings |
|---|---|---|
| Coverage | Only rated issuers | All obligors, including unrated private firms |
| Depth of analysis | Standardised methodology from public disclosure | Full borrower relationship data, cash flow and facility detail |
| Comparability | High, uniform across industries and regions | Low, specific to the institution |
| Transparency | Public | Internal and proprietary |
| Stability | Deliberately stable, rated through the cycle | Varies by design; can be point-in-time |

**Why depth is the genuine advantage.** A bank sees its borrower's full cash flow profile, account behaviour, covenant compliance and facility structure. An agency works from public disclosure and a standardised methodology designed for comparability across thousands of issuers. Internal systems also cover the large population of obligors that carry no agency rating at all, which is the practical reason IRB exists.

**The costs, which the wrong options invert.** Internal ratings are not public, are not comparable across institutions, and require supervisory validation precisely because they are opaque to outsiders.

a.reason: Internal systems can incorporate borrower-specific financial metrics and cash flow analysis in a depth that a standardised agency methodology does not reach.

b.reason: The statement is true, but it is an advantage of agency ratings, not of internal systems. The question asks for the advantage of internal ratings over agency ratings.

c.reason: Factually reversed. Internal ratings are proprietary and not public; agency ratings are published.

d.reason: Also an agency-side claim, and doubtful in itself. Agencies deliberately rate through the cycle and avoid frequent changes, so they are typically slower to reflect market news than market-based measures.

trap.explanation: Options (b) and (d) are both agency advantages presented in a question that asks for internal advantages, which is a direction error rather than a content error. A candidate who reads the options without re-checking the question's direction can find (b) entirely defensible, because uniformity across industries genuinely is an agency strength. Option (c) reverses a plain fact about transparency.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question: A credit analyst is explaining how a bank's internal rating grades map onto default probabilities. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Default probability rises non-linearly across the rating scale, so that each step down represents a progressively larger absolute increase in PD; a rating is therefore an ordinal ranking that must be calibrated to a PD before it can be used in pricing or capital.
Default probability rises linearly across the rating scale, so that the PD difference between AAA and AA equals the difference between B and CCC, which is what makes rating grades comparable.
A rating grade is itself a probability of default expressed on a letter scale, so no separate calibration is required before it can be used in a capital calculation.
Default probability is unrelated to the rating grade over short horizons, because ratings are assigned through the cycle and therefore describe long-run average behaviour only.

questions.solution:
Ratings are ordinal grades whose associated default probabilities increase geometrically rather than arithmetically, so a separate calibration step is required to convert a grade into a usable PD.

**The empirical shape.** One-year default rates by grade rise steeply and non-linearly.

| Grade | Indicative one-year PD | Multiple of the grade above |
|---|---|---|
| AAA | 0.01% | - |
| AA | 0.02% | 2x |
| A | 0.06% | 3x |
| BBB | 0.17% | 3x |
| BB | 1.1% | 6x |
| B | 4.1% | 4x |
| CCC | 16.4% | 4x |

Each notch down multiplies rather than adds. The step from A to BBB adds roughly 0.11 percentage points; the step from B to CCC adds more than eleven. A rating scale is therefore ordinal: it ranks borrowers reliably but the intervals between grades are not equal.

**Why calibration is required.** Capital formulas, pricing and expected loss all need a cardinal number:

$$EL = PD \times EAD \times LGD, \text{ which requires PD as a number, not a letter}$$

The bank must therefore map each internal grade to a long-run average default rate, estimated from its own default history or from external benchmarks, and validate that mapping periodically.

**The through-the-cycle caveat that option (d) exaggerates.** A through-the-cycle rating does describe long-run behaviour and is deliberately insensitive to the current point in the cycle. But that does not sever the relationship between grade and PD; it means the mapped PD is a cycle-average rather than a current estimate. Realised default rates in any single year will sit above or below the mapping depending on conditions.

a.reason: The relationship is non-linear, and a rating must be calibrated to a PD before it can be used quantitatively.

b.reason: Default probabilities rise geometrically, not linearly. Equal intervals across the scale would imply the AAA to AA step carries the same risk increase as the B to CCC step, which understates speculative-grade risk by orders of magnitude.

c.reason: A rating is an ordinal grade, not a probability. Treating a letter as a number skips the calibration step and would leave the capital formula with no numeric PD input.

d.reason: Overstates the through-the-cycle point into a denial of the relationship. TTC ratings map to cycle-average default probabilities, which remain informative in every year; realised rates vary around the mapping rather than being unrelated to it.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the linearity trap and is the most consequential error in practice, because it makes a speculative-grade portfolio look far safer than it is. Option (d) is a scope error that takes a genuine property of TTC ratings and inflates it into independence. The anchor: ratings rank, PDs measure, and the gap between adjacent grades widens as quality falls.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify drawbacks in using the correlation-based credit portfolio framework
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question: A model validation team is documenting the limitations of the correlation-based credit portfolio framework used to compute the bank's credit VaR. Which of the following correctly identifies its principal drawbacks?

options.text: Default correlations are very difficult to estimate because joint defaults are rare and credits are illiquid; the Gaussian copula understates tail dependence, so simultaneous extreme defaults are less likely under the model than in reality; and results are highly sensitive to a parameter that cannot be observed.

Default correlations are readily observable from equity markets, so the framework's weakness is computational cost rather than parameter uncertainty; the Gaussian copula overstates tail dependence and therefore produces conservative capital numbers.
The framework's principal drawback is that it cannot accommodate portfolios with more than a few hundred exposures, since the correlation matrix grows factorially with the number of names.

The framework has no material drawbacks for portfolios of investment-grade credits, since default correlations for high-quality names are close to zero and the resulting loss distribution is approximately normal.

questions.solution:
The correlation framework is fragile precisely where it matters most: the parameter driving the tail is unobservable, sparsely estimated, and modelled with a copula that understates joint extreme outcomes.

**Three connected drawbacks.**

| Drawback | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Estimation difficulty | Joint defaults are rare and credits illiquid, so correlation is inferred from proxies rather than observed |
| Understated tail dependence | The Gaussian copula assigns near independence to extreme joint outcomes, which contradicts observed default clustering |
| Extreme output sensitivity | Small changes in an unobservable parameter move credit VaR and tranche values materially |

**Estimation.** Default correlation is inferred rather than observed. Defaults are rare, joint defaults rarer still, and credits are illiquid so no market price reveals the dependence. Asset correlations are typically proxied from equity index correlations, which imports a different dependence structure.

**Tail dependence.** The Gaussian copula has zero tail dependence: as outcomes become more extreme, the probability of two names failing together approaches independence. Empirically defaults cluster far more in crises than that implies, which is the specific technical failure exposed in 2007 and 2008.

**Sensitivity.** Senior tranche values and portfolio credit VaR are acutely sensitive to correlation. A small change in an unobservable input moves the output materially, so the model's precision is illusory.

**Why the matrix size point in option (c) is wrong.** The number of distinct pairwise correlations is:

$$n(n - 1) / 2, \text{ which is quadratic, not factorial}$$

For 500 names that is 124,750 pairs, which is burdensome but tractable, and factor models reduce it to $n$ loadings anyway.

a.reason: Estimation difficulty, understated tail dependence, and extreme sensitivity to an unobservable parameter.

b.reason: Two polarity flips. Correlations are not readily observable, and the Gaussian copula understates rather than overstates tail dependence, so the framework is optimistic rather than conservative in the tail.

c.reason: The pair count is quadratic, $n(n-1)/2$, not factorial, and factor models reduce the parameterisation to one loading per name. Portfolio size is a computational inconvenience, not the framework's principal weakness.

d.reason: An absolute claim, and the most dangerous statement in the set. Investment-grade correlations are low but not zero, credit loss distributions are never approximately normal because they are bounded below and skewed, and it is precisely senior, high-quality exposures whose valuation is most sensitive to the correlation assumption.

trap.explanation: Option (b) reverses the direction of the copula's failure, which matters because it converts a source of understated risk into a source of conservatism. Option (d) is the absolute claim that produced the senior tranche mispricing of the last credit crisis: low individual default probabilities combined with an assumption of near-zero correlation made AAA tranches appear almost riskless.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe how Credit VaR can be calculated using a simulation of joint defaults; describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question: A quantitative analyst is documenting the steps required to compute portfolio credit VaR by simulating joint defaults under a single factor model. Which of the following correctly describes the procedure?

options.text: Convert each name's default probability into a threshold using the inverse normal; on each path draw one common factor and an idiosyncratic shock per name, combine them into an asset return, record a default where the return falls below the threshold, aggregate losses across names, and read the required quantile of the resulting loss distribution net of expected loss.

Draw an independent standard normal for each name on each path, record a default where it falls below the name's default probability expressed as a percentage, and take the average loss across paths as the credit VaR.
Simulate each name's default time from its own hazard rate independently, then apply the portfolio correlation as a multiplier to the resulting loss distribution before reading the quantile.
Compute each name's standalone credit VaR analytically and sum them, since credit VaR is additive across exposures within a portfolio.

questions.solution:
Joint default simulation generates correlated latent asset returns from a common factor, converts them into defaults through name-specific thresholds, and reads credit VaR as a quantile of the resulting loss distribution less expected loss.

**The procedure.**

| Step | Operation |
|---|---|
| 1 | Set each name's default threshold as $k_i = N^{-1}(PD_i)$ |
| 2 | Draw one common factor $m$ for the path, plus an idiosyncratic shock for each name |
| 3 | Form each name's latent asset return from the factor loading and the idiosyncratic term |
| 4 | Record a default where the asset return falls below that name's threshold |
| 5 | Aggregate losses across names, applying exposure and loss given default |
| 6 | Repeat over many paths, then read the required quantile less expected loss |

**The two mechanics that make it work.** The threshold is the inverse normal of the default probability, so the marginal default probability is exactly right for every name:

$$k_i = N^{-1}(PD_i), \text{ so } P(a_i < k_i) = PD_i$$

And the shared factor $m$ creates the dependence, since every name loads on the same draw:

$$a_i = \beta_i m + \sqrt{1 - \beta_i^2}\, \epsilon_i, \text{ giving pair correlation } \beta_i \beta_j$$

**Why the common factor is essential.** Without it, defaults are independent, the law of large numbers flattens the loss distribution, and credit VaR collapses toward zero for a granular portfolio. The factor is what produces the bad years in which many names fail together, and those years are the entire content of the tail.

**The final subtraction.**

$$\text{Credit VaR} = \text{quantile of portfolio loss} - \text{expected portfolio loss}$$

a.reason: Thresholds from the inverse normal, a common factor plus idiosyncratic shocks, aggregation, and a quantile net of expected loss.

b.reason: Independent draws produce no default correlation, which removes the tail the exercise exists to measure. Comparing a standard normal draw directly against a default probability expressed as a percentage is also a unit error, since the comparison must be against the inverse normal threshold. And taking the average loss gives expected loss, not a quantile.

c.reason: Correlation cannot be applied as a multiplier after the fact. It must enter inside the simulation, because it changes the shape of the loss distribution rather than scaling it. Simulating independently and then adjusting produces a distribution with the wrong tail.

d.reason: Credit VaR is sub-additive for a diversified portfolio, so summing standalone figures overstates portfolio risk and would eliminate any diversification benefit. It also requires no simulation, which contradicts the premise of the question.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the subtle one: it accepts that correlation matters and then applies it in the wrong place. Correlation must be generated, not applied. Option (b) contains three separate errors and is worth reading carefully as a catalogue: no dependence, a unit mismatch at the threshold, and a mean reported where a quantile was required.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation
questions.reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about the modelling of default correlation in CreditMetrics and in Vasicek's model?

options.text: Vasicek's model calculates default correlation using multiple Gaussian copulas to reflect varying economic conditions across sectors.
CreditMetrics employs a single-factor model that simplifies the correlation of defaults to a common economic influence affecting all entities equally.
Vasicek's model uses a single systematic factor representing overall economic conditions to model default correlations, affecting all entities in the portfolio.
CreditMetrics uses sector-based risk adjustments in addition to a Gaussian copula for modelling default correlations specifically tied to individual industries.

questions.solution:
Vasicek's model reduces all dependence to one systematic factor with a common correlation, whereas CreditMetrics uses a full asset return correlation matrix derived from equity indices.

Both models use a Gaussian copula to link individual credit outcomes, but they differ fundamentally in how much structure they impose on the dependence.

| Feature | Vasicek | CreditMetrics |
|---|---|---|
| Dependence structure | One systematic factor, a single correlation parameter | Full asset return correlation matrix |
| Source of correlation | Assumed or regulatory prescribed | Equity index correlations by country and industry |
| Scope of credit events | Default only | Default and rating migration, mark to market |
| Solution method | Closed form, asymptotic | Monte Carlo simulation |
| Principal use | Basel IRB capital formula | Portfolio credit VaR |

**Vasicek's single factor.** Each obligor's latent asset return is driven by one common factor plus an idiosyncratic term:

$$a_i = \sqrt{\rho} \times m + \sqrt{1 - \rho} \times \epsilon_i$$

where $m$ is the single systematic factor common to all obligors and $\epsilon_i$ is idiosyncratic. All pairwise correlations collapse to the single parameter $\rho$. This drastic simplification is what makes the model analytically tractable and is why it underpins the Basel IRB capital formula: a formula requiring a full correlation matrix could not be written into regulation.

**CreditMetrics.** Estimates a full asset return correlation matrix, typically inferred from equity index correlations mapped to each obligor's country and industry. Dependence therefore varies pair by pair, at the cost of requiring simulation rather than a closed form.

**What they share.** Both map correlated normal draws through thresholds to produce correlated credit outcomes, which is the Gaussian copula construction.

a.reason: Vasicek's model is defined by having one factor, not multiple sector copulas. The option describes a multi-factor extension and attaches it to the wrong model.

b.reason: The single-factor description belongs to Vasicek, not CreditMetrics. A direct role misassignment between the two models, and the mirror image of the correct answer.

c.reason: Vasicek uses a single systematic factor representing overall economic conditions.

d.reason: CreditMetrics does use a Gaussian copula and does map obligors to country and industry indices, but describing this as sector-based risk adjustments in addition to the copula misstates the mechanism: the industry mapping is how the correlation matrix is estimated, not an adjustment layered on top.

trap.explanation: Options (b) and (c) are the two halves of one role misassignment, and the item is decided entirely by which model owns the single-factor description. Option (d) is subtler: every noun in it is real and associated with CreditMetrics, but the relationship between them is wrong. The memory hook: Vasicek is one factor and one correlation number because a regulator has to be able to write it down; CreditMetrics is a full matrix because a bank can simulate.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question:
A risk team is preparing training material on the interplay between recovery rates and default rates, following a rise in corporate bond defaults triggered by an economic downturn.

Which of the following best describes how recovery rates are typically influenced by default rates during economic downturns?

options.text: Recovery rates increase as default rates increase, because more defaults provide more data for improving recovery strategies.
Recovery rates decrease as default rates increase, due to market saturation with defaulted securities and reduced asset valuations.
Recovery rates are independent of default rates, being determined solely by the original credit rating of the bond issue.
Recovery rates and default rates are inversely proportional, due to the high liquidity of defaulting securities in economic downturns.

questions.solution:
The negative empirical relationship between recovery rates and default rates, and the supply and valuation mechanism that produces it.

Recovery rates and default rates are negatively correlated. Hull documents the relationship empirically: in years with high default rates, average recovery rates are markedly lower.

The mechanism has two parts, and both must be stated.

**Supply.** A downturn produces many simultaneous defaults, so a large volume of distressed assets reaches the market at once. Forced sellers meet a limited pool of distressed-debt buyers, and prices fall.

**Valuation.** The same macroeconomic conditions that trigger defaults also depress the value of the collateral and the going-concern value of the defaulted firms. Recovery is a claim on assets whose worth has fallen for the same underlying reason the borrower failed.

**Why this matters for loss estimation.** PD and LGD are not independent. Expected loss computed with a through-the-cycle average recovery rate understates downturn losses, because the high-default states are exactly the states where recovery is poorest. This is why regulators require downturn LGD for capital purposes rather than a long-run average.

$$\text{Downturn: PD rises AND LGD rises together, so expected loss rises more than proportionally}$$

a.reason: Polarity flip, with a superficially sensible justification. More default observations may improve future modelling but cannot raise contemporaneous recovery prices; the causation runs the other way.

b.reason: Recovery rates fall as default rates rise, driven by an oversupply of defaulted securities and by depressed asset valuations.

c.reason: Independence is precisely what the empirical evidence rejects, and assuming it is the modelling error that leads to understated downturn losses. Original credit rating influences the expected recovery but does not insulate realised recovery from the cycle.

d.reason: The direction is right but the reasoning is wrong, which is what disqualifies it. Defaulted securities in a downturn are illiquid, not highly liquid; illiquidity is part of why prices fall. The option also overstates the relationship as strictly inversely proportional, whereas it is a negative empirical correlation, not a fixed proportionality.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the trap for a candidate who selects on direction alone. It states the correct direction and then supplies a mechanism that is factually backwards, and adds an absolute-sounding proportionality claim. On a four-statement item where two options share a direction, the discrimination has moved to the reasoning, so read the justification clause with the same care as the claim. Option (c) is the modelling assumption that the reading exists to warn against.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define a credit default swap and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both parties
questions.reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
questions.question:
An investor has bought five-year credit default swap protection on a corporate reference entity with a notional of USD 10 million, at a spread of 200 basis points per annum paid quarterly. Two years into the contract the reference entity defaults. The cheapest-to-deliver obligation is trading at 35% of face value.

Which of the following statements about this transaction is correct?

options.text: Under cash settlement the protection seller pays USD 3.5 million, and the protection buyer's obligation to pay the spread continues to the original maturity.

Under physical settlement the protection buyer delivers bonds with a face value of USD 10 million and receives USD 10 million, and the buyer additionally pays the spread accrued since the last payment date.
Under either settlement method the protection buyer receives USD 3.5 million, because that is the market value of the deliverable obligation.
The protection seller's payoff is unaffected by the recovery rate, since the contract is written on the occurrence of a credit event rather than on the severity of loss.

questions.solution:
CDS mechanics: the obligations of protection buyer and seller, the two settlement methods, accrued premium at default, and the termination of premium payments.

**The two legs of a CDS.**

| Leg | Party | Obligation |
|---|---|---|
| Premium leg | Protection buyer | Pays the CDS spread periodically on the notional, until maturity or a credit event, whichever comes first, plus accrued premium at default |
| Protection leg | Protection seller | Pays notional $\times (1 - \text{recovery})$ on a credit event, either in cash or by buying the delivered bonds at par |

**Payoff size.** Both settlement methods deliver the same economic value:

$$\text{Payoff} = \text{notional} \times (1 - \text{recovery rate}) = 10{,}000{,}000 \times (1 - 0.35) = \text{USD } 6.5 \text{ million}$$

Under cash settlement the seller simply pays USD 6.5 million. Under physical settlement the buyer delivers bonds with a face value of USD 10 million, currently worth USD 3.5 million, and receives USD 10 million in cash, a net gain of USD 6.5 million. Identical.

**Two mechanics that generate the distractors.** First, the credit event terminates the contract, so premium payments stop; they do not run to the original maturity. Second, because default rarely falls on a payment date, the buyer owes the accrued premium from the last payment date to the credit event date.

a.reason: Two errors. The cash settlement payment is notional times $(1-R) = $ USD 6.5 million, not USD 3.5 million, which is the value of the bonds retained. And the credit event terminates the contract, so the spread does not continue to the original maturity.

b.reason: Physical settlement is exchange of the deliverable obligation at par, and accrued premium since the last payment date is payable.

c.reason: USD 3.5 million is the recovery value, that is, what the bonds are worth. Protection compensates for the portion not recovered, so the payoff is USD 6.5 million.

d.reason: A CDS is triggered by a credit event but the size of the payment depends directly on the recovery rate. If it did not, the contract would be a fixed-payout binary instrument, which standard CDS are not.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (c) both substitute the recovery value (USD 3.5 million) for the loss (USD 6.5 million), which is the same $1-R$ input-twin error that recurs in hazard rate calculations elsewhere in this syllabus. Option (d) is the trigger-versus-severity confusion: the credit event determines whether the seller pays, the recovery rate determines how much. Option (a) adds the continuation-of-premium error, which matters because the premium leg's early termination is precisely what a protection seller is compensated for bearing.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question:
Analysts are assessing credit risk in a portfolio of corporate bonds using the CDS-bond basis together with comparisons of default probabilities from historical data and from credit yield spreads.

- Tech Innovations' CDS spread is 300 basis points and its bond yield spread is 270 basis points, giving a CDS-bond basis of +30 basis points.
- Historical data shows an average seven-year cumulative default probability of 2.3% for a company of this credit quality.
- The credit spread on a five-year bond issued by Tech Innovations is 320 basis points, with an assumed recovery rate of 45%.

Which option accurately describes the analysis and provides the best assessment of Tech Innovations' credit risk?

options.text: The CDS-bond basis is positive, indicating lower default risk than bond yield spreads alone suggest; however the default probability from credit spreads is higher than historical averages, implying overvaluation of risk.

The positive basis suggests the market perceives a higher risk of default than bond yield spreads indicate, and the default probability from credit spreads is lower than historical data, indicating undervaluation of risk.

The positive basis may indicate inefficiencies or specific risks not captured by the bond market, and the default probability from credit spreads is higher than historical data, suggesting market participants expect worsening conditions.

The analysts incorrectly calculated the basis as positive when it should be negative, given the high CDS spread over the bond yield spread. The default probability from credit spreads aligns with historical data, indicating stable risk assessment.

questions.solution:
Definition and sign of the CDS-bond basis, and the systematic gap between spread-implied and historically estimated default probabilities.

**Part 1. The CDS-bond basis.**

$$\text{CDS-bond basis} = \text{CDS spread} - \text{bond yield spread} = 300 - 270 = +30 \text{ basis points}$$

The sign is confirmed: CDS exceeds bond spread, so the basis is positive. In theory the two should be close, because buying a bond and buying protection on it approximately replicates a risk-free position. A persistent non-zero basis therefore points to frictions rather than to a pure credit view: bonds trading away from par, cheapest-to-deliver optionality in the CDS, counterparty risk, funding costs, and differences in liquidity between the two markets.

**Part 2. Spread-implied against historical default probability.**

$$\lambda = s \div (1 - R) = 0.0320 \div (1 - 0.45) = 0.0320 \div 0.55 = 5.82\% \text{ per annum}$$

Compounded over seven years, the implied cumulative default probability is:

$$1 - e^{-0.0582 \times 7} = 1 - 0.6654 = 33.5\%$$

against a historical seven-year cumulative figure of 2.3%. The spread-implied probability is an order of magnitude larger, which is the normal and well documented relationship.

The stem compares a five-year spread with a seven-year historical figure, which is a horizon mismatch. The qualitative conclusion, implied far exceeds historical, is unaffected.

a.reason: The first clause reverses the meaning of a positive basis: a higher CDS spread indicates the protection market prices more risk, not less. The second clause is right about direction but mislabels a higher implied probability as overvaluation without justification.

b.reason: The first clause is defensible, but the second is factually wrong: the implied probability of roughly 33.5% is far higher than the historical 2.3%, not lower.

c.reason: A positive basis points to frictions or risks not reflected in the bond market, and the spread-implied default probability substantially exceeds the historical figure.

d.reason: The basis is correctly computed as positive; a CDS spread above the bond yield spread is by definition a positive basis. The second clause is also wrong, since the two probability estimates diverge by more than an order of magnitude.

trap.explanation: Option (d) attacks the arithmetic rather than the interpretation, which is attractive to a candidate unsure of the sign convention. Fix the convention: basis equals CDS minus bond spread, so a higher CDS spread means positive. Option (b) is the more dangerous distractor because its first half is correct and only the comparison direction in the second half is wrong, so a candidate who validates only the opening clause will accept it. On two-part options, both halves must hold.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap, total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation
questions.reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
questions.question: A risk analyst is preparing a briefing note on the principal categories of structured credit product. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A collateralised loan obligation is backed by a pool of corporate loans, a collateralised bond obligation by a pool of bonds, and a synthetic CDO obtains its credit exposure through credit default swaps rather than by purchasing the assets.
A synthetic CDO is backed by a pool of physical assets purchased by the SPV, whereas a cash CDO obtains its exposure through credit default swaps.
In a collateralised debt obligation, credit tranching and time tranching are the same mechanism, since both allocate losses in order of seniority.
A collateralised loan obligation differs from a collateralised bond obligation only in that the CLO issues a single tranche while the CBO issues multiple tranches.

questions.solution:
The taxonomy of structured credit products by collateral type and by whether exposure is obtained physically or synthetically.

Two independent classification axes are in play, and confusing them generates most of the errors here.

**Axis 1: what the collateral is.**

| Product | Collateral |
|---|---|
| Collateralised loan obligation (CLO) | A pool of corporate loans, typically leveraged loans |
| Collateralised bond obligation (CBO) | A pool of bonds |
| Collateralised mortgage obligation (CMO) | Mortgage pass-through securities, time tranched |
| Collateralised debt obligation (CDO) | The general category, covering loans, bonds or other debt |

**Axis 2: how the exposure is obtained.** A cash CDO buys the assets, funding the purchase by issuing notes. A synthetic CDO does not buy anything: the SPV sells protection through credit default swaps on a reference portfolio and invests the note proceeds in safe collateral. Credit risk is transferred without the assets moving, which is faster, cheaper and avoids the need for a true sale.

**The two tranching mechanisms, which option (c) conflates.** Credit tranching allocates losses in order of seniority, so the equity tranche absorbs the first losses. Time tranching allocates principal repayments in sequence, so one class is repaid before another begins. They are independent: a deal can have both, and time tranching redistributes prepayment risk rather than credit risk.

a.reason: CLO on loans, CBO on bonds, and synthetic CDOs obtain exposure through credit default swaps rather than purchase.

b.reason: The definitions of cash and synthetic are exactly reversed. A cash CDO buys the assets; a synthetic CDO takes exposure through derivatives.

c.reason: Credit tranching allocates losses by seniority; time tranching allocates principal repayments in sequence and addresses prepayment risk, not credit risk. Treating them as one mechanism is a sibling swap.

d.reason: Both CLOs and CBOs are multi-tranche structures. The difference between them is the collateral, loans versus bonds, not the number of tranches.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is a clean polarity flip on the cash versus synthetic definition, and it is the single most examined distinction in this area. Option (c) is the credit versus time tranching sibling swap, which is worth holding precisely because both are described as sequential and both appear in the same documents: credit tranching orders losses, time tranching orders principal.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify the default probabilities used to value a CDS; describe the valuation of a synthetic CDO
questions.reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
questions.question: A structurer is valuing a tranche of a synthetic collateralised debt obligation. Which of the following correctly describes the two valuation approaches and the role of the Gaussian copula?

options.text: The spread payments approach equates the present value of the premium leg received by the protection seller with the present value of the expected protection payments on the tranche, and the Gaussian copula is used to generate correlated default times across the reference portfolio so that the tranche loss distribution can be simulated.

The spread payments approach discounts the tranche's coupon at the risk-free rate and ignores default, while the Gaussian copula is used to calibrate the recovery rate assumption for each reference name.
The two approaches are alternatives that produce identical values by construction, since the copula is simply a numerical implementation of the spread payments identity.

The Gaussian copula generates independent default times for each reference name, and the spread payments approach then aggregates them, so that tranche value depends on the individual default probabilities but not on any correlation assumption.

questions.solution:
A synthetic CDO tranche is valued by equating premium and protection legs, and the loss distribution required for the protection leg is generated by simulating correlated default times through a Gaussian copula.

**The two legs.** A synthetic CDO tranche is economically a portfolio credit default swap. The investor sells protection on a slice of the reference portfolio.

$$PV(\text{premium leg}) = s \times \sum_t E[\text{outstanding tranche notional at } t] \times DF(t)$$
$$PV(\text{protection leg}) = \sum_t E[\text{tranche loss in period } t] \times DF(t)$$

The fair spread is the value of $s$ that equates the two.

**What the copula supplies.** The protection leg requires the distribution of portfolio losses, which depends entirely on how defaults cluster. The Gaussian copula generates that dependence.

| Step | Operation |
|---|---|
| 1 | Map each name's cumulative default probability to a default time through the marginal distribution |
| 2 | Draw correlated standard normals, typically through a single common factor plus idiosyncratic terms |
| 3 | Convert each correlated normal into a default time using the inverse of that name's marginal |
| 4 | Aggregate losses across names in each simulation path |
| 5 | Apply the tranche attachment and detachment points to obtain the tranche loss |
| 6 | Average across paths to obtain expected tranche loss, then discount |

**Why correlation is the pricing variable.** Tranche loss depends on where portfolio losses fall relative to the attachment and detachment points. Higher correlation fattens both tails, which harms the senior tranche and benefits the equity tranche. Correlation is therefore the single most important input, and it is the one that cannot be observed.

**Why option (d) is fatal.** Independent default times would make tranche value depend only on individual probabilities, which would remove the entire rationale for tranching. The copula exists to introduce dependence, not to avoid it.

a.reason: Premium leg equated to protection leg, with the Gaussian copula generating correlated default times to produce the tranche loss distribution.

b.reason: Ignoring default would value the tranche as a risk-free bond, which defeats the purpose. The copula generates correlated default times; it is not a recovery rate calibration device.

c.reason: They are not alternatives producing identical values by construction. The spread payments approach is the valuation identity; the copula is the method for populating the loss distribution that the identity requires. One is the equation, the other is the input.

d.reason: A fatal error. The copula's entire purpose is to introduce dependence. Independent default times would leave tranche value insensitive to correlation, which contradicts the observed sensitivity of senior and equity tranche prices to correlation assumptions.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the substantive trap and it inverts the copula's function, converting a dependence-generating device into an independence assumption. Option (c) is a scope error that confuses the valuation identity with the simulation method, treating a formula and its input as competing approaches. The sentence to hold: the spread payments approach is the equation; the copula supplies the loss distribution that equation needs.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the credit risks of derivatives
questions.reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
questions.question: A dealer is valuing a credit default swap on which it has bought protection, and must account for the credit risk of the protection seller. Which of the following correctly describes the adjustment?

options.text: The risk-free value of the swap is reduced by a CVA term reflecting the joint event that the protection seller defaults while the swap has positive value to the buyer, and the adjustment is larger the higher the correlation between the seller and the reference entity.

The risk-free value is reduced by a CVA term computed from the seller's default probability alone, since the correlation between the seller and the reference entity affects the timing of the loss but not its size.
No adjustment is required, because a credit default swap is collateralised by definition and the protection buyer's exposure is therefore always zero.

The risk-free value is increased by a DVA term reflecting the buyer's own default probability, and no adjustment is made for the seller, since the buyer bears no exposure to the seller once the premium has been paid.

questions.solution:
A purchased CDS carries counterparty exposure to the protection seller that is inherently wrong-way: the swap is most valuable precisely when credit conditions have deteriorated and the seller is least able to pay.

**The exposure being valued.** A purchased CDS has positive value to the buyer when the reference entity's credit has deteriorated. That is exactly when the buyer needs the seller to perform.

$$\text{Risky value} = \text{Risk-free value} - CVA$$
$$CVA = LGD_{seller} \times \sum_t EE(t) \times PD_{seller}(t) \times DF(t)$$

**Why correlation is central rather than incidental.** The standard CVA formula above assumes exposure and seller default are independent. For a CDS that assumption is untenable. Both the value of the protection and the seller's default probability are driven by the same credit cycle, so the correct quantity is expected exposure conditional on the seller defaulting, which exceeds unconditional expected exposure.

| Correlation between seller and reference entity | Value of the protection | CVA |
|---|---|---|
| Zero | Close to the risk-free value | Modest |
| Positive | Reduced | Larger |
| Approaching one | Approaching zero | Approaching the full risk-free value |

**The limiting case.** If the seller and the reference entity were perfectly correlated, the protection would be worthless: the seller would fail in every state in which the protection pays. Buying protection on a bank from that same bank is the extreme instance.

**The practical consequence.** Correlation must be modelled explicitly, typically through a copula linking the seller's default time to the reference entity's. Ignoring it materially understates CVA and overstates the value of the protection, which is why concentration in a small number of correlated protection sellers, as with the monolines, proved so damaging.

a.reason: The risk-free value is reduced by CVA, and the adjustment grows with the correlation between the protection seller and the reference entity.

b.reason: Correlation affects the size of the expected loss, not merely its timing, because the relevant quantity is exposure conditional on seller default. This is the wrong-way risk the whole adjustment is designed to capture.

c.reason: An absolute claim. Credit default swaps are not collateralised by definition, and even fully collateralised positions retain residual exposure through the threshold, the minimum transfer amount and the margin period of risk.

d.reason: Reverses the parties. The protection buyer is exposed to the seller for the life of the contract, not merely until the premium is paid, because the premium is paid periodically and the contingent payout lies in the future. DVA reflects the buyer's own default and does not remove the need for CVA.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the sharpest, because it correctly identifies CVA as the adjustment and then demotes correlation to a timing effect. That is a scope error at the precise point where CDS valuation differs from ordinary derivative valuation. Option (c) is the absolute claim, and option (d) is a role misassignment between buyer and seller exposure.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Summarize netting and close-out procedures (including multilateral netting), explain their advantages and disadvantages, and describe how they fit into the framework of the ISDA master agreement
questions.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
questions.question: A legal and risk working group is documenting how netting operates under an ISDA Master Agreement. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Payment netting reduces settlement risk by combining same-day, same-currency cash flows, while close-out netting reduces credit exposure on default by collapsing all transactions in the netting set to a single net amount; close-out netting depends on enforceability in the counterparty's jurisdiction, and multilateral netting across three or more parties generally requires a central counterparty.

Payment netting reduces credit exposure on default while close-out netting reduces settlement risk on a daily basis; both are automatically enforceable in every jurisdiction because they are contained in a standard-form agreement.
Close-out netting permits the non-defaulting party to enforce only those transactions that are favourable to it and to repudiate the rest, which is what produces the exposure reduction.
Multilateral netting is available bilaterally under any ISDA Master Agreement, since the agreement covers all transactions between the two parties and can be extended to third parties by notice.

questions.solution:
Payment netting addresses settlement risk and close-out netting addresses default exposure; both sit under the Master Agreement, and enforceability rather than drafting is the binding constraint.

**The two forms of netting.**

| | Payment netting | Close-out netting |
|---|---|---|
| Risk addressed | Settlement risk | Credit exposure on default |
| When it operates | Ongoing, on each payment date | On a default or termination event |
| Mechanism | Combines same-day, same-currency flows into one payment | Collapses all transactions in the netting set to one net amount |
| Key constraint | Operational systems | Legal enforceability in the relevant jurisdiction |

**Why close-out netting is the important one.** Without it, an insolvency administrator could cherry-pick: enforce contracts favourable to the estate and repudiate the rest. The non-defaulting party would owe on its out-of-the-money trades and rank as an unsecured creditor on its in-the-money ones.

$$\text{Without netting: exposure} = \sum_i \max(V_i, 0)$$
$$\text{With close-out netting: exposure} = \max\left(\sum_i V_i, 0\right)$$

Option (c) describes cherry-picking itself, which is what netting prevents and is the opposite of the protection it provides.

**The disadvantages.** Enforceability is jurisdiction dependent and must be supported by a legal opinion; netting sets can be fragmented across entities and product types, reducing the benefit; and netting concentrates the relationship, so a single close-out crystallises a large amount at once.

**Multilateral netting.** Bilateral agreements cannot net A's exposure to B against B's exposure to C. That requires a common counterparty to all parties, which is what novation to a CCP achieves.

a.reason: Payment netting for settlement risk, close-out netting for default exposure, enforceability as the binding constraint, and a CCP required for genuine multilateral netting.

b.reason: The two functions are transposed, and the enforceability claim is false. A standard-form agreement does not guarantee enforceability; netting opinions are obtained jurisdiction by jurisdiction precisely because it varies.

c.reason: This describes cherry-picking by an insolvency administrator, which is the risk close-out netting exists to eliminate. It has the protection exactly backwards.

d.reason: An ISDA Master Agreement is bilateral by construction and cannot be extended to third parties by notice. Multilateral netting requires a structure in which all participants face the same counterparty.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the most instructive wrong answer because it inverts the direction of the protection: it grants the non-defaulting party the very right that netting removes from the administrator. Option (b) is a role misassignment between the two netting types plus an absolute claim on enforceability, and the enforceability half is the one that costs real money when it fails.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Provide examples of trade compression of derivative positions, calculate net notional exposure amount, and identify the party holding the net contract position in a trade compression
questions.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
questions.question:
Three dealers hold the following interest rate swaps on identical terms, differing only in notional and direction. In each contract the first named party is the fixed rate payer.

| Contract | Fixed rate payer | Fixed rate receiver | Notional |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bank A | Bank B | USD 250 million |
| 2 | Bank B | Bank C | USD 180 million |
| 3 | Bank C | Bank A | USD 130 million |

Following a multilateral compression exercise, what is the total notional remaining and which party holds the net fixed-paying position?

options.text: USD 120 million, with Bank A paying fixed
USD 250 million, with Bank A paying fixed
USD 120 million, with Bank B paying fixed
USD 560 million, with no net position

questions.solution:
Compression replaces a set of offsetting contracts with a smaller set carrying the same net risk, so each party's net position is computed and the redundant gross notional is eliminated.

**Step 1. Compute each bank's net fixed-paying position.** Paying fixed is positive, receiving fixed is negative.

| Bank | Net fixed-paying position |
|---|---|
| Bank A | + USD 120 million (net payer: pays 250, receives 130) |
| Bank B | - USD 70 million (net receiver: receives 250, pays 180) |
| Bank C | - USD 50 million (net receiver: receives 180, pays 130) |

The three net positions sum to zero, as they must, since every contract has two sides.

**Step 2. Identify the surviving position.** Bank A is the only net fixed payer, on USD 120 million. Bank B is net receiving fixed on USD 70 million and Bank C on USD 50 million, so Bank A's position is split between them.

$$\text{Compressed structure} = \text{Bank A pays fixed to Bank B on USD 70 million and to Bank C on USD 50 million}$$

**Step 3. Notional reduction.**

$$\text{Gross notional before} = 250 + 180 + 130 = \text{USD 560 million}$$
$$\text{Notional after} = \text{USD 120 million, a reduction of 78.6\%}$$

**What compression achieves and what it does not.** Market risk is unchanged: every party's net exposure to rates is identical before and after. What falls is gross notional, and with it operational burden, settlement flows, leverage ratio exposure, and counterparty exposure where netting is imperfect. The circular chain A to B to C to A is what makes the reduction possible: USD 130 million of offsetting notional runs round the full loop and is eliminated from every leg.

a.reason: USD 120 million remaining, with Bank A the net fixed payer.

b.reason: USD 250 million is the largest single contract, retained as though compression simply removed the smaller trades. Compression nets across the whole chain rather than selecting the dominant contract.

c.reason: The notional is right but the direction is wrong. Bank B receives fixed on USD 250 million and pays on USD 180 million, so it is a net receiver of fixed on USD 70 million; Bank A is the only net fixed payer.

d.reason: USD 560 million is the gross notional before compression, and the claim of no net position is contradicted by Bank A's net long fixed-paying exposure of 120.

trap.explanation: The sign convention is the whole exercise: paying fixed in one contract and receiving fixed in another offset, and reversing the convention for a single contract flips the answer. Option (d) is the intermediate-result trap, reporting gross notional as though compression had not occurred. Option (c) is caught by noting that Bank B receives more fixed (250) than it pays (180), so it is a net receiver, not a payer.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of termination provisions and explain their advantages and disadvantages; identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction
questions.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
questions.question: A credit officer is reviewing the termination provisions in a proposed ISDA schedule. Which of the following correctly distinguishes events of default from termination events and identifies the risk that additional termination events create?

options.text: Events of default arise from a party's own failure, such as non-payment or bankruptcy, and generally allow the non-defaulting party to terminate all transactions; termination events are typically no-fault, such as illegality or a tax event, and may affect only the transactions concerned. Additional termination events tied to a rating downgrade create cliff risk, since they force close-out or collateral posting precisely when the counterparty is least able to fund it.

Events of default are no-fault occurrences such as illegality, while termination events arise from a party's own failure such as non-payment; additional termination events reduce risk unambiguously because they allow early exit before losses accumulate.

Both categories require fault on the part of one party, and the only difference is the length of the grace period; rating-linked triggers are prudent because a downgraded counterparty should always be closed out immediately.
Termination provisions are standardised and non-negotiable under the ISDA framework, so neither party can add triggers linked to credit quality.

questions.solution:
Events of default are fault-based and permit close-out of the whole netting set; termination events are typically no-fault and narrower; rating-linked additional termination events introduce cliff risk that can accelerate a counterparty's failure.

**The two categories.**

| | Events of default | Termination events |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Fault-based: failure to pay, bankruptcy, misrepresentation, cross-default | Typically no-fault: illegality, tax event, merger without assumption |
| Scope of close-out | All transactions in the netting set | Often only the affected transactions |
| Who may terminate | The non-defaulting party | May be either party, depending on the event |
| Negotiated additions | - | Additional termination events, frequently rating linked |

**The mechanics on close-out.** Following an event of default the non-defaulting party designates an early termination date, values all transactions in the netting set, applies close-out netting, and arrives at a single close-out amount owed one way or the other.

**The advantage of termination provisions.** They allow a party to exit before exposure grows further, which is the core credit protection the framework provides.

**The disadvantage, which is the examinable half.** Additional termination events linked to a credit rating create a cliff effect. On breach of the trigger the counterparty must post collateral or face close-out, and both demands arrive at the moment it is least able to meet them. The trigger therefore accelerates the distress it was designed to protect against, and does so simultaneously across all counterparties with the same trigger.

The illustration is AIG's downgrade in 2008, which triggered collateral calls across many agreements at once. The protection was individually rational and collectively destabilising, which is the standard criticism of ratings triggers.
