a.reason: Events of default are fault-based and allow full close-out; termination events are typically no-fault and narrower; rating-linked additional termination events create cliff risk.

b.reason: The two categories are transposed, and the claim that additional termination events reduce risk unambiguously ignores the cliff effect entirely. An early exit right is valuable only if it can be exercised without precipitating the failure it anticipates.

c.reason: Termination events are characteristically no-fault, so the claim that both require fault is wrong. The assertion that a downgraded counterparty should always be closed out immediately is an absolute claim that ignores both the cliff effect and the commercial value of the relationship.

d.reason: The ISDA Schedule exists precisely so that parties can negotiate amendments to the standard terms, and additional termination events linked to credit quality are among the most commonly negotiated provisions.

trap.explanation: Option (b) combines a role misassignment between the two categories with an absolute claim that early termination rights are unambiguously good. The cliff effect is the reason they are not: a trigger that fires across an entire market at once converts a downgrade into a funding crisis. Option (d) misstates the architecture by forgetting that the Schedule is the negotiated layer.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the rationale for collateral management; describe the role of a valuation agent
questions.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
questions.question: A collateral operations manager is briefing new staff on why the function exists and on the role of the valuation agent. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Collateral management exists to reduce counterparty credit exposure to a residual level and thereby to free credit lines and support larger trading volumes; the valuation agent computes the mark-to-market of the netting set and the resulting margin call, and is typically one of the two parties, which is why disputes arise and why a third-party agent may be appointed.

Collateral management exists to eliminate counterparty credit exposure entirely; the valuation agent is always an independent third party appointed by the regulator, which is why valuation disputes are rare in practice.
Collateral management exists primarily to generate funding for the receiving party through rehypothecation; the valuation agent's role is limited to custody of the posted assets.

Collateral management exists to convert credit risk into market risk on the posted securities; the valuation agent is the custodian bank, which independently determines both the exposure and the eligible collateral schedule.

questions.solution:
Collateral reduces exposure to a residual level and expands trading capacity; the valuation agent computes exposure and the margin call, and is usually a party to the trade, which is the structural source of disputes.

**The rationale.** Collateral does three things.

| Purpose | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Reduce credit exposure | Margin is called as exposure grows, leaving only a contractual residual |
| Reduce economic and regulatory capital | Lower exposure at default reduces the capital charge |
| Free credit lines | Capacity released supports greater trading volume with the same counterparty |

The commercial driver is often the third: a credit line freed by collateralisation can support more business with the same counterparty. Collateral is therefore an enabler of volume as much as a risk control.

**What collateral does not do.** It leaves a residual:

$$\text{Residual exposure} \approx \text{Threshold} + \text{Minimum Transfer Amount} + \text{exposure over the margin period of risk}$$

so option (b)'s claim of elimination is wrong.

**The valuation agent.** The party responsible for calculating the mark-to-market of the netting set, applying the credit support annex parameters, and issuing the margin call. Under a standard bilateral agreement this is one of the two parties, frequently the dealer.

**Why that matters.** The party computing the call has an interest in the result. Where the two parties value the same portfolio differently, using different models, curves or snapshot times, a dispute follows. That structural conflict is why agreements specify dispute resolution procedures, and why a third-party valuation agent is sometimes appointed for complex or illiquid portfolios.

a.reason: Exposure reduced to a residual and capacity freed; the valuation agent computes exposure and the call and is usually a party to the trade.

b.reason: An absolute claim on elimination, and a factual error on the agent. Valuation agents are not regulator-appointed independents, and valuation disputes are common rather than rare, which is why formal dispute procedures exist.

c.reason: Rehypothecation is a consequence available under some agreements, not the rationale for collateral management, and it is restricted or prohibited for initial margin. The valuation agent computes exposure; custody is a separate function.

d.reason: Collateral does introduce market risk on posted securities, but describing that as the purpose inverts cause and side effect. The custodian holds assets and does not determine exposure or the eligible collateral schedule, which is negotiated between the parties.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the recurring absolute claim that collateral eliminates rather than reduces exposure, paired with a plausible-sounding but false assertion of independence. The structural point worth carrying: the party calculating the call is usually a party to the trade, which is why disputes are a routine operational feature rather than an exception.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of collateral and the types of collateral that are typically used; differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality
questions.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
questions.question: A dealer is negotiating a credit support annex with a hedge fund client. Which of the following correctly describes collateral types and the difference between one-way and two-way agreements?

options.text: Cash and government securities dominate posted collateral, with corporate and equity collateral attracting larger haircuts; under a one-way agreement only one party posts, which is common where credit quality is asymmetric, whereas under a two-way agreement either party posts depending on the direction of the mark-to-market. Thresholds and independent amounts are frequently linked to credit ratings.

Corporate bonds and equities dominate posted collateral because they offer a higher return to the poster; under a one-way agreement both parties post simultaneously to equalise exposure, while a two-way agreement restricts posting to the weaker party.
Only cash may be posted as collateral under an ISDA credit support annex, which is why haircuts are unnecessary; one-way and two-way agreements differ only in the frequency of margin calls.
Collateral type is prescribed by regulation and cannot be negotiated; one-way agreements are prohibited under the ISDA framework because they create an asymmetric credit exposure.

questions.solution:
Collateral eligibility trades liquidity against yield, one-way agreements reflect asymmetric credit quality, and rating-linked parameters tighten terms automatically as credit deteriorates.

**Collateral types and why the mix looks as it does.**

| Collateral type | Typical haircut | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Cash | Zero | Instantly valued and liquid; the dominant form of variation margin |
| Government securities | Small, rising with maturity | Highly liquid, low credit risk |
| Corporate bonds | Larger | Credit risk and lower liquidity |
| Equities | Largest | High volatility and, if issued by the counterparty or its sector, wrong-way collateral |

Cash dominates because it is instantly valued, instantly liquid and carries no haircut. The haircut on any security buffers the risk that its value falls during the margin period of risk, so it scales with volatility and illiquidity.

$$\text{Credit given} = \text{market value} \times (1 - \text{haircut})$$

**One-way against two-way.**

| Feature | One-way CSA | Two-way CSA |
|---|---|---|
| Who posts | Only the weaker-rated party | Either party, depending on which side is out-of-the-money |
| Typical counterparty | A dealer facing a lower-rated counterparty, such as a hedge fund | Two similarly-rated dealers or institutions |
| Symmetry | Asymmetric by design | Symmetric |
| Parameter linkage | Thresholds and independent amounts are often set against the weaker party alone and tightened on downgrade | Thresholds and independent amounts can apply to both sides, often graduated by each party's rating |

A one-way agreement in the dealer's favour is common with hedge funds and other lower-rated counterparties. It is asymmetric by design and is permitted, contrary to option (d).

**Linkage to credit quality.** Thresholds and independent amounts are frequently tied to the counterparty's rating, tightening automatically on downgrade. That protects the stronger party and creates the cliff effect discussed under termination events: the call arrives when funding is hardest.

a.reason: Cash and government securities dominate, one-way agreements reflect asymmetric credit quality, and parameters are frequently rating linked.

b.reason: Two errors. Cash and government securities dominate, not corporate bonds and equities, because eligibility is driven by liquidity rather than yield. And the definitions of one-way and two-way are transposed.

c.reason: Securities are routinely posted, which is precisely why haircut schedules are negotiated. The one-way against two-way distinction concerns who posts, not call frequency.

d.reason: Collateral eligibility is negotiated in the credit support annex, within regulatory constraints for margined trades, and one-way agreements are permitted and widely used. Asymmetry is the intended feature, not a prohibition.

trap.explanation: Option (b) contains a role misassignment on the one-way and two-way definitions wrapped around a plausible but wrong claim that collateral is selected for yield. Eligibility is selected for liquidity: the receiver needs to be able to sell it quickly at a predictable price, which is the opposite of a yield-seeking criterion.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain aspects of collateral including funding, rehypothecation, and segregation; assess the impact of collateral on counterparty risk and funding, with and without segregation or rehypothecation
questions.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
questions.question: A treasury team is assessing how segregation and rehypothecation affect the funding cost and counterparty risk of posted collateral. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Segregation protects the poster by preventing the receiver from using the collateral, but it increases the poster's funding cost because the assets cannot be reused; rehypothecation reduces the funding cost by allowing the receiver to reuse the collateral, but exposes the poster to loss of the collateral if the receiver defaults.

Segregation reduces the poster's funding cost because segregated assets remain on the poster's balance sheet, while rehypothecation increases funding cost by removing the assets from circulation; neither affects counterparty risk.
Rehypothecation and segregation are mutually reinforcing: collateral that is segregated may still be rehypothecated, so the poster obtains protection and funding relief simultaneously.
Segregation applies only to variation margin and rehypothecation only to initial margin, which is why initial margin is the cheaper of the two to fund.

questions.solution:
Segregation and rehypothecation sit at opposite ends of a trade between the poster's protection and the system's funding efficiency, and the two are mutually exclusive for the same collateral.

**The trade.**

| | Segregated | Rehypothecable |
|---|---|---|
| Receiver may reuse | No | Yes |
| Poster's protection if the receiver defaults | Strong, assets are ring-fenced and returned | Weak, an unsecured claim for equivalent assets |
| Funding cost to the poster | Higher, assets are locked away | Lower, reuse creates value in the chain |
| Typical application | Initial margin under the uncleared margin rules | Variation margin, where permitted |

**Segregation.** The collateral is held with a third-party custodian and ring-fenced. If the receiver defaults, the poster gets its assets back rather than ranking as an unsecured creditor. The cost is that nobody can use those assets, so they must be funded outright for the life of the trade. This is why initial margin is required to be segregated under the uncleared margin rules, and why initial margin is the expensive one to post, which is the reverse of option (d)'s claim.

**Rehypothecation.** The receiver may reuse the collateral, for example to post onward or to fund its own positions. That reuse creates value in the system and reduces the effective funding cost. The poster's protection is correspondingly weaker: it holds a contractual claim for the return of equivalent assets, not the assets themselves.

**Why they are mutually exclusive, which disposes of option (c).** Segregation is defined by the prohibition on reuse. Collateral that can be rehypothecated is by definition not segregated.

**Where this leads.** The funding cost of posting collateral that cannot be reused is the origin of margin valuation adjustment, alongside funding valuation adjustment in the xVA family.

a.reason: Segregation protects the poster at a higher funding cost; rehypothecation lowers the cost at the price of the poster's protection.

b.reason: Both directions are reversed, and the closing claim that neither affects counterparty risk is the central error: the poster's exposure to the receiver's default is precisely what segregation addresses.

c.reason: The two are mutually exclusive for the same collateral. Segregation is defined by the prohibition on reuse, so segregated collateral cannot be rehypothecated.

d.reason: The application is reversed. Initial margin is the type required to be segregated, and it is therefore the more expensive to fund, not the cheaper.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is a double polarity flip on both funding directions, and it is caught by asking a single question: can the assets be used by anyone while they are posted? Segregated assets cannot, so they cost more to fund. Option (c) is the scope error of treating two mutually exclusive states as compatible, and it is attractive because both sound like desirable features.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the various regulatory capital requirements
questions.reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
questions.question: A regulatory capital analyst is summarising the capital requirements a bank faces on its over-the-counter derivative book. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: The bank holds default risk capital against counterparty exposure at default, computed under the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk or an internal model method; it separately holds a CVA capital charge for the mark-to-market volatility of CVA; and centrally cleared exposures attract a lower but non-zero charge, including capital against default fund contributions.
The bank holds a single capital charge against counterparty exposure at default, and CVA is excluded from capital because it is already reflected in the fair value of the derivative.
Capital is required only for uncleared derivatives; centrally cleared exposures attract no capital charge, since the CCP guarantees performance and the exposure is fully margined.

The internal model method computes exposure at default as the sum of current exposure and an add-on prescribed by the regulator, which is why it produces the same result as the standardised approach for any given portfolio.

questions.solution:
Counterparty risk attracts two distinct capital charges, default risk and CVA volatility, and central clearing reduces but does not eliminate the requirement.

**The three components.**

| Charge | What it covers | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Default risk capital | Loss if the counterparty defaults | EAD from SA-CCR or the internal model method, risk weighted |
| CVA capital charge | Mark-to-market volatility of CVA as credit spreads move | Introduced under Basel III |
| Cleared exposures | Trade exposure to the CCP, plus default fund contributions | Low risk weight for qualifying CCPs, but not zero |

**Why the CVA charge exists separately.** Default risk capital covers the loss if the counterparty actually fails. But the great majority of losses attributed to counterparty risk in 2008 and 2009 arose from mark-to-market moves in CVA as credit spreads widened, without any default occurring. Basel III added the CVA capital charge specifically to capitalise that volatility, which is the regulatory recognition that counterparty risk has a market risk component.

**Exposure at default under the internal model method.**

$$EAD = \alpha \times \text{effective EPE, with } \alpha \text{ set at 1.4 by default}$$

The alpha multiplier grosses up for correlation and concentration effects the model does not capture. Option (d) confuses this with the current exposure method, which is the add-on approach, and the two do not coincide.

**Central clearing.** Cleared trade exposures attract a low risk weight, typically 2% for qualifying CCPs, and there is a separate charge against default fund contributions, because those are genuinely at risk in a member default. Lower is not zero, which disposes of option (c).

a.reason: Default risk capital, a separate CVA charge, and a reduced but non-zero requirement for cleared exposures including default fund contributions.

b.reason: CVA is not excluded from capital. Basel III added a dedicated CVA charge precisely because CVA volatility caused the majority of counterparty-related losses in the crisis without defaults occurring.

c.reason: An absolute claim. Cleared exposures attract a low risk weight rather than none, and default fund contributions carry their own charge because they are mutualised and genuinely at risk.

d.reason: Describes the current exposure method, not the internal model method. The IMM computes EAD as alpha times effective EPE from a simulated exposure profile, and it does not produce the same result as a standardised add-on approach.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the sharpest, because its reasoning sounds principled: if CVA is already in fair value, charging capital for it looks like double counting. It is not, because fair value captures CVA's level while the capital charge captures its volatility. Option (c) is the recurring absolute claim that central clearing eliminates rather than reduces risk.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities; explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact when there is correlation between transaction values
questions.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
questions.question: A counterparty risk analyst is explaining how contractual features and portfolio aggregation shape an exposure profile. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: More frequent payments reduce exposure by resetting the accumulated mark-to-market more often, and an exercise date on an option truncates the profile because the position either terminates or converts; aggregating transactions under an enforceable netting agreement reduces exposure below the sum of the individual profiles, and the reduction is largest when transaction values are negatively correlated.

More frequent payments increase exposure because each payment date creates a settlement risk window, and exercise dates have no effect on the profile since the underlying risk continues regardless; aggregation reduces exposure most when transaction values are positively correlated.

Payment frequency affects only operational cost and not the exposure profile, since exposure depends solely on the volatility of the underlying; aggregation has no effect on exposure unless the transactions are in the same currency.
More frequent payments reduce exposure, and aggregation reduces exposure by an amount that is independent of correlation, since netting is a legal mechanism rather than a statistical one.

questions.solution:
Cash flow timing truncates the accumulation of mark-to-market value, and netting benefit depends on how transaction values co-move.

**Payment frequency.** Exposure on a swap is the accumulated difference between what has been paid and what has been received since the last settlement. Each payment resets part of that accumulation to zero.

| Feature | Effect on the exposure profile |
|---|---|
| More frequent payments | Lowers the profile; less mark-to-market accumulates between resets |
| Exercise date | Truncates the profile; the position terminates or converts |
| Principal exchange at maturity | Raises the profile toward maturity; the largest flow is last |
| Aggregation under netting | Lowers total exposure below the sum of individual profiles |

A quarterly-paying swap therefore has a lower exposure profile than an otherwise identical annual-paying swap, because value has less time to build between resets.

**Exercise dates.** An option's exposure profile is truncated at the exercise date. Either the option is exercised, converting into the underlying position with its own profile, or it expires worthless and exposure falls to zero. A Bermudan or American feature creates multiple such points and generally lowers the profile relative to a European equivalent.

**Aggregation.** Under an enforceable netting agreement:

$$EE_{\text{netting set}} = E\left[\max\left(\sum_i V_i, 0\right)\right] \leq \sum_i EE_i$$

The inequality is strict whenever transactions can take opposite signs. The netting factor for $n$ equal trades with average correlation $\rho$ is:

$$\text{Netting factor} = \sqrt{n + n(n-1)\rho} \div n$$

which equals 1 at $\rho = 1$, meaning no benefit, and falls as correlation declines. The benefit is therefore greatest at negative correlation, which disposes of option (b).

a.reason: Frequent payments reduce exposure, exercise dates truncate the profile, and netting benefit is greatest when transaction values are negatively correlated.

b.reason: Payment dates do create settlement risk windows, but that is a distinct short-dated risk and does not raise the pre-settlement exposure profile, which is what the question concerns. Exercise dates plainly do affect the profile, and the correlation direction is reversed: netting benefit falls as correlation rises.

c.reason: Payment frequency directly affects how much value accumulates between resets. Netting also operates across currencies within a netting set, provided the agreement so provides.

d.reason: The first clause is right and the second wrong. Netting is legally enabled but its magnitude is statistical: it depends entirely on how the transaction values co-move, which is why the netting factor is a function of correlation.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the sharpest because it correctly identifies netting as a legal mechanism and then draws the wrong inference. The law makes netting possible; correlation determines how much it is worth. Option (b) is a correlation misuse, associating stronger correlation with a larger benefit, which is the same error that appears in portfolio diversification.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation; explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins
questions.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
questions.question: A CVA desk is refining its calculation to reflect an enforceable netting agreement and a credit support annex. Which of the following correctly describes how each is incorporated?

options.text: Netting is incorporated by computing expected exposure on the netted portfolio rather than trade by trade, so that CVA is computed once for the netting set and allocated to trades through incremental or marginal CVA; collateral is incorporated by replacing the exposure profile with the collateralised residual, which is driven by the threshold, the minimum transfer amount and the exposure accruing over the margin period of risk, with segregated initial margin further reducing it.

Netting is incorporated by computing CVA trade by trade and then subtracting a netting benefit adjustment at the portfolio level; collateral is incorporated by setting expected exposure to zero for any netting set covered by a credit support annex.
Netting has no effect on CVA because CVA is driven by the counterparty's credit spread rather than by exposure; collateral reduces CVA only to the extent that the collateral itself is credit risky.
Both are incorporated by applying a fixed regulatory multiplier to the uncollateralised CVA, since the alpha factor of 1.4 already reflects typical netting and collateral arrangements.

questions.solution:
Netting changes the exposure profile that enters CVA, so CVA becomes a netting set quantity requiring allocation; collateral replaces that profile with a residual governed by the CSA parameters and the margin period of risk.

**Netting in CVA.** CVA is computed from expected exposure, so netting enters by changing the exposure profile itself:

$$CVA_{\text{netting set}} = LGD \times \sum_t EE_{\text{netted}}(t) \times PD(t) \times DF(t)$$

Because EE is computed on the net portfolio, CVA becomes a property of the netting set rather than of any individual trade, and it is non-additive:

$$CVA_{\text{netting set}} \leq \sum_i CVA_i^{\text{standalone}}$$

Allocation to trades therefore requires incremental CVA for pricing a new trade and marginal CVA for attributing the existing charge.

**Collateral in CVA.** The exposure profile is replaced by the collateralised residual.

| CSA parameter | Direction of effect on CVA |
|---|---|
| Higher threshold | Increases CVA; more exposure left uncollateralised |
| Higher minimum transfer amount | Increases CVA |
| Longer margin period of risk | Increases CVA; exposure accrues over a longer unprotected window |
| Higher initial margin | Decreases CVA; absorbs the residual |

**Why collateral does not take CVA to zero, which disposes of option (b).** Three residual terms survive. The threshold is uncollateralised by agreement. The minimum transfer amount allows exposure to drift before any call. And the margin period of risk is the window between the last effective call and close-out, over which exposure can move freely:

$$\text{Residual exposure} \approx \text{Threshold} + MTA + \sigma\sqrt{\text{margin period of risk}}$$

**Initial margin.** Segregated initial margin sits over and above variation margin and absorbs part of that residual, which is why it materially reduces CVA and why it creates a funding cost captured by MVA.

a.reason: Netting enters through the netted exposure profile and requires incremental or marginal allocation; collateral replaces the profile with a residual governed by threshold, MTA, margin period of risk and initial margin.

b.reason: Computing trade by trade and subtracting an adjustment is not how netting enters; the netted profile must be simulated directly. And setting exposure to zero under a CSA ignores every residual term, which is the substance of this objective.

c.reason: CVA depends on both the credit spread and the exposure profile. Denying the exposure dependence removes half the formula and would make netting and collateral irrelevant, which contradicts the entire counterparty risk framework.

d.reason: Alpha is a regulatory capital multiplier applied to effective EPE, not a CVA pricing device, and it does not substitute for modelling netting and collateral explicitly.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the trap and it contains the absolute claim that a credit support annex takes exposure to zero. It does not, and the three surviving terms are precisely what this objective names. Option (c) is a dropped term at the conceptual level, discarding exposure from a formula that requires it. The direction to hold: every CSA parameter that leaves more exposure uncollateralised raises CVA, and initial margin is the only one that lowers it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modelling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches
questions.reading: Reading 99: Gregory, Wrong-Way Risk
questions.question: A model development team is selecting an approach for modelling wrong-way risk in its CVA calculation. Which of the following correctly characterises the available methods?

options.text: Hazard rate approaches make the counterparty's default intensity a function of the same variables that drive exposure; structural approaches link default to the counterparty's asset value; parametric approaches impose a simple functional relationship between the default intensity and portfolio exposure, calibrated to the historical link between exposure and credit spreads; and jump approaches allow a discrete move in exposure or value at default, which is the only family that reproduces the limited effectiveness of collateral.

Hazard rate approaches link default to the counterparty's asset value; structural approaches make the default intensity a function of exposure drivers; parametric approaches are the most flexible and require no functional assumption; and jump approaches are used only for equity derivatives.
All four methods produce equivalent CVA figures for a given portfolio, differing only in computational cost, which is why the parametric approach is preferred in practice.

Only structural approaches can capture wrong-way risk, because default must be linked to an economic cause; hazard rate, parametric and jump approaches are reduced form and are therefore incapable of generating dependence between exposure and default.

questions.solution:
The four families differ in how they link exposure to default, and only a jump approach reproduces the discontinuity that defeats collateral.

**The four families.**

| Family | How exposure and default are linked | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| Hazard rate | Default intensity is made a function of the variables driving exposure | Integrates naturally with reduced form CVA machinery |
| Structural | Default occurs when the counterparty's asset value crosses a threshold correlated with exposure | Economically interpretable |
| Parametric | A simple imposed function linking the hazard rate to portfolio value, calibrated to the historical relationship between exposure and credit spreads | Simple and transparent, but relies on the historical relationship holding |
| Jump | A discrete move in exposure or value at the moment of default | The only family that reproduces the failure of collateral |

**Why the jump family matters most in practice.** Collateral works by calling margin as exposure grows. That works against a continuous deterioration. Specific wrong-way risk frequently materialises as a discontinuity: a sovereign devalues overnight, a reference entity defaults, a counterparty gaps wider on an announcement. Exposure leaps before any call can be made and settled.

$$\text{Continuous models} \rightarrow \text{margin keeps pace} \rightarrow \text{collateral appears highly effective}$$
$$\text{Jump models} \rightarrow \text{exposure gaps between calls} \rightarrow \text{substantial residual exposure remains}$$

A firm observing that collateral underperforms in stress should therefore prefer a jump approach, because continuous approaches will not reproduce what it is seeing.

**The trade-off across families.** Parametric approaches are simple, transparent and easy to communicate, but they impose the answer through the chosen functional form. Hazard rate and structural approaches are economically grounded but harder to calibrate. Jump approaches are the most realistic for specific wrong-way risk and the most demanding to parameterise, since jump size and intensity are rarely observable.

a.reason: The four families are correctly characterised, and only the jump family reproduces the limited effectiveness of collateral against discontinuous moves.

b.reason: The hazard rate and structural descriptions are transposed. Parametric approaches are also the least flexible, since they impose a functional form rather than deriving one, and jump approaches are not confined to equity derivatives.

c.reason: The methods produce materially different CVA figures, particularly in the tail, which is the entire reason a choice must be made. Preferring the parametric approach for computational convenience would discard the dependence structure the exercise exists to capture.

d.reason: Reduced form models generate dependence readily by making the default intensity a function of common variables. Restricting wrong-way risk modelling to structural approaches is an absolute claim contradicted by the standard hazard rate methods.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is a role misassignment between the two economically grounded families, and it is difficult because both descriptions are individually accurate. Option (c) is the equivalence trap: methods that model dependence differently cannot give the same answer. The practical anchor: if you observe collateral failing in stress, you need a jump model, because a continuous model cannot produce that behaviour.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio and on a derivative portfolio; differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio
questions.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
questions.question:
A stress testing team is running a severe recession scenario over a loan portfolio with the following baseline and stressed parameters.

- Exposure at default: USD 800 million, unchanged in the stress
- Baseline probability of default: 1.5%; stressed probability of default: 5.0%
- Baseline loss given default: 40%; stressed loss given default: 55%

Which of the following gives the stressed expected loss and the stress loss?

options.text: Stressed expected loss USD 22.0 million; stress loss USD 17.2 million
Stressed expected loss USD 22.0 million; stress loss USD 22.0 million
Stressed expected loss USD 4.8 million; stress loss USD 17.2 million
Stressed expected loss USD 40.0 million; stress loss USD 35.2 million

questions.solution:
Stressed expected loss is the loss computed with stressed parameters; stress loss is the incremental amount above the baseline expected loss, which is what the stress scenario actually adds.

**Step 1. Baseline expected loss.**

$$EL_{\text{baseline}} = EAD \times PD \times LGD = 800 \times 0.015 \times 0.40 = \text{USD } 4.8 \text{ million}$$

**Step 2. Stressed expected loss.** Recompute with the stressed parameters. Note that both PD and LGD stress, which is the downturn LGD effect: recovery deteriorates in the same conditions that raise default.

$$EL_{\text{stressed}} = 800 \times 0.050 \times 0.55 = \text{USD } 22.0 \text{ million}$$

**Step 3. Stress loss.** The incremental loss attributable to the scenario:

$$\text{Stress loss} = EL_{\text{stressed}} - EL_{\text{baseline}} = 22.0 - 4.8 = \text{USD } 17.2 \text{ million}$$

| Measure | Definition | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline expected loss | EAD x baseline PD x baseline LGD | USD 4.8 million |
| Stressed expected loss | EAD x stressed PD x stressed LGD | USD 22.0 million |
| Stress loss | Stressed expected loss less baseline expected loss | USD 17.2 million |

**Why the compounding is so severe.** PD rises by a factor of 3.33 and LGD by a factor of 1.375, and they multiply:

$$\text{Stress multiple} = 3.33 \times 1.375 = 4.58, \text{ so expected loss rises 4.58-fold}$$

Stressing PD alone would give $800 \times 0.05 \times 0.40 = $ USD 16.0 million, understating the result by USD 6.0 million. Holding LGD at its baseline is the most common error in loan portfolio stress testing.

**The derivative portfolio analogue.** For derivatives the stressed quantity is the exposure itself, since exposure is market driven. The scenario is applied to the risk factors, the exposure profile is re-simulated, and the stressed exposure is combined with stressed PD and LGD. Exposure is fixed for a loan and variable for a derivative, which is the structural difference between the two stress tests.

a.reason: Stressed expected loss of USD 22.0 million and stress loss of USD 17.2 million.

b.reason: Reports the stressed expected loss twice. Stress loss is the incremental amount, so the baseline expected loss of USD 4.8 million must be subtracted. A dropped term.

c.reason: Reports the baseline expected loss of USD 4.8 million as the stressed figure while giving the correct stress loss. The two are transposed relative to their definitions.

d.reason: USD 40.0 million is $800 \times 0.05$, that is, the stressed PD applied to exposure with LGD omitted entirely. The stress loss then follows from the same error.

trap.explanation: Two named traps. The dropped term in option (b) is failing to subtract baseline expected loss, which conflates the level with the increment. The omitted LGD in option (d) is the more dangerous modelling error, because holding recovery at its through-the-cycle average in a downturn scenario systematically understates stress loss; PD and LGD deteriorate together, which is why downturn LGD is a regulatory requirement.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA; calculate the stressed CVA and the stress loss on CVA; calculate the DVA and explain how stressing DVA enters into aggregating stress tests of CCR
questions.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
questions.question:
A counterparty risk team is stressing its bilateral CVA position for a credit spread widening scenario. The following figures apply to a single counterparty.

- Expected positive exposure: 4.0% of notional; expected negative exposure: 3.0% of notional
- Counterparty credit spread: 150 basis points at baseline, widening to 450 basis points under stress
- The firm's own credit spread: 100 basis points at baseline, widening to 250 basis points under stress

Which of the following gives the stress loss on CVA and the stress gain on DVA, each expressed as a running spread?

options.text: Stress loss on CVA 12.0 basis points; stress gain on DVA 4.5 basis points
Stress loss on CVA 18.0 basis points; stress gain on DVA 7.5 basis points
Stress loss on CVA 12.0 basis points; stress gain on DVA 7.5 basis points
Stress loss on CVA 18.0 basis points; stress gain on DVA 4.5 basis points

questions.solution:
Stressing CVA means recomputing it with stressed credit spreads and taking the increment; DVA moves in the opposite direction and partially offsets, which is why bilateral aggregation must be done net.

**Step 1. Baseline and stressed CVA.** CVA uses the counterparty's spread against expected positive exposure.

$$CVA \approx EPE \times s_{\text{counterparty}}$$
$$CVA_{\text{baseline}} = 0.040 \times 150 = 6.0 \text{ bps}$$
$$CVA_{\text{stressed}} = 0.040 \times 450 = 18.0 \text{ bps}$$
$$\text{Stress loss on CVA} = 18.0 - 6.0 = 12.0 \text{ basis points}$$

**Step 2. Baseline and stressed DVA.** DVA uses the firm's own spread against expected negative exposure.

$$DVA \approx ENE \times s_{\text{own}}$$
$$DVA_{\text{baseline}} = 0.030 \times 100 = 3.0 \text{ bps}$$
$$DVA_{\text{stressed}} = 0.030 \times 250 = 7.5 \text{ bps}$$
$$\text{Stress gain on DVA} = 7.5 - 3.0 = 4.5 \text{ basis points}$$

**Step 3. Aggregate.**

$$\text{Net stress impact on BCVA} = -12.0 + 4.5 = -7.5 \text{ basis points}$$

| Component | Baseline | Stressed | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| CVA, a charge | 6.0 bps | 18.0 bps | -12.0 bps, a loss |
| DVA, a benefit | 3.0 bps | 7.5 bps | +4.5 bps, a gain |
| Net bilateral impact | | | -7.5 bps |

**Why stressing DVA matters for aggregation, which is the examinable point.** In a systemic scenario the firm's own spread widens alongside its counterparties'. Stressing CVA alone overstates the loss, because it ignores the accounting gain the firm books on its own deteriorating credit. Aggregating a counterparty risk stress test therefore requires both legs.

**The caveat that must accompany the number.** The DVA gain is an accounting gain that cannot be monetised without defaulting or repurchasing one's own debt, and it is excluded from regulatory capital. Reporting the net figure without that caveat overstates the firm's true resilience.

a.reason: Stress loss on CVA of 12.0 basis points and stress gain on DVA of 4.5 basis points.

b.reason: Reports the stressed levels of 18.0 and 7.5 rather than the changes from baseline. The intermediate-result trap: both figures are correct quantities answering the wrong question.

c.reason: The CVA figure is the correct increment but the DVA figure is the stressed level of 7.5 rather than the increment of 4.5. Internally inconsistent.

d.reason: The mirror image of option (c): the CVA figure is the stressed level and the DVA figure is the increment.

trap.explanation: The intermediate-result trap dominates: the stressed levels are easy to compute and the subtraction of the baseline is the step most often skipped. Options (c) and (d) are the two half-consistent versions, and both are eliminated by checking that the two figures are computed the same way. The second trap, not offered here but live in practice, is the spread pairing: EPE goes with the counterparty's spread and ENE with your own, and reversing them corrupts both legs.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR
questions.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
questions.question: A model risk committee is reviewing the bank's counterparty credit risk stress testing programme. Which of the following correctly identifies the common pitfalls?

options.text: Stressing credit factors while holding exposure fixed, so that wrong-way risk is missed; applying scenarios that are severe but not internally coherent across risk factors; ignoring collateral and margin dynamics, so that the funding consequences of the scenario are absent; and treating the aggregate result as a single number without decomposing it by counterparty and driver.

The principal pitfall is excessive severity, since scenarios that are too extreme produce results management will not act on; the remedy is to calibrate scenarios to the worst outcome observed in the past five years.
The principal pitfall is that stress testing duplicates the value at risk framework, so a bank operating a validated VaR model does not need a separate counterparty stress testing programme.

The principal pitfall is computational: because exposure must be re-simulated for every scenario, banks should stress only the largest counterparties and extrapolate the result to the remainder of the portfolio.

questions.solution:
Counterparty stress testing fails most often through incomplete stressing, incoherent scenarios, omitted collateral dynamics, and undecomposed results.

**The four pitfalls.**

| Pitfall | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Stressing credit but not exposure | Wrong-way risk is missed entirely; the loss is understated |
| Severe but incoherent scenarios | Results cannot be interpreted or acted upon |
| Ignoring collateral and margin dynamics | The funding consequences of the scenario are invisible |
| Reporting a single aggregate number | No decomposition by counterparty or driver, so no management action follows |

**Why holding exposure fixed is the most serious.** Counterparty risk is the product of exposure and default, and in a genuine crisis both move together. Stressing credit spreads while leaving the exposure profile at its baseline assumes independence, which is precisely the wrong-way risk assumption the whole framework exists to reject:

$$\text{Stress loss} = f(\text{stressed exposure}, \text{stressed PD}, \text{stressed LGD}), \text{ all three must move}$$

**Why coherence matters.** A scenario in which credit spreads widen sharply while equity markets rally and volatility falls is severe on one axis and internally contradictory. Incoherent scenarios produce results that cannot be interpreted or acted on.

**Why collateral dynamics matter.** In stress, margin calls rise, collateral values fall, haircuts widen and rating triggers fire. A stress test that ignores this misses the transformation of credit risk into funding liquidity risk, which is how collateralised counterparties actually fail.

**On severity, which option (b) inverts.** Calibrating to the worst outcome of the past five years is a documented weakness, not a remedy. Stress scenarios must extend beyond observed history, because the events that matter have not yet happened.

a.reason: Incomplete stressing, incoherent scenarios, omitted collateral dynamics and undecomposed results are the recognised pitfalls.

b.reason: Inverts the severity problem. Stress scenarios are criticised for being insufficiently severe, and calibrating to recent observed history is itself a pitfall, since it guarantees the scenario cannot exceed what has already happened.

c.reason: Stress testing and VaR are complements. VaR is a probabilistic measure calibrated to historical distributions; stress testing is scenario based and deliberately explores outcomes the distribution assigns negligible probability. Neither substitutes for the other.

d.reason: Extrapolating from the largest counterparties misses concentration in smaller names and, more importantly, misses correlated exposures across the portfolio. Computational cost is a constraint to be managed, not a justification for a partial test.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the polarity flip on severity, and it is attractive because insufficient management engagement with stress results is a genuine complaint. The remedy it proposes, anchoring to recent history, is the disease rather than the cure. Option (c) is the substitution trap: a validated VaR model tells you about the centre of the distribution and says nothing about the scenarios stress testing exists to explore.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure; describe the treatment of excess spread and estimate the value of the overcollateralization account; explain the tests on excess spread that a custodian must perform
questions.reading: Fabozzi, Securitisation Cash Flows and Structures
questions.question:
A three-tiered securitisation is backed by a USD 500 million collateral pool paying a weighted average coupon of 9.0%. The liabilities and costs for the first year are as follows.

- Senior notes: USD 400 million at 5.0%
- Mezzanine notes: USD 60 million at 8.0%
- Equity tranche: USD 40 million, receiving residual cash flow
- Servicing and administrative fees: 0.5% of the collateral balance
- Realised collateral losses in year 1: USD 6.0 million
- The overcollateralisation account opens at zero and captures excess spread up to a target of USD 15 million

What is the excess spread available in year 1, and what is the closing balance of the overcollateralisation account?

options.text: Excess spread USD 11.7 million; overcollateralisation account USD 11.7 million
Excess spread USD 17.7 million; overcollateralisation account USD 15.0 million
Excess spread USD 11.7 million; overcollateralisation account USD 15.0 million
Excess spread USD 45.0 million; overcollateralisation account USD 15.0 million

questions.solution:
Excess spread is collateral interest less note coupons, fees and realised losses; it is diverted to the overcollateralisation account until the target is reached, and only the surplus above the target flows to equity.

**Step 1. Work down the waterfall in priority order.**

| Item | Calculation | USD million |
|---|---|---|
| Collateral interest | 500 x 9.0% | 45.0 |
| Less senior note coupon | 400 x 5.0% | (20.0) |
| Less mezzanine note coupon | 60 x 8.0% | (4.8) |
| Less servicing and fees | 500 x 0.5% | (2.5) |
| Less realised collateral losses | given | (6.0) |
| Excess spread | | 11.7 |

$$\text{Excess spread} = 45.0 - 20.0 - 4.8 - 2.5 - 6.0 = \text{USD } 11.7 \text{ million}$$

**Step 2. Apply the overcollateralisation test.** The custodian compares excess spread against the target.

$$\text{Target} = \text{USD } 15.0 \text{ million}; \quad \text{available} = \text{USD } 11.7 \text{ million}; \quad 11.7 < 15.0$$

The account is not yet at target, so the entire USD 11.7 million is trapped and nothing flows to the equity noteholders in year 1.

$$\text{Closing OC account} = 0 + 11.7 = \text{USD } 11.7 \text{ million}$$

**Step 3. What year 2 would look like.** Only USD 3.3 million of further excess spread is needed to reach the target. Once the account is full, subsequent excess spread is released to equity, which is why the equity tranche's cash flows are back-loaded and highly sensitive to early losses.

**The custodian's tests, which are the examinable mechanism.** At each payment date the trustee runs coverage tests before releasing cash. The overcollateralisation test compares collateral value to note balances; the interest coverage test compares collateral interest to note interest. If either fails, excess spread is diverted to pay down senior notes or to build the reserve rather than being released. That diversion is the deleveraging mechanism protecting senior holders.

**Why losses are deducted here.** Realised losses are absorbed by excess spread first, before any tranche is written down. Excess spread is therefore the first layer of credit enhancement, ahead of overcollateralisation and subordination.

a.reason: Excess spread of USD 11.7 million, all trapped in the overcollateralisation account, which closes at USD 11.7 million.

b.reason: USD 17.7 million omits the USD 6.0 million of realised losses, a dropped term. Losses are absorbed by excess spread before anything is released, so they must be deducted. The account balance of USD 15.0 million then follows from the inflated figure.

c.reason: The excess spread is right, but the account cannot exceed what has been paid into it. Reporting the target of USD 15.0 million rather than the actual balance of USD 11.7 million confuses a cap with a balance.

d.reason: USD 45.0 million is gross collateral interest, before any coupons, fees or losses. The intermediate-result trap at the very first line of the waterfall.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the sharpest, because it computes excess spread correctly and then reports the target as the balance. A target is a ceiling, not an amount received. Option (b) is the dropped term on realised losses, which matters conceptually as well as arithmetically: excess spread is the first loss absorber, so losses must pass through it. Option (d) stops at gross interest.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate
questions.reading: Fabozzi, Securitisation Cash Flows and Structures
questions.question:
A mortgage analyst is measuring prepayment on a seasoned pool. In the most recent month the pool prepaid 0.55% of its beginning scheduled balance. The pool is 20 months seasoned.

Which of the following is nearest to the annualised constant prepayment rate and the corresponding PSA speed?

options.text: CPR 6.40%; approximately 160 PSA
CPR 6.60%; approximately 110 PSA
CPR 0.55%; approximately 100 PSA
CPR 6.40%; approximately 107 PSA

questions.solution:
The single monthly mortality rate is annualised into a CPR by compounding survival, and PSA expresses that CPR as a percentage of a benchmark ramp that rises 0.2% per month to 6% at month 30.

**Step 1. Convert the monthly rate into an annual CPR.** The single monthly mortality rate is $SMM = 0.55\%$. Prepayment compounds through survival, so:

$$CPR = 1 - (1 - SMM)^{12}$$
$$CPR = 1 - (1 - 0.0055)^{12} = 1 - 0.99450^{12} = 1 - 0.93597 = 6.40\%$$

Note that simply multiplying by 12 gives 6.60%, which overstates the rate. Prepayment probabilities compound rather than add, for the same reason cumulative default probabilities do.

**Step 2. Compute the benchmark PSA rate for this seasoning.** The 100 PSA benchmark ramps linearly:

$$100 \text{ PSA CPR} = 6\% \times (\text{month} \div 30), \text{ for month} \leq 30, \text{ and } 6\% \text{ thereafter}$$

At month 20: $6\% \times (20 \div 30) = 4.00\%$

**Step 3. Express the observed speed relative to the month-20 benchmark.**

$$\text{PSA speed} = \text{observed CPR} \div \text{benchmark CPR} = 6.40\% \div 4.00\% = 1.60, \text{ that is, } 160 \text{ PSA}$$

| Quantity | Formula | Value |
|---|---|---|
| SMM | given | 0.55% per month |
| CPR | $1-(1-SMM)^{12}$ | 6.40% |
| 100 PSA benchmark at month 20 | $6\% \times (20/30)$ | 4.00% |
| PSA speed | CPR $\div$ benchmark | 160 PSA |

Option (a) pairs the compounded CPR of 6.40% with 160 PSA, the speed measured against the month-20 ramp value of 4%, which distinguishes it from (b) (linear CPR against the terminal 6%), (c) (SMM reported as CPR) and (d) (correct CPR against the terminal 6%, giving 107 PSA).

**The forecasting methods behind the convention.** Static approaches apply a single assumed speed. Econometric models regress prepayment on refinancing incentive, seasoning, seasonality and burnout. Option-theoretic models treat prepayment as the exercise of the borrower's embedded call and value it accordingly. All three feed a projected CPR path, which is then expressed as a PSA speed for comparability.

a.reason: $CPR = 1-(1-0.0055)^{12} = 6.40\%$, and $6.40\% \div 4.00\% = 1.60$, that is, 160 PSA against the month-20 ramp value. It is the only option applying both the compounding formula and the seasoning-adjusted benchmark.

b.reason: CPR of 6.60% is $0.55\% \times 12$, the linear annualisation error. Prepayment compounds through survival, so the multiplication overstates the rate.

c.reason: CPR of 0.55% is the monthly SMM reported as an annual figure, a unit error, and the PSA speed does not follow from it.

d.reason: The CPR is right but the PSA figure is computed against the fully seasoned 6% benchmark rather than the month-20 ramp value of 4%, which understates the seasoning adjustment that should be applied.

trap.explanation: Two named traps. The linear annualisation in option (b) is the same error as multiplying a hazard rate by the horizon rather than exponentiating, and it recurs across this syllabus. The seasoning error in option (d) is specific to PSA: the benchmark is a ramp, so the comparison at month 20 must be against the month-20 value, not against the terminal 6%.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Analyze the credit risks and other risks generated by retail banking; explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk; discuss the dark side of retail credit risk
questions.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
questions.question: A risk officer is contrasting the bank's retail and corporate credit portfolios for the board. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Retail portfolios are granular and statistically predictable, so idiosyncratic risk diversifies away and the residual is systematic; corporate portfolios are lumpy and require name-by-name analysis. The dark side of retail is that a new product's loss experience may look benign for years before deteriorating, so apparent stability can mask an unseasoned book.

Retail portfolios are lumpy and require name-by-name analysis, while corporate portfolios are granular and statistically predictable; the dark side of retail is that individual borrowers default unpredictably, which makes statistical modelling impossible.
Retail credit risk is fully diversifiable because of the number of borrowers, so a granular retail book requires no capital beyond provisions for expected loss.
The dark side of retail credit risk refers to the operational risk of processing high transaction volumes, and it is unrelated to the credit performance of the portfolio.

questions.solution:
Retail books are diversified into systematic risk and modelled statistically; the dark side is that unseasoned or novel products can hide deteriorating credit quality behind benign early loss experience.

**The structural contrast.**

| | Retail credit risk | Corporate credit risk |
|---|---|---|
| Number of exposures | Very large | Relatively few |
| Individual exposure size | Small | Large; a single name can matter |
| Analysis | Statistical, pooled, automated | Name by name, judgement led |
| Residual risk after diversification | Systematic: unemployment, house prices, rates | Idiosyncratic and systematic both material |
| Data availability | Abundant | Sparse for any single name |

**Why retail can be modelled statistically.** With hundreds of thousands of similar exposures, idiosyncratic risk diversifies away and the loss rate becomes predictable. That is what makes scorecards, cut-offs and pooled loss rates workable, and it is the opposite of the corporate case where a single name can dominate.

**The dark side, which is the examinable term.** The very predictability that makes retail attractive can conceal deterioration.

| Mechanism | Effect |
|---|---|
| No loss history for a new product | Early experience is mistaken for the steady state |
| Seasoning lag | Defaults arrive with a lag, so a rapidly growing book looks better than it is |
| Systematic risk | When it materialises it hits the whole book at once, not name by name |

The mechanism has three parts. A new product has no loss history, so early experience is mistaken for steady state. Seasoning means defaults arrive with a lag, so a rapidly growing book looks better than it is because the denominator is full of loans too young to have defaulted. And the risk is systematic, so when it materialises it materialises across the whole book at once rather than name by name.

**Why option (c) is dangerous.** Diversification removes idiosyncratic risk, not systematic risk. A retail book remains fully exposed to unemployment, house prices and interest rates, all of which affect every borrower simultaneously. Capital is required precisely for that residual.

a.reason: Retail is granular and statistical with a systematic residual; the dark side is that unseasoned or novel products can look benign before deteriorating.

b.reason: The two portfolio characterisations are transposed, and the claim that statistical modelling is impossible for retail is the reverse of the truth: large numbers are what make it possible.

c.reason: An absolute claim. Diversification removes idiosyncratic risk, not systematic risk. A retail book remains exposed to macroeconomic factors affecting all borrowers together, and capital is required for exactly that.

d.reason: Operational risk in high-volume processing is real but is not what the dark side of retail credit risk refers to. The term describes a credit phenomenon: the concealment of deteriorating quality behind favourable early loss data.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the trap with real-world consequences, and it is the reasoning that underwrote subprime expansion: many small loans feel individually trivial and collectively safe. The scope error is treating diversification as removing all risk rather than only the idiosyncratic component. Option (b) is a straight role misassignment obtained by exchanging the two portfolio types.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare and contrast foreign currency defaults and local currency defaults; explain the consequences of a country's default
questions.reading: Retail and Sovereign Credit Risk
questions.question: A sovereign analyst is explaining why a country's local currency rating typically exceeds its foreign currency rating, and what follows from a default. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: A sovereign can create the currency in which local currency debt is denominated, so local currency default is rarer and is usually a choice made to avoid the inflation that monetisation would cause; consequences of default include loss of market access, a banking crisis, a severe output contraction and frequent political turnover.

A sovereign can create foreign currency reserves through taxation, so foreign currency default is rarer than local currency default; consequences are limited to a temporary rise in borrowing costs, since sovereigns cannot be liquidated.
Local and foreign currency defaults are equally likely, since a sovereign's ability to pay depends only on its fiscal position, and rating agencies therefore assign a single rating covering both.
Local currency default has never occurred historically, which is why local currency debt is treated as risk free in capital calculations regardless of the sovereign's rating.

questions.solution:
Monetary sovereignty makes local currency default rarer but not impossible, since monetisation carries an inflation cost; sovereign default has severe and well documented economic and political consequences.

**Why the two differ.**

| | Local currency debt | Foreign currency debt |
|---|---|---|
| Can the sovereign create the currency | Yes | No |
| Binding constraint | Willingness, given the inflation cost of monetising | Ability, given reserves and export earnings |
| Relative default frequency | Lower | Higher |
| Typical rating | Higher | Lower |

A sovereign borrowing in its own currency can always create the money to pay. Default is therefore a choice rather than an incapacity, and it is chosen where the inflation, currency depreciation and credibility cost of monetising exceeds the cost of restructuring. That is why local currency defaults are rarer but, contrary to option (d), do occur, Russia in 1998 being the standard example.

Foreign currency debt can only be serviced from reserves or export earnings, neither of which the sovereign controls. Ability to pay therefore binds, which is why foreign currency ratings are lower and foreign currency defaults more frequent.

**The consequences of default.**

| Consequence | Description |
|---|---|
| Loss of market access | The sovereign is shut out of capital markets, at least temporarily |
| Banking crisis | Domestic banks holding the sovereign's debt suffer losses, often triggering a banking crisis |
| Severe output contraction | GDP contracts sharply around the default episode |
| Frequent political turnover | Default episodes are commonly accompanied by changes in government |

**The willingness against ability distinction.** This is what separates sovereign credit analysis from corporate. A sovereign cannot be liquidated and its assets cannot generally be seized, so recovery depends on negotiation. The relevant question is not only whether the sovereign can pay but whether it will, which is why political risk carries weight that has no corporate analogue.

a.reason: Monetary sovereignty makes local currency default rarer and a matter of choice, and default carries severe economic and political consequences.

b.reason: Reverses the mechanism. A sovereign cannot create foreign currency; taxation raises local currency. Foreign currency default is therefore more frequent, and the consequences are far more severe than a temporary rise in borrowing costs.

c.reason: The two are not equally likely, and agencies assign separate local and foreign currency ratings precisely because the constraints differ. The gap between the two is itself informative.

d.reason: Local currency defaults have occurred, Russia in 1998 being the best known. Treating local currency sovereign debt as risk free regardless of rating is an absolute claim and a documented weakness of some capital frameworks.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is a polarity flip on the mechanism, attaching monetary sovereignty to the wrong currency, and it compounds the error by minimising the consequences. Option (d) is the absolute claim that local currency debt is riskless, which is exactly the assumption that made the euro area sovereign crisis so damaging for bank balance sheets holding domestic government bonds.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative; explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term
questions.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
questions.question: A dealer is decomposing the all-in cost of an uncleared over-the-counter derivative. Which of the following correctly identifies the xVA components and what each prices?

options.text: CVA prices the counterparty's default risk; DVA prices the dealer's own default risk as a benefit; FVA prices the funding cost of the uncollateralised exposure; MVA prices the funding cost of posting initial margin; and KVA prices the cost of the regulatory capital the trade consumes over its life.

CVA prices the dealer's own default risk; DVA prices the counterparty's default risk; FVA prices the market risk of the position; MVA prices the cost of margin calls received; and KVA prices the counterparty's cost of capital.
The xVA components are alternative names for the same adjustment, and applying more than one to a single trade double counts the cost of counterparty risk.
xVA applies only to cleared derivatives, since uncleared trades are fully collateralised under the margin rules and therefore carry no valuation adjustment.

questions.solution:
Each xVA term prices a distinct economic cost of running a derivative position, and together they convert a risk-free valuation into an all-in price.

**The chain from risk-free value to all-in price.**

$$\text{All-in value} = \text{Risk-free value} - CVA + DVA - FVA - MVA - KVA$$

| Component | Prices | Sign to the dealer |
|---|---|---|
| CVA | The counterparty's default risk against positive exposure | Negative, a charge |
| DVA | The dealer's own default risk against negative exposure | Positive, a benefit |
| FVA | Funding cost of the uncollateralised exposure | Negative |
| MVA | Funding cost of posting initial margin, which cannot be reused | Negative |
| KVA | Cost of the regulatory capital the trade consumes over its life | Negative |

**Why the family grew.** The pre-crisis convention was to value derivatives off a single risk-free curve and to treat counterparty risk as a credit limit question. Each subsequent adjustment recognises a cost that was previously borne without being priced: default risk, then own-credit, then funding, then margin funding, then capital.

**The overlap debate worth knowing.** DVA and FVA are widely argued to overlap, since both derive from the dealer's own credit and funding position. Recognising both in full is regarded by many as double counting, which is why practice varies and why the two are frequently reported together.

**Why option (d) fails.** Uncleared trades are not fully collateralised. Thresholds, minimum transfer amounts and the margin period of risk leave a residual, and initial margin requirements create the very funding cost that MVA prices. Cleared trades have their own adjustments, but the family originated with bilateral uncleared exposure.

a.reason: Each component is matched to the cost it prices, with DVA the only positive term.

b.reason: CVA and DVA are transposed, FVA is misdescribed as market risk rather than funding cost, MVA is attached to margin received rather than initial margin posted, and KVA is attributed to the counterparty rather than the dealer. Every component is misassigned.

c.reason: The components price distinct costs and are additive, not alternatives. The only genuine double counting concern is the DVA and FVA overlap, which is a specific and acknowledged issue rather than a general property.

d.reason: Uncleared derivatives are the origin of the xVA framework. They are not fully collateralised: thresholds, minimum transfer amounts and the margin period of risk leave residual exposure, and initial margin requirements create the funding cost MVA exists to price.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is a comprehensive role misassignment, and it is worth working through because each individual clause is a plausible sentence in isolation. The organising question that resolves the whole family: whose default, whose funding, whose capital? CVA is theirs, DVA is yours, FVA and MVA are your funding, KVA is your capital.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard; describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing
questions.reading: Reading 96: Gregory, Central Clearing and Risk Intermediation
questions.question: A clearing member is assessing the balance a central counterparty strikes between initial margin and default fund contributions. Which of the following correctly compares them?

options.text: Initial margin is defaulter-pays and sized to each member's own portfolio risk, so it aligns cost with risk taking and limits moral hazard; default fund contributions are mutualised and consumed after the defaulter's own resources, which spreads loss but weakens the link between a member's risk and its cost, so a CCP relying more heavily on the default fund creates greater moral hazard.

Default fund contributions are defaulter-pays and sized to each member's own risk, while initial margin is mutualised across members; relying more heavily on initial margin therefore creates greater moral hazard.

Initial margin and default fund contributions are both mutualised, which is why central clearing eliminates counterparty risk for surviving members and why moral hazard is not a concern in a cleared market.
Moral hazard is absent from central clearing under any funding structure, because the CCP monitors member positions in real time and can close out a deteriorating member before losses arise.

questions.solution:
Initial margin is risk sensitive and defaulter-pays, aligning cost with risk; the default fund is mutualised and therefore weakens that alignment, which is the source of moral hazard in a cleared market.

**The comparison.**

| | Initial margin | Default fund contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Who bears the loss | The defaulting member | Mutualised across surviving members |
| Sizing | Risk sensitive, to the member's own portfolio | Largely activity based, less risk sensitive |
| Position in the waterfall | First | Fourth, after CCP capital |
| Effect on cost of clearing | Raises the funding cost directly | Lower direct cost |
| Effect on moral hazard | Limits it, cost tracks risk | Increases it, cost is shared |

**The moral hazard mechanism.** A member's initial margin rises with the risk of its own portfolio, so risk taking is costly to the taker. A default fund contribution is sized largely on activity and is consumed only after the defaulter's own resources, so a member bears only a fraction of the cost of its own risk and shares in the cost of others'. The more a CCP leans on the mutualised layer, the weaker the link between risk taking and cost, and the greater the incentive to take risk.

$$\text{Waterfall order: defaulter's IM} \rightarrow \text{defaulter's default fund} \rightarrow \text{CCP capital} \rightarrow \text{surviving members' default fund} \rightarrow \text{assessments}$$

**The cost of clearing trade-off.** Higher initial margin raises the funding cost of clearing, which discourages participation and pushes activity toward uncleared markets. Lower initial margin makes clearing cheap but shifts loss coverage onto the mutualised layer. CCPs must balance loss coverage, cost and incentive alignment simultaneously.

**Advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.** Multilateral netting, transparency, standardised margining and orderly default management against concentration of risk in a systemically important node, procyclical margin calls, and the loss mutualisation that creates the moral hazard described above.

a.reason: Initial margin is defaulter-pays and risk sensitive; the default fund is mutualised and weakens the risk-to-cost link, so heavier reliance on it increases moral hazard.

b.reason: The two are transposed on both dimensions. Initial margin is the defaulter-pays, risk-sensitive resource, and relying more heavily on it reduces rather than increases moral hazard.

c.reason: Initial margin is not mutualised, and central clearing does not eliminate counterparty risk; it converts bilateral exposure into exposure to the CCP and its waterfall. The claim that moral hazard is not a concern is an absolute claim contradicted by the mutualised layer.

d.reason: Real-time monitoring reduces but cannot eliminate moral hazard, and a CCP cannot generally close out a member before losses arise; the losses are already embedded in the portfolio when the default occurs.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the role misassignment between the two resources and it reverses the moral hazard conclusion as a consequence, which makes it internally consistent and therefore hard to reject on logic alone. The discriminator is whose money is at risk: margin is yours, the default fund is everyone's, and shared cost always weakens the incentive to control risk.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe counterparty risk and differentiate it from lending risk; compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods
questions.reading: Gregory, The xVA Challenge
questions.question: A chief risk officer is explaining to the board why counterparty credit risk is managed jointly by the credit and market risk functions rather than by either alone. Which of the following best captures its dual nature and the implications for the trading business?

options.text: It is a credit risk because the loss is triggered by counterparty default, and a market risk because the size of that loss depends on market-driven exposure; the practical implication is that CVA must be priced into trades and hedged with market instruments, so a dedicated CVA desk sits between the trading desks and the counterparty.
It is a credit risk only, since the loss requires a default event; market factors affect the timing of default but not the size of the loss, so the credit function should own it exclusively.
It is a market risk only, since exposure is marked to market daily; default is already captured in the credit spread used to discount the position, so no separate credit treatment is required.

It is treated as both, but the two treatments are alternatives rather than complements: an institution using CVA for pricing should not also hold regulatory capital against counterparty exposure, since this double counts the same risk.

questions.solution:
Counterparty credit risk requires a default event and a market-determined exposure, so it must be priced, hedged and capitalised using tools from both disciplines.

**The two components, and why both are necessary.**

$$\text{Loss on counterparty default} = \text{exposure at the time of default} \times \text{loss given default}$$

The credit element supplies the trigger: no default, no loss. The market element supplies the magnitude: the exposure at that moment is whatever market movements have made it, and could be zero or many multiples of today's value.

| Element | Discipline | What it determines | Tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| Counterparty defaults | Credit risk | Whether a loss occurs at all | Default probability, credit spreads, ratings |
| Exposure at the moment of default | Market risk | How large the loss is | Simulation of market factors, EE and PFE profiles |

**Why an ordinary loan is not like this.** A loan has a known outstanding balance, so only the credit element is uncertain. A derivative's exposure is itself a random variable, which is why counterparty credit risk cannot be managed with loan-book tools alone.

**Implications for the trading business.** Three follow directly.

**Pricing.** CVA is a valuation adjustment charged at trade inception, so counterparty risk enters the price rather than sitting as an unpriced exposure.

**Hedging.** Because CVA moves with both credit spreads and market factors, it can be hedged with single-name and index credit default swaps for the credit component and with market instruments for the exposure component. That is a trading activity, not a credit approval activity.

**Organisation.** A dedicated CVA desk internalises the charge from the trading desks and manages the resulting portfolio, which is why the function sits alongside trading rather than within credit approval.

**Capital.** Basel III requires both a default risk charge and a separate CVA capital charge for the mark-to-market volatility of CVA itself, which is the regulatory recognition that the risk has a market component.

a.reason: Credit provides the trigger and market provides the magnitude, with the practical consequences of pricing, hedging and a dedicated CVA function.

b.reason: Market factors determine the size of the exposure, not merely the timing of default. This is the defining difference between a derivative exposure and a loan, and denying it removes the reason exposure must be simulated at all.

c.reason: Marking to market measures the current value of the position, not the loss on default. A credit spread used in discounting reflects the issuer of an instrument, not a bilateral counterparty's default against a two-way exposure, and it says nothing about exposure at the future moment of default.

d.reason: Pricing and capital are complements, not alternatives. Basel III requires capital for default risk and a separate CVA capital charge, precisely because CVA itself is volatile. Charging CVA at inception does not remove the requirement to hold capital against subsequent moves.

trap.explanation: Options (b) and (c) are the two single-discipline reductions, and each is attractive to a specialist: a credit officer finds (b) natural and a market risk officer finds (c) natural. The item is answered by insisting on both the trigger and the magnitude. Option (d) is a scope error that treats pricing and capital as substitutes; the double counting claim sounds principled and is contradicted by the Basel III framework, which imposes both charges deliberately.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk
questions.reading: Reading 99: Gregory, Wrong-Way Risk
questions.question: A central counterparty provides clearing and settlement for over-the-counter derivative transactions. Following recent high-profile clearing member defaults, how should it re-evaluate its risk assessment strategy to address wrong-way risk?

options.text: Maintain the status quo, since CCPs by design inherently mitigate wrong-way risk through robust practices such as margin calls and clearing fund contributions.
